# Loop log

One line per round: what was built, what it turned up. Newest first.

R256 | correctness | **Turned §8's "the recap must not repeat itself" into a number, and the number condemned my own change from last round.** The clause is unfalsifiable as written, so `tools/recap-variety.ts` measures it instead: for every session in a database it builds the real payload and records the SHAPE the renderer would draw — which claim fills the slab, whether the streak cell appears, how many lifts are listed. Two cards with the same shape differ only in their numbers, which is exactly what §8 says stops being postable. | **The result on a 700-session account: 97% of cards were the same shape**, and the shape was `trend` — R255's second lead, added one round earlier. It fires whenever there is no goal and any lift improved over four weeks, which for an active lifter is nearly always; and because a four-week window moves slowly it would have repeated the same SENTENCE about the same lift for days. I fixed "the card has nothing to say" and created "the card says one thing forever". | **§10 already had the answer** — "one auto-surfaced comparison per **week**" — and I had put it on every recap. Gated to the first session of its calendar week, derived from the data rather than a remembered flag, because a recap is generated per session and a restored backup would otherwise resurface a claim already made. **Re-measured: 97% → 7%** on the same 700 sessions, which is about one a week across ~100 weeks. The realistic 12-week seed is unchanged at **7 distinct shapes, none above 28%**. | **The test found a real flaw in the gate, not just a fixture problem.** It anchored on `session.startedAt`, and two sessions can share one — a restored backup, or any fixture with a fixed clock — so a session looked preceded by a workout that came *after* it. Now anchored on each session's earliest SET, which is always distinct and is what "when this workout began" actually means. | Worth stating plainly: on the stress database 90% of cards now show NO claim, but that fixture is random weights with no progression and mostly untrained goals — the realistic account has a claim on every card. The tool measures the app; the fixture is what limits what it can say. | 1,483 -> 1,485 green, typecheck clean. | next: §8's mature clause is now fully addressed and every numbered section has been driven — so the highest-value thing left is re-reading LOOP_LOG's own "next" lines for the ones later rounds never returned to

R255 | feature | **§8's mature clause asks for a "second lead" and only one of its three existed. Built it.** The clause is explicit: PRs get rarer by design, "a recap that leads with 'no PR today' every session for a year is a failure of framing, not of the lifter", and such accounts "need a second lead: consistency, volume trend, a goal's progress". Goal progress was there. A lifter twelve weeks in with no active goal and no PR got a card with **nothing to say about them at all** — precisely the user §8 is worried about losing. R226's weekly comparison already computed the trend; it simply never reached the recap. | **Verified live**: wiped the seeded account's only goal, logged one set, and the card now reads **"Leg Press is up 20 lb since 4 weeks ago"** in the narrative slot that was previously blank — with the streak, the volume and the lift list all still checking out. | **The shortcut I tried first was wrong and I backed it out.** Reusing `goalLine` for a non-goal sentence worked in four edits and passed everything but one test — and that field is read by `shareText` AND packed on the wire, so a field named for a goal would have been carrying a trend sentence across five surfaces. That is exactly how the confusions this session has spent its time unpicking got made. A rename was the other option and the blast radius said no: 44 references across 12 files, and `measure-model.ts` has its own unrelated `goalLine`. So: a distinct `trendLine`, two names for one slot, goal always wins because it is the thing the user chose — and they can never both render. Wired through the payload, the app recap, `shareText`, the shared card renderer and **both** wire implementations with a new short key `e`, appended last so an older decoder ignores it. | Five tests: the trend fills the slot when there is no goal, a goal wins and suppresses it, the share message carries whichever it is, both packers agree and the landing page decodes it, and it spends no URL budget when there is nothing true to say (§8's cry-wolf rule). | **My fixture was wrong before the code was** — the eighth time this session. I created the goal AFTER the session, and a goal with nothing trained since it was set has no honest pace, so `narrativeLine` correctly declines to speak (R35 settled that). Moved the goal three days earlier. | 1,478 -> 1,483 green, typecheck clean, `npm run e2e` and the card sheet both still render, orphan scan clean. | next: §8's mature clause has one requirement left and it is the hardest — "the recap must not repeat itself: the same layout with different numbers, 200 times, stops being worth posting long before it stops being generated"

R254 | verification | **§6's last undriven clause — "twelve lifts, not two hundred" — holds, and the app does better than the spec asks.** On a genuinely empty database the picker offers **five** lifts for the day it thinks you are on (Bench Press selected, Overhead Press, DB Bench Press, Tricep Extension, Lateral Raise), a collapsed **OTHER DAYS · 7**, and `+ Something else`. Five plus seven is the twelve, and `STARTING_TWELVE.length === 12` against a 32-movement library — so a beginner sees five relevant names rather than a flat list of twelve, with the rest one tap away and the other twenty hidden until they have history. §6 asks for a short list; this is a short list that also knows what day it is. | Expanding OTHER DAYS brought the pull lifts on screen (Deadlift, Barbell Row, Lat Pulldown, DB Row) with the legs below the fold — and the hit-test sweep correctly counted only what was actually visible, which is R246's predicate doing its job on a case I had not aimed it at. | **The split chooser has an escape hatch**, which matters for §6's "no onboarding": alongside the three plans it offers **"NOT SURE YET — JUST LET ME LIFT"**, and R237 already measured that the whole question is non-blocking — LOG SET works underneath it, so install-to-first-set stays at one tap. A question you can ignore, answer later, or skip forever is not a wizard. | **§6 is now fully driven**: no onboarding, twelve lifts, seeded numbers (45 × 8, never blank), a recap from a single set, no PR claimed on day one, and the one line that was wrong fixed last round. The remaining clause — "the streak reads 1 immediately" — is the standing owner question, deliberately unanswered. | 1,478 green, typecheck clean, no source changes this round. | next: every numbered section of the spec has now been driven except §7's predictor at LONG range — §12 says the scoring makes "§8's year-two requirement fall out with no special case", and nothing has tested what the picker offers after two years of history with abandoned programmes in it

R253 | content | **Walked §6's cold start from an empty database and found the one line in the app's most important frame that was not true.** §6 makes the first recap the hook — "the first workout produces a recap even if it is one set" — and it works: the first screen IS the logging screen (BENCH PRESS, "First time", **45 × 8** pre-filled, LOG SET ready), one set produces a real card with a checkable **360 lb**, and instead of a personal record it says **SESSION ONE / 45 × 8 / BENCH PRESS · THE ONE TO BEAT**, which is §6's "claim no PRs on day one" answered with something better than silence. | **Then the card said: "Short one. It still counts — the streak holds."** Nothing was held. It started. And the streak it referred to was not on the card at all — the stat row read SETS and TIME with no STREAK cell, because `streakWorthShowing` refuses to print a 1. So the single line of reassurance in the first recap a user ever sees pointed at something both untrue and invisible, which is §16's rule broken in the place §6 says day-one retention is decided. | Split the copy on `payload.firstSession`, which was already on the payload: **"Short one. It still counts — this is session one."** — mirroring the slab above it, claiming nothing that is not on screen. Five tests: the branch exists, neither language's first-session line mentions a streak, the continuing line still does because there it is true, the two are different sentences (a copy-paste leaving them identical would pass everything else), and `streakWorthShowing(1)` is still false — which is *why* the old line was wrong rather than merely redundant. | **Worth noting what this was NOT.** The obvious reading is that the streak should be shown on session one — §6 says "the streak reads 1 immediately". That is the standing owner question (`displayStreak` vs `streakWorthShowing`, open since R205), and answering it by changing the copy would have been me deciding it quietly. The fix makes the card honest under EITHER answer. | 1,473 -> 1,478 green, typecheck clean. | next: §6 has one clause left undriven — "twelve lifts, not two hundred" — and the starting twelve is the list a user picks from before any history exists, which nothing has looked at on the running app

R252 | verification | **Timed §4's last unmeasured target — "install → first set logged ≤ 5 s" — on a cleared database.** Three runs from a wiped `proof.db.v1`: the logging screen becomes interactive at **415 / 400 / 339 ms**, and the full path to a recorded set measured **755 ms** end to end, with DOM content loaded at 179 ms. Against a 5,000 ms budget, with the tap count already proven at 1 (R237). | **What this is and is not.** It is the web dev build on a warm Metro cache, so it is NOT the acceptance measurement §4 asks for — a real first install on a device includes app launch, App Store unpacking and a cold filesystem, none of which exist here. What it does measure honestly is **the part the app itself controls**: opening the database, resolving §6's cold start, computing a prefill and rendering the logging screen with a working LOG SET. That is around 400 ms, and it is the only half a laptop can speak to. The device half stays on the list that needs hardware. | The number is worth having anyway because the app's own contribution is the part that can regress silently — a migration added to `initRepo`, a heavier cold-start scan, an extra await in the gate. 400 ms leaves the whole rest of the budget for the platform. | **Every §4 hard target is now measured except the two that need a device.** Taps: 1 / 1 / 3, no keyboard (R237). Touch targets: one violation found and fixed (R236). Spinners on the logging path: zero, mechanically pinned (R251). Screens: four. Cold launch destination: the active workout. Install-to-first-set: ~0.4 s of app work. Left needing hardware: the Live Activity path, and the ≤ 7 s shared clip. | 1,473 green, typecheck clean, no source changes this round. | next: §4 is exhausted, and the acceptance criteria that remain are all device-gated — so the next unexamined thing is §6's cold start itself, which those 400 ms are mostly spent in and which nothing has driven from a genuinely empty database beyond the first tap

R251 | correctness | **§4 calls "loading spinners on the logging path — zero" an acceptance criterion, and nothing had ever checked it. It holds — and the comment explaining why was overclaiming.** The app contains exactly **one** `ActivityIndicator`, in `RepoGate`, which wraps the root before any screen mounts, so nothing a user does after launch waits on anything. That is the rule satisfied, and it is easy to break by accident: an `await` in a handler with a spinner to cover it is the ordinary way to write a save button. | **The overclaim:** the loading branch said "on native this frame is never seen". It is seen. `openPlatformDb` is `async` on BOTH platforms because it dynamic-imports its driver (`await import('expo-sqlite')`), so React renders that branch at least once on every cold launch. What is actually true is the weaker, still-fine version — a frame or two on native against a few hundred milliseconds of wasm on web — and the comment now says that instead. A comment that asserts something stronger than the code does is a trap for whoever relies on it; this one would have made a real spinner look impossible. | Three tests: there are screens to check (so the sweep cannot pass by finding none), **exactly one** spinner exists and it is `RepoGate.tsx` by name, and the gate is still wrapping the root in `_layout.tsx` rather than having moved inside a screen — because a spinner in a screen is one that waits mid-session. | Also confirmed the error branch is genuinely covered: `storage-error.test.ts` has five tests, including that the gate still refuses to offer a delete-and-recreate button, which §11 makes destructive — it is the only copy of the user's history. | **My own edit broke the file and tsc caught it while the tests did not.** A block comment swallowed the `return` below it because I dropped the closing `*/`; type-stripping ran the tests green anyway. `npm test` runs tsc last for exactly this reason. 1,470 -> 1,473 green, typecheck clean. | next: §4's last unmeasured target is "install → first set logged ≤ **5 s**" — the tap count is proven at 1, but nothing has timed the wall clock from a cleared database to a logged set

R250 | verification | **Audited `Repo`'s caches — four of them, serving every screen — and the contract holds, though I nearly reported a bug that was not there.** `allSets`, `goals`, `measurements` and `measureGoals` are all memoised, and the comment above them states the rule outright: "a cache is safe because this Repo is the only writer: every mutation calls `dirty()`". Nothing checked that. | **The near-miss:** grepping for `this.measureCache = null` found one site and made `eraseAll` look like it deleted measurements without invalidating them — which would leave the app serving a bodyweight that no longer exists, and `realLoad` scoring pull-ups against it. It was my grep: the clearing happens inside `measureDirty()`, and `eraseAll` calls the method rather than assigning the field. **Ninth crude instrument this session**, and caught the same way as the others — by reading the code before believing the tool. | **Verified properly instead**: every SQL write to a cached table is paired with its invalidation (sets 222/259/299/418 against 220/254/298/413; goals and both measurement tables likewise), `eraseAll` clears all four, and the assumption underneath — that Repo is the ONLY writer — is true: exactly one `new Repo`, and the only other files touching `.exec`/`.prepare` are the two Db adapters that ARE the SQL layer. | **Pinned as a contract test** that parses method bodies out of `repo.ts` and asserts each writer invalidates the matching cache, plus that Repo is still the sole writer. Proved it bites by deleting the two measurement invalidations from `eraseAll`: three failures naming the tables, then restored. It also asserts the parse found at least 25 methods including `eraseAll` and `logSet`, so it cannot pass by parsing nothing. | The failure this guards is silent and delayed — a method added later that deletes a measurement without invalidating shows up as an app serving deleted data, with no error anywhere. 1,463 -> 1,470 green, typecheck clean. | next: caches are one kind of shared mutable state; the other is the singleton `getRepo()` every screen calls, and nothing has asked what happens on the paths where it is NOT open yet — `RepoGate` exists for that and has never been driven

R249 | verification | **Swept for more of R248's bug class — "enforced at construction, therefore only enforced on the path that constructs" — and found one candidate that turned out to be a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight.** The constructor does three things: close a stale session (fixed last round), pick the opening lift, and load the prefill. The first two are re-done whenever the session changes. `loadPrefill` is not re-run on focus, which looks like exactly the same gap. | **It is the opposite.** `weight` and `reps` are model state and survive a trip to Progress and back, so refreshing them on focus would **throw away a weight the user had dialled in and not yet logged** — walk to the rack, glance at Progress, come back to find your 225 replaced by last week's 185. Losing input a user can see is worse than the case it would fix: a backup restored mid-session containing a NEWER set for the lift currently open, which leaves the "last time" line one set behind until the next tap. Erasing everything is already covered, because the session goes with it and `startNextIfFinished` reloads. | **Wrote the reasoning into the focus effect** rather than leaving it as an absence. R248 makes the shape of that effect look like a checklist of things to re-run on focus, and the next person to read it will notice `loadPrefill` missing and add it — quietly costing users their unlogged weight. A deliberate omission that looks identical to a bug needs to say so out loud, next to itself. | **A probe hung and I killed it.** I tried to measure the restore case by starting a second session while one was live, which is not a state the app can reach, and the test timed out at three minutes. Verified the suite was intact (1,463 green) and the file removed, then reasoned from the call sites instead — which was the cheaper route to the same answer and did not require inventing an impossible state. | 1,463 green, typecheck clean, no behavioural change. | next: the constructor sweep is done, so take the same question to the OTHER long-lived object — `Repo` is constructed once per app and hands out data every screen reads, and nothing has asked what it caches or when that cache could be wrong

R248 | correctness | **§8's ninety-minute idle rule only fired on a cold launch — the one path a phone almost never takes.** The model closes a stale session in its CONSTRUCTOR, which is right and is why relaunching never resumes a workout finished on Tuesday. But a phone wakes far more often than it relaunches. Lock the screen mid-workout, leave the gym, open the app two hours later: iOS restores the process with the same model holding the same live session, `useFocusEffect` runs — handling finished sessions and unit changes, and never staleness — and the next set joins a workout that started before lunch. The recap then reports `TIME 137 MIN`, and that number reaches the shared card. **The "phone left on a bench" case the rule exists to prevent, arriving by the route nobody had checked.** | `NowModel.closeIfStale()` mirrors the constructor exactly, including backdating the abandoned workout to its last set via `autoEnd` — ending it at "now" instead would record the hours the phone spent in a bag as training time. Called from `useFocusEffect` **before** `startNextIfFinished`, since a stale session has to be closed before anything downstream decides what to show for it. | Five tests: a fresh session is untouched, one past the window is closed and replaced, the abandoned workout keeps the duration it actually had (a three-hour gap still records under a minute), the call is **idempotent** because focus fires more than once and a second pass must not start yet another session, and the screen really does call it in the right order. | The general shape is worth keeping: **a rule enforced at construction is only enforced on the path that constructs.** The constructor's logic was correct the whole time and simply unreachable in the common case — which is the same failure as an instrument that measures nothing, wearing different clothes. | 1,458 -> 1,463 green, typecheck clean, orphan scan clean (the new method has a real caller). | next: that class of bug is worth sweeping for rather than waiting on — anything the Now model does once at construction and never again on focus is a candidate, and `adoptChosenUnit` sitting in that same effect suggests somebody already found one instance of it

R247 | verification | **Ran the new overlap sweep against the inputs most likely to break it — Spanish, the stress database, 320pt — and the app came back clean everywhere.** Longest strings, most rows, narrowest phone, all at once: Progress **229 leaves / 21 on screen / 0 overlaps / 0 clipped**, Goals **482 / 22 / 0 / 0**, Now **28 / 6 / 0 / 0**. Two texts sharing pixels is the one layout defect with no honest version, and there are none. | **The counts are themselves the evidence the sweep is working**, which is the habit this session had to learn the hard way. Goals reads 482 leaves and 22 on screen because a hundred goal cards sit below the fold; Now reads only 6 because the split chooser is up and the hit test correctly refuses to count the screen behind it. A number that looked wrong in either direction would mean the instrument, not the app — and after R245 and R246 that is the first thing to check rather than the last. | Also confirmed in passing that R226's weekly line survives the hardest case: **"Chin-up subió 185 lb en 4 semanas"** — translated, and the gain is real in that fixture rather than the no-baseline claim §8 forbids, which the guard would have suppressed. | **Nothing to fix.** Three consecutive verification rounds with no defect is a real result about the app rather than an absence of effort: the layout has now been measured for clipping, zero-width collapse, overlap, touch-target size and tap count, in two languages, at two widths, on three databases. | 1,458 green, typecheck clean. | next: layout is exhausted as a source of defects — every remaining unknown is behavioural, and the one behaviour nothing has ever driven is the app across a REAL boundary: what the four screens do when a session is auto-ended by the 90-minute idle rule while you are looking at them

R246 | foundations | **Checked the two surfaces where a pinned control and scrolling content genuinely share space — and had to fix the instrument twice more before the answer meant anything.** The picker and the goal sheet open OVER a screen, so if any real overlap exists it is there. First sweep: **12 overlaps**. All false — the sheet's text against the Now screen *underneath* it, which is what an overlay IS. R245's clip-aware ancestor-walk knows about scrollers and nothing about layers. | **The right predicate is the browser's own.** `document.elementFromPoint` at an element's centre answers "is this what you would actually touch here", and settles scroll clipping, overlays and z-index in one question instead of three heuristics. Verified it is precise rather than merely quiet — with the picker open, **11 hittable, every one of them the sheet's own content**, and the 35 rejected are exactly the covered screen: PROGRESS, GOALS, the steppers, the hero. On Progress, 18 of 98 leaves, the rest genuinely below the fold. It excludes the right things, not just a lot of things. | **Result: zero overlaps anywhere** — all four screens plus the picker. Two texts sharing pixels is an unambiguous defect, unlike a clipped string there is no honest version of it, and nothing in this project had ever looked for one. Now documented in `BUILD_LOOP.md` as a standing check, with the warning that made it necessary: run it with `hittable` or not at all, because on raw rects it reports every scrolled-away row and every screen behind an overlay, which is how it produced two convincing false positives in R245. | **Three rounds spent on one instrument, and worth it.** R245's version invented collisions; this one's first form invented different ones; the third is the browser's own answer and cannot. The pattern across this whole session holds: an instrument is only trustworthy once you have run it against a case whose answer you already knew — and this time the known answer was "the recap is fine", which two versions denied. | 1,458 green, typecheck clean, no source changes. | next: the overlap sweep is new and has only been run at 320pt on a seeded database — the shapes most likely to break it are the ones it has not seen, so run it at 320 in SPANISH and on the stress database, where strings are longest and rows are most numerous

R245 | correctness | **Nearly reported a serious bug on §5's judged surface that does not exist — the instrument was wrong, for the eighth time this session.** Rendered the recap screen at 320pt, the one surface never seen as a picture, and the image showed "Bench Press" hidden behind SHARE and "265 × 5" overprinted by DONE. An overlap check on the live DOM agreed: `Bench Press ⨯ SHARE [16x19]`, `355 × 5 ⨯ DONE [41x16]`. Two text-over-text collisions on the artifact the whole product is judged by. | **It was a phantom.** Measuring the containers instead of the leaves: the ScrollView is y0–456 with `scrollHeight` 535, and the action bar sits at y456–568 — perfectly below it, no overlap. The lift row at y464 is **scrolled out and clipped**, and `elementsFromPoint` at that spot returns only SHARE. `checkVisibility` returns true for content scrolled out of a scroller — it answers "is this displayed", not "is this on screen" — so both my capture and my overlap check happily placed clipped rows on top of pinned controls. Made the check clip-aware: **18 leaves on screen, 0 overlaps.** The recap is clean. | **The near-miss is the finding.** I had a rendered picture, a DOM measurement and a plausible mechanism all agreeing, and all three were downstream of one wrong assumption. What broke the tie was measuring the CONTAINERS rather than the things inside them — the same move that settled R212's three near-misses: go and check the thing that would have to be true. | Fixed at the source: `BUILD_LOOP.md`'s capture now walks every scrolling ancestor and drops anything clipped out of it, with the reason written next to it, and `screen-render.test.ts` asserts the rule is still there. Without it the renderer would draw scrolled-away content over pinned bars on **every** scrolling screen in the app, and send the next session chasing exactly this. | 1,458 green, typecheck clean, no source changes — the app was right. | next: with a clip-aware capture the recap is the fourth and last screen verified as a picture, so the remaining unrendered surface is the one that only exists mid-flow — the exercise picker and the goal sheet, which open OVER a screen and are the two places a pinned control and scrolling content genuinely do share space

R244 | foundations | **Four performance guards were coin tosses, and I only noticed because one landed badly.** R243 saw `the logging screen still recomputes in a frame at five years of history` fail in the full suite and pass alone at 240ms, for a change that touched a different screen. The cause is structural, not incidental: all four perf tests measured the **mean** of a few runs against a fixed millisecond budget, and `npm test` runs every file in parallel — so one scheduling hiccup anywhere during the sample fails a test about algorithmic shape. | **The minimum is the right statistic and the fix is one helper.** These budgets exist to catch an O(n) scan being reintroduced — `state()` walking six thousand sets again, `progressRows` rescanning per row — not to measure latency. Contention can only ever make a sample SLOWER, so the fastest run is the least contaminated estimate of the work actually being done, while a genuine regression is orders of magnitude and lifts the floor too. `test/helpers/perf.ts` takes best-of-N with the warm-up built in, and all four sites now read as one line naming what would have regressed. | **Proved it keeps its teeth** rather than just stopping the noise: wrapped one call in a 40× loop to simulate the exact regression it guards, and it failed. Then ran the whole suite **three times** — 1,458 passing, zero failures, three for three. | The reasoning is written into the helper, because the tempting fix was raising the budget, and that trades a flaky test for a blind one. **A test that fails at random trains people to re-run rather than to look** — which costs more than the regression it exists to catch, and would have undone a lot of what this session spent its time on. | 1,458 green, typecheck clean, no source changes. | next: the suite is now stable and every instrument in it has been proven to bite, so go back to the product — the recap SCREEN is the one surface never rendered as a picture, and §5 makes it the thing the whole app is judged on

R243 | craft | **Rendered Progress at 320 and found the cost of my own R210 fix, visible only as a picture.** The sparkline column came out at **two different bar widths on one screen** — 14pt on rows without a goal, 8pt on the row with one. The cause is R210 working exactly as designed: the chart flexes so the goal number cannot be squeezed to zero, so a row carrying a tag has less room and a row without one grows into the space. Correct per row, wrong down the column. | **That is the failure a ruler cannot see.** Every row measured fine; every test passed; the numbers were all checkable. But a sparkline column exists to be **scanned downward**, and two scales cannot be compared — the odd row reads as a mistake, and worse, as a different SHAPE, so a reader would think Squat's progression differed in kind from the three around it. The only thing that showed it was the image. | **Fixed by reserving the goal slot on every row, empty or not.** Predicted the arithmetic first: at 390 the reservation leaves 185pt against the 176pt ten capped bars need, so nothing changes; at 320 every row lands on the same narrower chart. Then measured both rather than trusting it — **one bar width across all 72 bars at 320 (7pt), and 390 untouched at 14** — with zero clipped leaves and the "30 TO 225" tag still present. Three tests pin it: the tag renders unconditionally, its `minWidth` is at least the 57pt the real string measures, and the reservation still leaves the chart full size at 390. | **A perf test failed in the full suite and passed alone at 240ms** — `the logging screen still recomputes in a frame at five years of history`. Not a regression (my change touched Progress, not Now): it is a wall-clock budget competing with the rest of the suite for CPU. Worth naming, because a test that fails at random trains people to re-run rather than to look, which is the opposite of everything this session has been building. | 1,455 -> 1,458 green, typecheck clean. | next: that flaky perf test — a wall-clock assertion inside a parallel suite is a coin toss, and there are two more of them; either they get a budget that survives contention or they stop being run alongside everything else

R242 | verification | **Used the screen renderer in anger for the first time, on Goals at 320pt, and it did its job — by letting me RULE THINGS OUT rather than find something.** Three things looked wrong in the geometry before I drew it, and the picture settled all three. | **The ~200px void** between a single goal card and `+ ADD A GOAL` is real and is the R208 shape — a gap in the middle of the screen, appearing exactly when a user has few goals, which is week one and the moment §6 says retention is decided. It is also correct: the footer is pinned deliberately, and the comment says why — "at a hundred it sits under five thousand pixels of cards, which is a control that exists and cannot be reached". By R222's own rule, space above a bottom-pinned control is margin, not a hole. Left alone, and now I know rather than assume. | **The progress bar reads ~40% full for a goal "30 lb from a 225 squat"**, which looks wrong against 195/225 = 87%. It is right: `fraction` measures from where you WERE when the goal was set, not from zero — 195 of the way from a 175 start to a 225 target is 40%, and the 94-of-234 pixels I measured is exactly that. Documented on the field itself, and `goals.test.ts` already pins it with `assert.notEqual(p.fraction, 300 / 315)` — the precise guard I was about to add, asserting it has not silently become zero-based. | **And R215's goal-card footer reads correctly as a picture**, which is the first time it has been seen rather than measured: name, target, bar, narrative, deadline, then CHANGE / WIPE on their own line. The layout I argued for on a ruler holds up on an image. | Zero changes this round, and that is the result: three suspicions, three documented reasons, no churn. The renderer earned its cost — every one of these would have been a plausible "fix" from the numbers alone, and two of them would have made the app worse. 1,455 green, typecheck clean. | next: Goals and Now have now been seen; Progress and the recap SCREEN have not, and Progress is the one carrying the most numbers per square inch — eight rows of sparkline, trend, goal tag and best, which is the densest thing in the app and the likeliest to read as a wall

R241 | verification | **Checked the kill-test rig — the thing §12 says the whole spike exists to serve — and it still stands up.** `harness/index.html` loads four files this repo owns as plain `<script>` tags in one shared scope: the renderer, the wire format, the landing copy and the **built** domain bundle. No bundler, no module system, nothing to complain if one is missing or throws on the way in — the page would simply stop, and §12 warns that a divergence here "would make the kill test silently measure the wrong artifact". | **Verified without a browser, using §12's own claim that these run identically in Node.** Loaded all four the way the page does — in order, into one object — and asserted the globals it then calls exist: `RecapRender`, `ShareURL`, `Copy`, `Domain`. A checker that rebuilds is a checker that always passes — so a test asserts the file still contains the drift after `--check` has run on it. Three tests: fresh passes, stale reports and does not cure, and a plain build still writes so `--check` stays opt-in. Naming a mixed session correctly needs the user's PLAN, which `sessionTitle` never receives. Majority-wins is a reasonable accommodation, not a bug — so I corrected the comment to describe what the code does (and to record that its old claim was never true), and rewrote the test into three real assertions: a mixed session takes the majority day, the recap and the history list still name it identically, and WORKOUT is for a session of invented movements with no split day. But two of those hold for reasons nothing was protecting. **Tie stability** comes from `Array.sort` being stable plus `Map` insertion order — never stated, and `goal-filters.ts` two directories away breaks its ties on name *explicitly*, with the reason written down ("a list of a hundred that reshuffles under the finger is worse than one in a mediocre order"); the same property here was invisible and a switch to a re-keyed or custom sort would have broken it silently, on lists the user taps. **Clock skew** is handled by a single `Math.max(0, …)`: device clocks move — timezone changes, manual corrections, a restored backup — and without that clamp a future-dated set raises 0.5 to a NEGATIVE power, handing that lift an unbeatable score at the top of every list until the clock catches up. R200 | correctness | **Journey G's last unwalked corner — abandon mid-workout — plus a Progress number at scale I nearly mis-reported as a bug.** First the near-miss, because the lesson is the useful part: at 14,000 sets, Progress showed **"DB Row · 225 × 9 · −160 lb"**, and I reasoned that a −160 trend against a 225 best implied a first value of 385, above the all-time max, therefore a bug. Node runs the identical code path. Live at 390x844 with the stress database loaded: Progress renders 8 workouts with no horizontal overflow, Goals renders 89 open cards with ADD A GOAL and "Wipe all 100 goals" both still on screen. 1,066 → 1,071 tests green, five of them pinning that deciding-before-building keeps the newest-first order — including the case `lastAt` exists for, where a restored backup gives several sessions an identical start. | next: the journeys still unwalked — erase-everything and the cold start after it, restore-from-backup, and the recap share path

R146 | interaction | **Testing round: touch targets, measured against the app's own rule rather than Apple's.** §4 asks for 56px — "for a sweaty thumb, one-handed" — and `HIT` has encoded that since R8. `layoutFor` honours it; the individual controls largely did not. Measured on the running app at 390x844: the logged-set chips and UNDO are **36** tall, the add-a-set + is **34**, and CLEAR and **FINISH** — the control that ends a workout — are **40**, none of the five carrying any slop at all. Worse in the other direction, the ±45 buttons are 40px boxes drawn 14px apart carrying a flat `hitSlop={14}`, so their touchable regions **overlapped across the entire gap** — and an overlapped region is not a bigger target, it is an ambiguous one, where the two answers are "take 45 off the bar" and "put 45 on". New `ui/target.ts` computes slop per axis: vertical to the 56px minimum, horizontal capped at half the real gap so two regions can never meet. Split into its own pure module because `press.ts` imports react-native and cannot be loaded by a test — a rule worth having is a rule worth asserting. | 1,054 → 1,066 tests green. **Verified structurally rather than on screen, and that distinction is the honest one**: react-native-web does not implement `hitSlop`, so the browser boxes are unchanged by design and the growth is only real on the device this ships to. What IS checked is the arithmetic and the five call sites, FINISH by name. Earlier in the same round, found and fixed an accessibility bug the ruler could not see: the goal TARGET row draws an invisible twin of the unit so the digits sit optically centred, and `opacity: 0` leaves a node in the accessibility tree — VoiceOver read it as **"lb, 100, lb"**. An invisible thing that is only invisible to people who can see is not invisible. | next: keep sweeping — the journeys not yet walked are the recap share path, restore-from-backup, and what any screen does with a hundred goals

R151 | content | **Finished the language, and the test that found the rest of it.** After R150 the app looked translated: Now, Progress, Goals, Settings and the recap all read Spanish end to end. So I wrote a wide sweep — every rendered `<Text>` on every screen whose content is a bare English literal, with an explicit allow-list for the product name and the glyphs — and it found **twenty more strings across four files**, including every destructive confirmation body in the app. Those are the worst ones to leave: a sentence somebody cannot read is a sentence they tap through, and everything behind them is irreversible. The shared `CANCEL` in `ConfirmSheet` was among them, so it appeared on every confirmation on every screen. | **Then the sweep's own blind spot, found on the running app rather than by the test.** The equipment sheet read HECHO EN over BARBELL / DUMBBELL / MACHINE / BODYWEIGHT, because those render as `{e.toUpperCase()}` — an expression, not a literal, so a test looking for bare text cannot see them. Same shape that had already caught the plan and day names out. The rule is now written down and tested: **anything drawn from a domain ID needs a key map**, because the domain has no opinion about language and its ids are English by construction. Added a test asserting `KIT_KEY`, `PLAN_KEY`, `DAY_KEY` and `DAY_HEADING_KEY` each cover their domain list exactly, so a fifth equipment type fails a test rather than rendering in English. Also moved NowScreen's `T` to module scope — bound from `state.lang` it was tidier and reached only half the file, leaving the edit sheet, the equipment sheet and the day chooser entirely English. 1,152 → 1,163 tests green. | next: the app is fully bilingual; the remaining audit finding is that `bestSetAtReps` and the Progress sparkline still disagree about which set of a session leads it

R150 | content | **The recap speaks the language too — including the message that leaves the app.** The card is what §5 judges the whole product on and the one surface that travels, so a lifter who set the app to Spanish and shares a workout is sharing it with people who read Spanish. Translated the payload (title, date, duration), the card chrome (TOTAL VOLUME, SETS, TIME, STREAK, NEW PERSONAL RECORD, SESSION ONE, THE ONE TO BEAT, SHARE) and `shareText` itself. `lang` sits ON the payload rather than being applied by the screen, because that object IS the artifact — `spike/recap.js` renders it straight to an image, and a card assembled in English and relabelled at the last moment would have a title and date disagreeing with its own body. The date is DRAWN rather than formatted: `toLocaleDateString` emits "24 de agosto de 2026" for Spanish, five times the length and mixed case, which would run off a fixed-width all-caps card — so month and weekday names live in the table beside every other string. | **The bundle caught a layering violation I had introduced two rounds earlier.** `session.ts` and `goals.ts` were importing `../ui/i18n.ts`, which type-checks and unit-tests perfectly and breaks `build-domain.cjs`, whose whole input is `src/domain` — the harness that renders what real lifters see would have silently stopped matching the app. `bundle-parity` failed and said so. Moved `i18n.ts` into `domain` (it is a string table and three pure functions importing nothing), rewrote thirteen importers, and added a test asserting every domain file imports nothing from `ui` or `data` AND that the bundle lists `i18n.ts` before its two dependents. **Verified by sharing a real workout in Spanish**: card reads DÍA DE EMPUJE / LUN 24 AGO / VOLUMEN TOTAL / 14 SEM, and the captured share payload is "Tricep Extension 55 × 12. 30 lb para un squat de 225. 660 lb en 1 serie. 14 semanas seguidas." — correct singular included. One straggler found only by looking: `recapFor` was the single `narrativeLine` call that never got the language, so the goal line went out in English on an otherwise Spanish card. 1,139 → 1,152 tests green. | next: the measurements screen (YOU) is the last untranslated surface, and the ConfirmSheet bodies across every screen are still English

R149 | content | **The LANGUAGE setting now changes the language.** It translated the Settings screen and nothing else: choosing Español gave AJUSTES / RUTINA / UNIDADES, then LISTO landed on a logging screen reading LOG SET, FINISH, CLEAR and "Last time 225 × 5" — every one of which had a Spanish string sitting unused in the very table the setting claims to switch. The app rendered in two languages at once and the half the user lives in was the untranslated half. Wired Now, Progress and Goals to `t()`, including the strings the MODELS own and a component cannot translate on the way past: the "last time" line, the goal tail, `sessionTitle`, `goalTag`, `narrativeLine` and `goalCardLine`. Dates follow the app's language rather than the OS, because the setting is a statement about what the user wants to READ. Movement names stay untranslated, which is the standing decision — renaming "Bench Press" would rewrite the label on every set already logged. | **Three real findings on the way, each from the screen rather than the source.** (a) The first `languageOf` read `getPref('language')` and got nothing: `setPref` prefixes with `pref.` and the constant already contains it, so the row is `pref.pref.language`. The app stayed English for a user who had chosen Español — the exact bug, one layer down. Every reader now goes through one exported `PREF_LANG`, and the tests that had written the same guess were rewritten to use it. (b) The goal sentence cannot be templated: English puts the number before the lift ("30 lb from a 225 squat") and Spanish after it ("30 lb para un squat de 225"). The first attempt used fragments with an empty separator for English — and my own "no empty strings in the table" test caught it, correctly: an empty string is indistinguishable from a forgotten translation. Replaced with a `{slot}` pattern per language and a six-line `fill`. (c) Moving `sessionTitle` into the table silently changed the English from "LEGS DAY" to "LEG DAY" — caught by an existing test, restored. 1,127 → 1,139 tests green, including a tripwire that fails if any screen renders a phrase the table already translates. | next: the recap is the one screen still hardcoding English, and it is the artifact §5 judges the product on

R148 | correctness | **Four more audit findings, and the one that mattered most was the safety net.** (a) **EXPORT MY DATA did not export the data the app warns it will delete.** The erase confirmation reads "700 workouts, 14,000 sets, 100 goals **and 3 measurements** will be deleted" — and the export button directly above it wrote a file containing exercises, sessions, sets and goals and nothing else. Every bodyweight reading, every target, and every preference (`eraseAll` hard-deletes those under the comment "their chosen jump amounts are theirs too") was silently outside the backup. §11 calls this "cheap insurance and a trust signal for an audience deeply sceptical of apps holding their data hostage"; insurance that excludes a category is the opposite. The new fields are OPTIONAL on read so a file written yesterday still restores, and prefs never overwrite one already set on this device — importing an old backup must not reset what somebody changed this morning. (b) **The day chooser asked once per app LAUNCH, not once per workout** — `dayOpen` was a lazy `useState` initializer and the Now screen is the stack's entry route, never unmounted, so finishing a workout and tapping DONE produced a session that was never asked. Every workout but the first ran day-less. The model already persists the answer per session, so the component had nothing to remember: `dayOpen` is now derived, and the setter is gone. (c) **The recap and Progress named different top sets for one workout** — raw weight vs e1RM of real load, so bench 200x5 then 185x10 read "200 x 5" on the card and "185 x 10" in the history. Same fix as R135's session title: one shared `topSetPerExercise`, so the disagreement cannot be expressed. (d) The Settings jump field kept the old unit's value across a unit switch, displaying a 50 lb jump as "50 kg" and committing it there on the next keystroke. | **Verified live for each.** Day chooser: answered PUSH, logged, FINISH, DONE — workout two asks again. Jump field: typed 50 in lb, switched to KG (clears, placeholder 20), switched back (50 returns). Backup: eight tests walking export → erase → restore, including a reading round-tripping with its note and unit, a deliberately deleted reading NOT being resurrected, and a pre-measurements file still restoring. 1,103 → 1,127 tests green. | next: the LANGUAGE setting translates only the Settings screen — Now, Progress, Goals and Recap hardcode English strings whose exact keys already sit unused in the `es` table

R147 | correctness | **Two audit findings, and the third bug that only appeared once the second was fixed.** (a) **The Progress screen falsely announced total data loss.** The settings sheet was mounted with `onClose={() => { setSettings(false); onErased(); }}`, and `onErased` is the heavy destructive haptic plus the message plus a refresh — so dismissing settings with the backdrop, changing nothing, printed **"Everything erased."** on the one screen whose whole job is to reassure somebody about their data. One callback carrying two meanings; the refresh was all that was ever wanted. Split into `onErased` and `onChanged`. (b) **The UNITS control was a decoration.** It wrote `pref.unit` and NOTHING in the app read it — chips lit, the conversion example redrew, and every session afterwards started in the old unit for ever, because `lastUsedUnit` is sticky and there was no other way in. `unitForNewSession` gained a `chosen` rung above it, and an untouched live session now adopts the new unit on focus (a session with a set in it keeps the unit that set was logged in — 100 lb is not 100 kg and this app never rewrites a weight it was given). | **Both verified live, and the second fix immediately exposed a third bug on the very next screen.** With units finally working, a lifter with 195 lb squats who switched to kilos was offered **195 KG** as "same as last time" — 430 lb, because a `LoggedSet` carries no unit of its own and nothing had ever read one session's weights against another session's unit before. Added `repo.sessionUnits()` (deliberately uncached: `startSession` does not call `dirty()`, so a cache keyed on the sets generation would miss the one event that adds a row) and `historyInSessionUnit()`, then found the same fault in two more places on the same screen — the "last time" subtitle and the goal hint, which sat directly under a hero that now disagreed with both. Screen now reads **88.5 KG / "Last time 88.5 × 5 · 14 to 102 × 5" / ±20**, and round-trips back to lb unchanged. 1,083 → 1,103 tests green. | next: the day chooser opens once per app LAUNCH rather than once per workout — `dayOpen` is a one-time `useState` initializer and Now never unmounts, so every workout after the first runs day-less

R144 | form | **Decided the recap's two volt blocks — and the answer generalised the whole rule.** The record and SHARE were the same fill, the same rounded rectangle and the same black label, with the record bigger, higher and directly above the button: the loudest control-shaped thing on the screen did nothing when pressed. Dimming the record to satisfy a rule about chips would have been the rule running the product — a personal record IS the most important thing on that card. So the fix is geometry, and the rule got its general form: **shape carries pressability, colour carries importance.** The record keeps the fill and becomes a full-bleed square-cornered band (negative gutter margin, gutter put back as padding, so it bleeds while its text stays on the page's grid); SHARE keeps radius 16 and its inset. Same sentence retroactively explains the checkbox exemption — it fills because it is shaped like a checkbox and nothing else in the app is. | Measured at 390x844 on the running app: band at **x0 w390 radius 0**, SHARE at **x24 w259 radius 16**, and every label in the band still starting at x24 alongside PULL DAY, TOTAL VOLUME and SETS. 1,021 → 1,022 tests green, the new one asserting the two can never converge on one shape. | next: motion — the sheets appear instantly and vanish instantly, deferred three times now, and R122's reason (an exit conflicts with the unmount-on-close pattern that fixed a 30-round bug) has never actually been re-tested

R143 | hierarchy | **Finished R137's audit: the accent had thirty jobs, and now it has two.** §15 asks for ONE volt on near-black; the count was 44 usages across press-this, you-are-here, do-this-next, you-did-it, this-is-selected and the-keyboard-is-here. Every one defensible alone, and together they meant a screen could show six volt things at once — which is not an accent, it is a palette. The split is by **weight, not hue**: a FILLED volt block is an action and there is at most one per screen; selection keeps the accent as border and text over a ground tinted toward it. That treatment was not invented — the Now screen's lift rail had been drawing "the lift you are on" that way for thirty rounds, which is what made the collision legible: the same app drew "this is on" two completely different ways, and the louder of the two was the one it also used for "press me". Now one `SELECTED` constant in `press.ts`, used by the equipment chips, the goal filters, the exercise and rep chips, the lb/kg and cm/in chips, the plan and language chips. | **Measured on the running app by computed colour, not by eye.** Now: exactly one filled volt element on the whole screen, LOG SET at 390x72. Settings: was three solid volt blocks on a screen with no primary action at all, now zero filled and three outlined. Equipment sheet: selected chip reads #CCFF00 on #1A1F0A, unselected #C3CBD2 on #111417. Goals: the filter chip is outlined and the only volt fills left are 6px progress hairlines — kept, and the rule now says why: it governs CONTROLS, and a progress bar is the thing the screen is about rather than something you press. The checkbox keeps its fill as the single named exemption, stated in the style and enforced by name, because a tick in a filled box is the least ambiguous affordance there is. 1,005 → 1,021 tests green, sixteen of them a source rule that fails if any screen draws a state as loudly as an action. | next: the sheets still have no exit animation — deferred three times now, and R122's reason (it conflicts with unmount-on-close, which fixed a 30-round bug) has never actually been re-tested

R142 | foundations | **Measurements, fine-tune: the four surfaces that were still counting a pull-up as nothing.** Went in to make PR detection bodyweight-aware and found a bigger bug underneath it: **a strict pull-up could never set a personal record at all, and never could have.** `e1rm(0, reps)` is 0 however many reps you do, so `bestE1rm` was 0, so the e1RM branch hit its own `bestPrior <= 0` guard and returned empty — somebody going from 8 strict pull-ups to 15, about as visible as strength gains get, was told nothing for ever. Fixing it by comparing real load immediately introduces the opposite defect, a record earned by **gaining weight**, so the rule is that a record on the weight branch has to hold on BOTH scales: more total load AND more added weight than ever. At an unchanged bodyweight the two agree exactly, so it costs a real lifter nothing; they diverge only when the scale rather than the training moved the number. The reps branch deliberately has no such guard — getting there means no set in history ever reached that many reps. `realWeight` is a second field rather than a redefinition of `weight`, because `gain` is `weight - previousWeight` and mixing the scales would have printed a pull-up PR as **"-160 LB"**. | **Verified by training the app: four pull-up sessions, then twelve reps — "NEW PERSONAL RECORD · PULL-UP · BEST YET", which was unreachable an hour earlier.** But the live walk found three more surfaces still summing `weight * reps` by hand, each its own copy of the recap's volume: the Progress history said **0 lb** for the same session the recap called 2,960, and the running total under the logged sets counted **0 lb** while the set was being done. All three now go through `sessionStats` — R135 deleted a duplicated session TITLE for this exact reason, and this is the worse version, because two names read as a wording choice and two totals read as one of them being wrong. Also found: `realLoad` added a kg bodyweight to an lb bar and labelled the result kg (84 + 25 = 109, off by fifty), `perSessionTop` ranked a session's pull-ups by `e1rm(0, reps)` so the "top" set was whichever came first, and the change column reported **+0** for a lifter who gained 25 lb doing the same strict set. Goal progress is deliberately left on added weight — a "+25 x 5" target would otherwise read as smashed the moment a bodyweight was recorded. 979 → 1,005 tests green. | next: the volt-accent audit from R137 is still open — 30 distinct jobs for one accent, and §15 says one accent means one job

R141 | content | **Measurements, fine-tune: the shareable.** Wired `bodyweightMultiple` into the recap — the one line in this app that says something a weight alone cannot, because 315 means nothing until you know who lifted it. Four rules keep it from being noise: only the session's BEST set, only at or above 1x (below bodyweight the number is true and says nothing anyone wants said), never for the four movements whose load IS the lifter ("Pull-up at 1.0x bodyweight" is a tautology in an achievement's clothes), and null with no reading. The payload's `best` gained an `exerciseId` so it can tell a squat from a pull-up. | **Verified by finishing a real pull-up session — and the verification found something worse than what I was checking.** The multiple correctly stayed silent, and the recap read **"TOTAL VOLUME 0 LB"**: two sets of pull-ups logged at 0, and 0 x 8 is 0, on the artifact §5 judges the whole product on. A workout that says you moved nothing is worse than one that says nothing. `sessionStats` now takes measurements and counts real load — same session now reads **2,960 LB**. Optional parameter, so every existing caller is unchanged and it degrades to the old answer with no reading rather than throwing. 966 → 979 tests green, including one asserting a barbell is not counted twice just because a bodyweight exists. | next: PR detection still compares pull-ups by added weight, so 185+0 and 185+25 look like a tie at 0 vs 25 — and `bestSetAtReps` picks the session's top set the same way

R140 | foundations | **Measurements, piece three: something finally consumes it.** `realLoad` existed and changed nothing until a screen called it. Progress rows now carry `realBest`, so the four movements whose load is the lifter report what they actually moved. Two rules held: the number the user TYPED stays the headline (they will recognise 25, not 210), and a bodyweight lift with no reading on record shows nothing extra rather than inventing an operand — an ordinary lift never grows a second number at all. | **Walked the whole chain on the running app**: recorded 185 lb on the YOU screen, logged two Pull-up sets, and the Progress row now reads **"Pull-up · 0 × 8 · 185 lb"**. Before this it read "0 × 8" — a lifter's hardest pulling work filed as nothing at all, which is the defect the whole feature exists to fix. 963 → 966 tests green. | next: fine-tune the feature — the recap and PR detection still count a pull-up as the weight added, and `bodyweightMultiple` is written but nothing calls it

R139 | first impression | **Measurements, piece two: the screen.** A YOU screen off Progress — not a fifth destination on the logging path (§5), because nothing here is needed mid-set. One card per kind, driven entirely from `KINDS`, so a third kind is a row rather than a rewrite. Decisions worth keeping: a kind with no readings still gets a card, because this screen is the only place the app says bodyweight EXISTS and a kind you can only see after using it cannot be discovered; the empty state is a sentence at lead size rather than a dash at 38px, so an empty card does not shout a non-answer; the trend line names its own baseline ("Down 4.2 lb since Jun") because one kind measures over 90 days and the other over three years and nothing else on screen would say so; both units stay visible instead of a toggle, and switching them CONVERTS what you typed rather than silently reinterpreting 185 lb as 185 kg; and the entry prefills from the last reading, because a three-digit bodyweight is a number the app already knows (§4). The reason bodyweight matters is stated once at the bottom rather than badged on the card. | Recorded 185 lb end to end on the running app: sheet opens, value saves, card shows **185 lb**, height still reads "Not recorded yet". 963 tests green (18 new). **Found the same bug for the third time in this project:** the entry field had no `minWidth: 0`, so a flex item refusing to shrink below its content width pushed the LB and KG chips to x554 — entirely off a 390px screen. Fixed; input now ends at 244 with the chips at 256-368. | next: piece three — nothing yet CONSUMES a bodyweight, so pull-ups are still counted wrong on Progress and in the recap

R138 | foundations | **Measurements, piece one: the model and the store.** Schema v5 adds one `measurements` table for every kind rather than a bodyweight table and a height table — they differ only in what they measure, so waist or arm later is a new `kind` and no new schema. `domain/measure.ts` gives each kind its own profile: units (lb/kg, cm/in), a NOISE floor so a 0.4 lb swing reports flat instead of inventing a direction, plausible bounds as a typo guard, and — the detail that made height worth taking seriously — its own **window**. Bodyweight trends over 90 days, height over three years, because on one axis the first looks like noise and the second looks like a flat line that failed to load. Units are stored as entered and never rewritten, same rule as set weights. Then the payoff: `realLoad()` and `bodyweightMultiple()`. Four library movements (pull-up, chin-up, dip, push-up) log at weight 0 because the load IS the lifter, so a 200 lb person's +25 pull-up was recorded as 25 — their hardest pulling work filed as their lightest. Both return NULL rather than guessing when there is no reading, and both use the reading that applied ON THE DAY, because a set done at 190 lb does not get heavier because you gained weight since. | 916 → 944 tests green (52 new across measure / repo / real-load). Two findings on the way: the plausible-bounds ceiling of 1000 lb let "400" typed into a kilos field through at 881 lb, so the guard was decorative — now 700; and there is a test asserting `CARRIES_BODYWEIGHT` matches the library's own `kit: 'bodyweight'` list, because one decides the input and the other decides the truth and they must not drift. Migration tested from a real v4 database, not just a fresh install. | next: piece two — where measurements live on screen, and logging one

R137 | texture | INTERRUPTED, no code changed. Premise checked and found wrong first: I assumed set chips and rail chips looked alike, and they do not — a set is a solid soft-cornered block (radius 9, no border) and a rail chip is an outlined pill (radius 22, 1px border), so that was my misreading rather than the app's. Moved on to the real texture question and got as far as counting it: **the volt accent has 30 distinct jobs** — primary action, current lift, next suggestion, achieved goal, focus ring, goal tick, plan tick, PR slab, the header rule, the add-set +, the undo action, the sparkline's last bar. §15 says ONE accent; using it for "press this", "you are here", "do this next", "you did it" and "the keyboard is here" all at once means none of them owns it. | Paused here for a product brainstorm requested mid-round. | next: finish R137 — decide which of the 30 volt uses earn the accent and which should become a lighter treatment (weight, size, or the #C3CBD2 tier)

R136 | foundations | Regression sweep after 22 rounds of edits, because every one of them moved something and none of them re-checked the invariants R94/R95 fought for. Swept Now, Goals, the add-goal sheet, Settings and Progress at **390x844 and 320x568** — the smallest phone still shipping — checking for text past the right edge, text below the fold, and any horizontal page scroll, while correctly excusing anything inside a horizontal scroller. **Zero findings on every screen at both sizes.** Nothing changed, and that is the point: the press states, type collapse, palette fold, wrapping filter row, sparkline resize, nav regroup and reps reorder all landed without breaking the layout. Also declined to churn the recap's spacer — the 287px void only appears on a ONE-lift session, the two-spacer split is a considered decision that already cut it from 380, and re-litigating it without evidence would be motion for its own sake. | Live measurement, 5 surfaces x 2 widths. 893 tests green. | next: the audit is due at R138; before that, texture — the set chips and rail chips are the same shape, so a logged set and a lift you have not done yet look alike

R135 | hierarchy | Walked the recap at 390x844 and found the app contradicting itself. `buildRecap` defaults to `title: 'WORKOUT'` and the recap SCREEN passes no title, so the screen you see the instant you finish called every session ever recorded "WORKOUT" — while the shared card was handed "PUSH DAY" by its caller and the Progress history derived the day itself. Three surfaces naming one session, two answers, and the vague one was the one the user meets first. `sessionTitle()` now lives in session.ts and both `buildRecap` and `recentSessions` call it, so a disagreement is no longer expressible; an explicit title still wins, because the shared card names its own. Deleted the duplicate derivation from progress-model on the way. | Live: the recap header now reads **PUSH DAY**, matching what Progress calls the same session. 889+4 tests green, including one asserting the two surfaces return the identical string for a session whose lifts do NOT agree on a day. Also checked the header alignment I suspected — `alignItems: 'baseline'` is already there and correct; the differing y values are just cap height, so that observation was mine being wrong, not the app. | next: the recap's middle is 287px of void when a session has one lift — the flexGrow spacer that fixed a different case now over-corrects on a short workout

R134 | sound and haptics | The app's sense of touch stopped at the edge of one file: twelve haptic calls on the logging screen and **zero** on Goals, Progress and Settings. Stepping a rep count by one buzzed; wiping all thirty-one of your targets did not. Extracted `haptics.ts` with four verbs named by INTENT rather than intensity — `chose`, `did`, `undid`, `destroyed` — so the next screen cannot pick a weight at random, and wired them: wiping goals and erasing everything are `destroyed` (both erase routes, not just the one on the populated screen), undo is `undid` and deliberately the same weight as the thing it reverses, filters/sort/preferences are `chose`, committing a goal is `did`. Every call swallowed, because it is invoked from inside write paths and expo-haptics is a no-op on web that can still reject — a phone that cannot buzz must never cost a set. | 883+6 tests green. Cannot be felt from here, so it is verified structurally: coverage per screen, both erase paths, and that the catch is on the promise AND the synchronous throw. | next: the sheets still have no exit; R122's reason for deferring it stands, so the honest alternative is to make the disappearance less abrupt without touching the six call sites

R133 | feedback | Went looking at the app's one async action — export / restore — and found a regression I had caused myself. `backupBusy` was `#39414A`; R117 folded that into `#7C8792` for contrast, which is the same colour as `backupLink`. So the disabled state still existed in the code and **had no effect on screen**: during an export every control looked exactly as it had. Disabled text is exempt from the contrast floor precisely because it is meant to recede, so it says so with `opacity: 0.4` now — which no future legibility pass can fold away. Also gave the note a DURING state: it only ever spoke after the work finished, so the whole time a file was being written the screen showed its resting sentence. | 883 tests green (2 new), including a guard that the busy style is not simply the resting colour again. **The guard needed guarding too:** the contrast test greps source for banned hexes, and the comment explaining WHY #39414A was removed contains #39414A — so documenting the fix failed the test that enforces it, and the cheapest way to make that go away is to delete the explanation. It strips comments before matching now. Third heredoc backslash-eating incident of the session on the way; rewrote the extraction with the repo's own `region` helper, which takes plain strings and cannot be mangled. | next: motion — the sheets still have no exit, and R122 deferred it for a good reason that may now be testable

R132 | texture and art | Backlog (9). Measured the split chooser at 390px: the push/pull/legs and upper/lower blurbs wrap to two lines, FULL BODY's fits on one, so the three options came out **100, 100 and 82px** — a set of three choices where the last one looks like it did not finish loading. Gave the blurb its own two-line box instead, so the text stops deciding the row height — the shortest option gets a little air under it, which reads as spacing, where the ragged set read as a bug. | At 390 cold: all three rows **100px**, one distinct height. 881 tests green. | next: backlog (6) — skipping the split question changes nothing visible, so the one blocking question in the app can be answered with no acknowledgement at all

R131 | content | Read the two surfaces a user only sees when something has gone wrong. The storage-failure copy is genuinely good — it says the data is safe, and after two failed retries it stops repeating "closing and reopening usually clears it" and admits the problem is not temporary. But it then says **"send the message below"** and gives no destination and no way to lift the text off the screen: a `selectable` Text, which on a phone means dragging selection handles across a stack trace. An instruction nobody can follow. Added SEND THIS MESSAGE, handing the whole diagnostic (db name, error, and the storage-location note) to the system share sheet — a mechanism the app already has for the recap, so no new dependency. Caught, because `Share.share` REJECTS where no sheet exists and an unhandled rejection on the screen that already means "something is broken" would be the second failure in a row. Also reworded +not-found: "this version of the app doesn't have YET" promised something that may never come and named a version the reader cannot see; a dead link is usually just a dead link. | 881 tests green, including the standing sweep that asserts no `Share.share` is wired to a bare onPress — which is what proves the catch is there. The failure screen itself is not reachable without corrupting the store, so this round is verified structurally rather than live, and said so. | next: backlog (9) — the three split options are different heights because their blurbs wrap differently

R130 | accessibility | R117 covered contrast; this is the keyboard. Good news first: all **35 controls on the logging screen are tabbable**, none unreachable. Bad news: **not one of them showed focus** — `outline: none`, no box-shadow, and zero `:focus` rules in the entire stylesheet, because react-native-web resets the browser's outline on every Pressable and nothing put one back. A keyboard user could tab the whole app with no idea what they were about to press. `pressStyle` now adds a 2px volt ring at 2px offset on `focused` — one change covering every control already routed through it. The accent earns its place here more than anywhere: "where am I" is exactly the question one loud colour should answer. Also widened the state type, since RN core only declares `pressed` while RNW also passes `focused` and `hovered`. | Verified on both a `primary` and a `quiet` control: the inline style gains `outline: rgb(204, 255, 0) solid 2px; outline-offset: 2px` on focus and loses it on blur. 881 tests green. **Limitation, stated rather than papered over:** a hidden document sets `activeElement` but fires no focus event, so plain `.focus()` proves nothing here — the ring had to be exercised with a synthetic `focusin`, which is the delegated event React listens to. Real tab-key focus is unverified from this environment. | next: content — the RepoGate failure screen and +not-found have never been read in this loop, and they are what a user sees when something breaks

Nothing here needed optimising, so nothing was changed — inventing a fix the measurement does not support is how you make something slower while feeling productive. The sheet was not slow, it was invisible, and would be for any user whose frames stall. Rebuilt so the RESTING style is the visible one and the entrance is a transient state cleared on a `setTimeout` (timers fire when hidden): worst case it snaps visible, which is exactly the old behaviour.
