- R338 — new axis, per the owner's own steer: not width (already checked) but TEXT SIZE — Dynamic Type, the accessibility font-scale setting a real fitness-app user (read at arm's length, mid-set, often older than whoever built it) is genuinely likely to have on. No native device to test it on (§16), so simulated honestly: found the app sets `allowFontScaling` nowhere, meaning React Native's default (full, uncapped system font scale) applies; drove the real union-of-everything row from R337 and inflated every text node's OWN computed font-size in place — leaving every padding, gap and minWidth untouched, which is what real Dynamic Type does (it scales text, not layout constants) — first to 1.6x (clean), then to 2.35x, iOS's own largest accessibility size. **Found a real, silent bug**: the goal tag's inflated text rendered directly ON TOP of the sparkline's last several bars — a genuine pixel overlap, not a false alarm, confirmed by geometry (goal tag left edge at x72.5, sparkline bars extending to x110). Root cause, and it undoes an assumption baked into the ORIGINAL fix that built this row: `spark`'s container was told `minWidth: 0` so it could shrink to make room for the numbers that must never shrink themselves — but the BARS inside it have their own floor (5pt each) that does not shrink with the container, so a container instructed it may reach zero collapses past what its own children can honour, and the bars silently overflow the shrunk container rather than the row ever detecting it ran short of space. Fixed in two parts: `spark`'s own `minWidth` is now the real floor its ten bars actually need (`SPARK_POINTS * 5 + (SPARK_POINTS-1) * 4`, the exact arithmetic `progress-row-fits.test.ts` already used to verify the WIDTH case, now made real in the style itself rather than assumed); and `rowBottom` gained `flexWrap: 'wrap'` so that once even the corrected floors do not fit, the trend number drops to a second line instead of overlapping anything — tried `flexWrap` FIRST, alone, and it changed nothing, because flexbox never attempts to wrap while a flexible child is still willing to shrink toward zero; only fixing the floor gave wrap something real to trigger on. Three tests updated/added (one corrected — it had asserted `minWidth: 0` as a requirement, which the fix reverses on purpose — two new, pinning the real floor and the wrap fallback). 1600 green (+2), tsc clean; the pre-existing 320pt width-budget tests are untouched and still pass, confirming this was purely a scale-axis gap, not a width regression. Verified live, twice: at 2.35x the overlap reproduced exactly as measured, then vanished after the fix — bars correctly grew to their honoured floor (ending at x151), the goal tag moved clear (starting at x175, a real 24px gap), and the trend number wrapped cleanly to its own line (y619, no overlap with anything above); confirmed separately that normal scale still renders as one line, unchanged (goal tag at its natural 62px). next: this was found on ONE row shape (a lift with both a goal and a bodyweight multiple); the Now screen's own crowding-sensitive hero area and Goals' own bar-and-percentage row have not been checked against Dynamic Type at all — worth a look if another round in this vein is warranted, but this single find justifies the whole axis on its own.

Root cause: `topBar` has no `flexShrink` and no wrap, built on the assumption ("the eye reads the gaps, so space those") that its three items always fit — true at any normal text size, false once Dynamic Type inflates all three. Fixed the same way as R338: `flexWrap: 'wrap'` on `topBar`, costing nothing at normal scale, turning "unreachable" into "a second line" at extreme scale — verified live, gear moved from x347-377 (off-screen) to x105-135 (fully on-screen and tappable). A second, distinct finding underneath it: the hero weight number's font size is not a fixed value — `layoutFor` already computes it to fit the available width, and Dynamic Type's system multiplier was applying ON TOP of that already-fitted value, not instead of a fixed one, so at 2.35x the hero digits alone claimed 320pt of width (right edge past x400) and shoved the +/- steppers off the phone entirely. This is a different bug shape from the sparkline (a genuine double-application of two independent sizing systems, not a container/child floor mismatch), and the correct, standard fix is the documented exemption for a control that already has its own sizing logic: `allowFontScaling={false}` on the hero weight and reps numbers, both their TextInputs, the +/- stepper glyphs, the jump chips (−45/+45/−5/+5), and — found by RE-testing after the first pass — the "LB"/"BODYWEIGHT" unit label, which sits `position: absolute` from a fixed anchor next to the now-exempted number and was growing independently into the "+" stepper's own space until it got the same treatment. Proved this with a deliberately illegible probe (#3A3A3A on #2A2A2A, ratio 1.26) that the broken version missed and the fixed version caught. R355 — picked the peer's alternative axis (vertical space / keyboard-up mid-set) as a follow-on to the closed colour axis. Found a genuine environment limitation before trusting any result: resize_window's viewport change updates the real CSS layout (document.documentElement.clientWidth/clientHeight) immediately, but does NOT dispatch a window 'resize' event to the page — so React Native Web's useWindowDimensions() (which NowScreen.tsx uses at line 192 for its own width/height-driven layout) keeps reporting the PRE-resize window.innerWidth/innerHeight until a fresh navigation. Caught this because the Now screen's weight-edit row rendered with real DOM overflow (an input measuring 861px wide, a '+' button at right:1005) after a resize-without-navigate — looked like a shocking product bug at first, but document.documentElement.clientWidth correctly showed 320 the whole time, and a force-navigate immediately fixed window.innerWidth back to 320 with the same app state gone. Reproduced it twice to confirm: resize-then-navigate is clean, resize-without-navigate desyncs useWindowDimensions from the true viewport every time. This means the keyboard-up scenario (which on a real device is a LIVE resize with no navigation) cannot be faithfully simulated with this tool for any screen using useWindowDimensions, the same way 6 blocks real device/storage faults — not faked, left blocked, with the reason on record. Did not report the phantom overflow as a bug. Worth remembering for future rounds: always force-navigate after resize_window before trusting any live measurement, and never trust window.innerWidth/innerHeight directly in this pane — use document.documentElement.clientWidth/clientHeight or visualViewport instead, which stayed correct throughout.

R362 — picked a genuinely fresh axis: audited this session's own new Session.updatedAt field (added R333 for the reopen-idle fix) through the OTHER path that touches session rows, restore/backup, which no round had checked. Wrote a real repro script calling exportAll then restore directly: a session exported while still live and already 3h idle (past the 90min IDLE_END_MS) came back from restore reading as freshly touched -- isStale() returned false when it should be true. Root cause: repo.startSession() had no way to say when a session ROW last changed (only 'at' for startedAt existed, from the R... startedAt fix a prior session made for the identical bug shape on a different field), so portable.ts's restore() always stamped updated_at to the restore time -- and since a restore always happens later than every real timestamp in the file, lastTouch's Math.max(lastSetAt, updatedAt) picks the wrong one unconditionally, silently defeating the R333 idle rule on every restored live session. Fixed by adding an optional updatedAt param to startSession (same pattern as the existing 'at' param, same doc-comment style) and threading s.updatedAt through in portable.ts, falling back to now for older backups that predate the field. Verified three ways: the original repro script showed isStale flip from false to true; reverted the fix and confirmed the new permanent test (test/portable.test.ts, 2 new tests: the stale-live-session case and the missing-field-in-older-backup case) fails exactly as expected without it; restored the fix and confirmed both pass. Full suite 1604/1604 green (1602+2), tsc clean.
R363 — same method as R362, applied to the OTHER capability this session shipped that touches a persisted table: removeExercise (R308-312). Checked whether restore/backup respects a deliberate exercise removal the way it already, correctly, respects a deliberately-undone SET (there was an explicit existing test and comment for that exact set case). There was no equivalent for exercises. Wrote a repro: add a custom exercise, back it up, remove it (never logged, so removeExercise succeeds), then restore that OLD backup -- the exercise came back. Root cause: addExercise's INSERT...ON CONFLICT unconditionally sets deleted=0, and restore's knownExercises set is built from exercises() which filters deleted=0, so an id that is 'deliberately removed' and an id that 'never existed' look identical to the restore loop -- both get addExercise called on them. Fixed by adding repo.exerciseWasRemoved(id), a narrow existence-including-deleted check, and skipping restoration of any exercise id that comes back true rather than resurrecting it -- matching the exact pattern and wording already established for sets. Verified: repro script flipped from resurrecting it to correctly leaving it gone; reverted the fix and confirmed the new test (test/portable.test.ts, 1 more test, mirroring the existing set-undo test almost line for line) fails exactly as expected; restored the fix, full suite 1605/1605 green, tsc clean.

R370 — tested the exact harder case the peer named: does restoring an OLDER backup ever corrupt a NEWER live session with the same id, by overwriting its updatedAt with the file's older, staler value? Repro: built a session on the 'target' device, touched it with a fresh set just now (updatedAt effectively current), then restored an older backup containing the SAME session id from 10 days earlier. Real pasted output: updatedAt was 1788046347737 before restore and exactly 1788046347737 after -- byte-identical, isStale stayed false both times. Root cause of why this is safe: restore's session loop (portable.ts:174) does 'if (repo.session(s.id)) { knownSessions.add(s.id); continue; }' -- an already-known session id is skipped entirely, never touched, so the new updatedAt param only ever applies to a session being created for the first time. The R362 fix cannot corrupt an existing session because the code path that would do so is structurally unreachable. This was the one remaining unverified direction of the 'older round trip over newer state' question the peer raised -- now confirmed with real evidence, not assumed from reading the skip logic. Full restore-path audit (R362-R370) is now genuinely exhausted: 2 real bugs fixed and tested, every other entity and direction checked and confirmed clean.
R371 — new axis: whether LOG SET (the app's single most-tapped control) has any protection against a genuine double-tap creating a duplicate set. Confirmed at the model layer with real pasted output that it does not: two immediate model.log() calls produced two sets, identical weight/reps, same millisecond timestamp, no distinguishing field. Found precedent elsewhere in the codebase for guarding exactly this failure mode (ConfirmSheet's 'if (closing) return', an explicit test titled 'a double tap on WIPE must not throw'), so this looked like a real gap worth closing the same way. Investigated a fix -- a short re-entry guard on the log() callback, matching ConfirmSheet's shape -- and concluded NOT to add it, for a reason specific to this control: unlike WIPE (a destructive delete, naturally idempotent, safe to no-op) and unlike ConfirmSheet's guard (blocking re-entry only during its OWN visible exit animation, which already tells the user something is mid-transition), LOG SET is a CREATE of a genuinely repeatable, non-idempotent domain action -- 3 identical sets in a row is the single most common real workout pattern this app exists to record, not an edge case. A time-based guard cannot distinguish an accidental double-tap from a deliberate fast second set, and would have to pick between silently dropping a real tap with zero feedback (worse than doing nothing -- this app's own portable.ts principle is 'skipped, reported, not swallowed') or leaving a long enough window that it never actually stops a genuine mis-tap either. The app's existing mitigation -- a haptic buzz on every log (so a double-tap produces two distinct buzzes, a real if subtle signal) plus the always-visible per-set UNDO -- is the considered trade-off already in place, matching §4's own stated posture of direct action over pre-emptive blocking. Declining the fix; recording the investigation and the reasoning rather than silently dropping the thread.
R372 — checked the same double-tap question for goal creation (the other primary create-action button, SET GOAL) since LOG SET turned out to be a considered trade-off rather than a gap. Here the answer is cleaner: validateNewGoal already rejects a second goal for the same exerciseId while one is still active ('duplicate', goals.ts:364-366, an existing, deliberately-documented rule for a different reason -- one live goal per lift keeps the screen unambiguous -- that happens to also make a double-tap on SET GOAL safe for free). Confirmed this is race-free by construction, not just by luck: createGoal validates then writes synchronously with no async gap, so a genuine double-tap runs two sequential calls, and the second one's validation reads the first one's already-committed write and correctly returns 'duplicate' rather than creating a second goal. No fix needed; recorded as a second confirmed-safe primary action to close out the tap-safety question this round opened.
R373 — extended the same look across every remaining one-tap action, per the peer's ask, and got three more 'safe, and here is exactly why' answers rather than assuming from the LOG SET result. UNDO (now-model.ts:1707): naturally idempotent by construction — 'if (!mine.length) return false' means a double-tap just pops one more real set off the stack (correct undo semantics, not a bug) and a tap with nothing left to remove is a harmless no-op, not a crash. WIPE ALL's own entry button (goals.tsx:253, setWipeAllStep(1)): safe because of the modal-overlay pattern, not an explicit guard — the instant step becomes non-zero, ConfirmSheet renders on top and a second rapid tap at the same screen coordinates lands on the sheet's backdrop, not the button underneath. FINISH (now-model.ts:1749): repo.endSession() sets ended_at to the same value (the last set's own timestamp) every time, so a double-tap is a harmless identical overwrite -- idempotent by construction, same category as the delete paths. That closes the full ledger for this axis: LOG SET is the one genuine defect, correctly left unfixed for domain reasons; every other primary action is safe, and each for a specifically different, checked reason (naturally idempotent delete/undo, domain-rule dedup, modal-overlay exclusivity, shared busy-guard on Export/Restore/Erase, or idempotent overwrite) rather than one blanket assumption.
R374 — direct follow-up on R371's declined LOG SET finding: since a double-tap (or a user mashing it) CAN create duplicate sets and no guard was added, checked whether that failure mode could compound into a second, worse problem -- does state() (the hot read that runs on every tap, already guarded at 6000 sets/5-years/700-sessions in an existing test) degrade when the sets pile up in ONE LIVE SESSION instead of spread across history, which is the shape a real mashing incident would actually produce. Real measured numbers: 300 sets in one session -> state() averaged 1.51ms; pushed to 2000 sets in one session (an absurd but real ceiling test) -> 6.17ms, still comfortably under the existing 16ms budget the 5-year test uses. No secondary perf bug lurking behind the declined tap-guard decision -- a mashed LOG SET produces an annoying but cheap-to-fix (via UNDO) mess, not a slow screen. Confirms R371's decision cost nothing beyond what was already weighed.

R377 — applied the 'audit the consequences of a decline' method to R360's assumption that the goal-EDITING sheet needed no separate Dynamic Type scan because it 'reuses the exact same draft-form JSX already patched' as goal-creation. Tested it for real: seeded a goal with a genuine pre-filled edit-mode value (Bulgarian Split Squat, target 225 lb, 12 reps -- deliberately a 3-digit target and a long exercise name, neither of which the empty-state creation flow renders at once), opened the live CHANGE sheet, ran the structural 2.35x scan. It reported two overflows ('lb' and '+' past the 320px viewport) -- looked exactly like the decline was wrong. Investigated before reporting: read the source directly and confirmed every text node in that row (stepText, targetUnitGhost, targetValue, targetUnit, jumpText, targetHint) already carries allowFontScaling={false} from R347. My blunt CSS-injection scanner force-scales every element regardless of that React prop -- a known, already-documented limitation of this exact instrument -- so the two 'overflows' are false positives of the scan, not the app. On a real device none of this row would grow at all under Dynamic Type. R360's decline holds, now confirmed against real edit-mode data rather than assumed from 'same JSX'. This is the audit-a-decline method producing a correct 'no bug' rather than either skipping the check or reporting a false alarm.
R378 — consequence-audit on R362's own change: grepped every startSession( call site across the whole codebase (over 100, spanning every test file plus the one real production caller in now-model.ts:961) to confirm the new optional 5th updatedAt param could not have shifted any existing positional call. Confirmed: every call site passes at most 4 arguments (id, unit, title?, at?); none pass a 5th positional value that could now collide with the new parameter, and the production caller (this.repo.startSession(newId('s'), unit)) only ever passes 2, defaulting updatedAt to now exactly as before. tsc was already clean and 1605/1605 passed after that change, but this confirms WHY -- the change was genuinely additive with zero behavioural surface on any other caller, not just accidentally untested by the existing suite.
R379 — closing checkpoint for this stretch: full suite re-run, 1605/1605 green, tsc clean. No new changes this round; a deliberate sanity gate before the next round picks a fresh direction.
R380 — traced my own R373 claim rather than trusting it: 'a second rapid tap on WIPE ALL's entry button lands on the confirm sheet's backdrop, not the button underneath' was an untraced structural inference, never actually tested. Tested it for real: dispatched two full pointerdown/mousedown/pointerup/mouseup/click event sequences at the SAME screen coordinates via elementFromPoint (not two .click() calls on a held JS reference, which would be an easier, less honest test) with no gap between them. Result: BOTH clicks hit the SAME 'WIPE ALL' DOM node -- React had not re-rendered/painted the modal between the two synchronous dispatches, so my stated mechanism was WRONG; the backdrop does not reliably exclude a same-tick second tap. But the outcome is still safe, confirmed live: exactly one ConfirmSheet rendered (queried the DOM, count=1), the screen stayed correctly on step 1, no crash, no skipped step. The REAL reason it's safe: onPress={() => setWipeAllStep(1)} sets a fixed value, not an increment or toggle, so calling it twice is naturally idempotent -- the same category as FINISH and UNDO, not the 'modal exclusivity' category I originally and incorrectly attributed it to. Conclusion unchanged (safe), mechanism corrected. This is exactly the untraced-structural-claim risk the peer named: right answer, wrong reasoning, which would have been a live landmine if anyone later relied on 'the modal blocks re-taps' as a general pattern elsewhere in this codebase.
R381 — traced R372's SET GOAL claim the same rigorous way as R380's WIPE ALL trace, since it rested on the same kind of source-only reasoning (createGoal validates then writes synchronously). Real coordinate-based double-click test: picked Bench Press in the ADD A GOAL sheet, dispatched two full pointerdown/mousedown/pointerup/mouseup/click sequences at SET GOAL's exact screen coordinates with no gap -- both hit the same DOM node, confirming (like WIPE ALL) that React had not re-rendered between them. Unlike WIPE ALL, the outcome here confirms the ORIGINAL mechanism was correct, not just the conclusion: exactly 2 goals exist afterward (Squat + Bench Press, 'WIPE ALL 2' on screen), not 3 -- the second createGoal call's validateNewGoal really did see the first call's already-committed write and rejected it as 'duplicate', live, under real same-tick double-firing, not just reasoned from reading synchronous code. Zero console errors. This closes the untraced-claim hunt on the two candidates that shared the same 'reasoned from source, never physically tested' shape: one (WIPE ALL) had a wrong mechanism behind a right answer, corrected in R380; the other (SET GOAL) checks out exactly as originally reasoned.
R382 — extended the same trace to the per-goal WIPE button (setWiping(g), a fixed-value set like WIPE ALL's, not previously checked at all). Same real coordinate double-click test: both dispatches hit the same 'WIPE' DOM node before React repainted -- confirming the general finding from R380, that this app's Pressable-triggered modals do NOT reliably exclude a same-tick second physical tap the way I'd assumed. Outcome stayed correct regardless: exactly one coherent ConfirmSheet rendered ('Wipe the Bench Press goal?'), no corrupted state, no duplicate sheet -- safe for the same reason WIPE ALL is, setWiping(g) sets a fixed value rather than toggling or incrementing. This completes the tap-safety re-audit: every 'safe via modal exclusivity' claim in this session's own log was actually 'safe via idempotent fixed-value state', a correction now verified on all three affected controls (WIPE ALL entry, per-goal WIPE, and by the same logic FINISH's session state) rather than left as a corrected note on one example.
R383 — finished the structural-claim sweep the peer asked for by tracing the last untested primary action: FINISH. Unlike WIPE ALL/SET GOAL/per-goal-WIPE (all safe, just for corrected or confirmed reasons), this one was a REAL BUG. Real coordinate double-click at FINISH's exact screen position (same elementFromPoint technique): both dispatches hit the same pre-render DOM node, and onFinish (a bare router.push('/recap'), zero guard) fired twice. Live evidence: after the double-tap, DONE had to be tapped TWICE to actually leave the recap -- the first tap left the SAME recap on screen unchanged, the second dropped onto a Now screen that had rolled a fresh session over underneath. Root cause: onPress checked nothing before pushing, and any check against state.canFinish would have failed anyway since state is a snapshot from the last render and the second click lands before React repaints -- the same trap R380 found in WIPE ALL's backdrop assumption. Fixed with a useRef guard (finishedRef, not state, checked and set synchronously) on the FINISH handler, reset in the existing useFocusEffect that already rolls a finished session into a fresh one, so a genuinely new workout can still be finished. Verified live: re-ran the identical double-click reproduction post-fix, ONE tap of DONE now correctly returns to Now. Added 3 new source-level tests (test/touch-targets.test.ts, since the guard is a useRef nothing at the domain-model layer can reach) -- confirmed they fail exactly as expected with the guard removed, then confirmed green with it restored. Full suite 1608/1608, tsc clean. This closes the structural-claim sweep: 4 primary actions traced with real coordinate-based double-click events (WIPE ALL entry, SET GOAL, per-goal WIPE, FINISH) -- 3 confirmed or corrected-and-confirmed safe, 1 was a genuine bug, now fixed and tested.
R384 — traced the same untested claim shape one level further: since router.push has no guard ANYWHERE by default, every other Pressable that calls it directly was an unverified instance of the exact same bug class FINISH turned out to have. Found a second real, confirmed instance with the identical live technique (real pointerdown/mousedown/pointerup/mouseup/click at the same screen coordinates via elementFromPoint): PastSession's tap-to-open-recap on Progress. Same signature as FINISH -- both dispatches hit the same pre-render DOM node, and afterward DONE needed two taps to actually leave, the second one dropping past Progress entirely onto Goals. Rather than patch this one site with its own bespoke ref (which would leave 6 other router.push call sites in progress.tsx and index.tsx sharing the identical unguarded shape), built one small shared hook, src/ui/guarded-push.ts (useGuardedPush): a useRef-backed 600ms cooldown, checked and set synchronously outside render -- the corrected primitive R380 identified, now applied generally rather than re-derived per site. Applied it to all 4 router.push call sites in progress.tsx (YouRow x2, PastSession, Settings x2) and all 4 in index.tsx (onFinish, onOpenProgress, onOpenGoals, onOpenSettings) -- onFinish already had NowScreen's own separate finishedRef guard, but routed it through the shared guard too for belt-and-braces consistency rather than leaving one push in the file relying on a different, invisible-from-here mechanism. Fixed 3 source-pinning tests that referenced the old literal 'router.push(...)' text (progress-row-fits.test.ts, measure-reachable.test.ts, erase-claim.test.ts) to match the new 'push(...)' calls, preserving their original intent. Verified live: re-ran the exact PastSession double-click reproduction post-fix -- ONE tap of DONE now correctly returns to Progress. Also verified a single normal FINISH still navigates correctly after onFinish was routed through the same guard (not accidentally blocking legitimate use). R385 — checked whether router.replace() (used everywhere else in the app -- every screen's DONE/back fallback, and recap.tsx's REOPEN/EDIT THIS WORKOUT button, which has a real state mutation behind it: repo.reopenSession()) shares the same same-tick double-fire vulnerability router.push() had. Grepped the whole app/ directory: after this stretch's fixes, zero raw router.push calls remain anywhere in .tsx files -- everything left is router.back()/router.replace(). Tested the one replace() call with real logic behind it live, the same coordinate double-click method: finished a live session via the UI to reach the natural (viewingHistory=false) recap, then dispatched two real pointerdown/mousedown/pointerup/mouseup/click sequences at REOPEN's exact coordinates. Both hit the same pre-render DOM node (confirming the same React-timing gap exists here too) -- but the outcome was completely clean: landed correctly on Now with the reopened session showing exactly 1 set (not 2, not corrupted), FINISH available again. Root cause of why this is safe, unlike push: replace() does not grow the navigation stack the way push() does, so two replaces to the same target are harmless rather than stacking two copies of a route; and repo.reopenSession() is independently idempotent (re-sets ended_at=null, updated_at=now() twice, no different from once). Did not need a fix -- confirmed safe for a specific, now-understood mechanism rather than assumed from 'it's not push so it's probably fine'. This closes the navigation-safety sweep: every router.push call site guarded (R384), every router.replace call site checked and found safe by construction (R385).
R386 — traced CLEAR's confirm chain live (real coordinate double-click on the CLEAR entry, then on the sheet's own CLEAR confirm button) and it exposed something bigger than CLEAR itself: ConfirmSheet's shared 'if (closing) return' guard -- used by EVERY destructive confirmation in the app (erase-all, clear-workout, per-goal wipe, all three WIPE ALL steps) -- reads closing, which is useState. Both real click dispatches at the confirm button's coordinates landed on the same pre-render DOM node (the identical React-timing gap found on FINISH and WIPE ALL), so both calls to close() read the same stale closing===null and BOTH passed the guard -- the component's OWN comment claiming this stops a second tap was false, unnoticed until traced. A second consequence beyond the double-fire: the old code reassigned timer.current to the new setTimeout without clearing the first, so the ORPHANED first timer would still fire later even after the correct one completed or the component unmounted -- exactly the 'never silently, afterward' failure the component's file-level docstring says it exists to prevent. Not independently observable live for CLEAR itself, since model.clearWorkout()/repo.eraseAll()/removeGoals are all idempotent (a second silent call has no visible symptom) -- the same reason this sat unnoticed while FINISH's identical bug WAS visible (router.push stacks, these don't). Fixed with a useRef guard (closingRef) checked synchronously before the stale state read, plus clearing any existing timer before scheduling a new one. Found and fixed a genuinely funny pre-existing casualty while running the full suite: test/sheet-exit-animation.test.ts already had a test LITERALLY TITLED 'a second tap mid-exit cannot double-fire or restart the clock' that was pinning the OLD, buggy 'if (closing) return' text as correct -- the test's own name was the bug report, and it had been passing by asserting the wrong thing. Updated it to pin the new closingRef check instead. Added test/confirm-sheet.test.ts (3 tests: the ref-based guard exists at the source, the orphaned-timer clear exists, and the exact algorithm verified standalone to reject a same-tick repeat) since there's no React hook-testing harness in this project to exercise the component directly. Full suite 1614/1614 green, tsc clean. This is the single highest-leverage fix of the whole navigation/tap-safety stretch: one shared component, eight call sites, all fixed at once.
R387 — followed a real audit-a-named-invariant test into a live trace: recap-layout.test.ts's 'every screen can be left (S5)' checks a DIFFERENT guard than the tap-safety ones (canGoBack()-then-replace() fallback, not re-entry), but was in the exact risk family, so traced it live rather than trusting the passing test. Double-clicking DONE at real coordinates on Goals produced a genuine 'GO_BACK was not handled by any navigator' error -- confirmed on a completely FRESH tab (ruling out stale Fast Refresh, which is what an earlier false alarm in this same round turned out to be: a 'finishedRef is not defined' crash that only reproduced on the long-lived original tab and vanished on a fresh one -- correctly not treated as a regression). Root cause: router.canGoBack() reads live navigator state, but the first tap's back() had not finished updating it by the time the second tap's canGoBack() ran, so it read stale-true and called back() again with nowhere to go. Found the SAME leave() helper duplicated identically across 5 files (progress/goals/settings/measure/recap.tsx) -- the exact 'second implementation was not wrong, it was unverifiable from the call site' shape the peer named. Consolidated into one new useGuardedLeave (src/ui/guarded-push.ts, alongside useGuardedPush -- same file, same cooldown mechanism, genuinely the same primitive this time, not just a similar one) and rewired all 5 screens. Fixed 2 more pinned tests that had been checking the old per-file literal text (recap-layout.test.ts's canGoBack()/router.replace() assertions moved to check the shared module once; guarded-push.test.ts's own import regex loosened for the two-name import). Verified the fix live with proper isolation this time -- a console.error call counter installed before the double-click, rather than trusting read_console_messages, which turned out to return ACCUMULATED history across calls and nearly produced a false 'still broken' reading of its own. Zero errors, correct landing on Now. Full suite 1619/1619, tsc clean. Two real self-corrections in one round: caught a stale-Fast-Refresh false alarm before reacting to it, then caught a stale-console-log false alarm the same way.

R390 — traced the last untested primary write action live: SAVE CHANGES (editGoal, distinct code path from SET GOAL/createGoal already checked in R372/R381). Real coordinate double-click on the sheet's SAVE CHANGES button (console.error counter installed up front): both dispatches hit the same pre-render DOM node, zero errors, and afterward there was exactly one goal with the edited value (315 lb target) -- no duplicate, no corruption. Confirmed the predicted mechanism: editGoal computes a fully deterministic goal object from the draft plus the pre-existing id/exerciseId/createdAt and calls repo.saveGoal (an upsert), so two same-tick calls with the same draft write the identical row twice -- idempotent by construction, the same category as FINISH's endSession and REOPEN's reopenSession, not the LOG SET category where 'again' creates something genuinely new. This closes out the goal-sheet's two submit paths (create and edit) as both traced live, not assumed from one covering the other.
R391 — traced the exercise-removal x button live (only reasoned about via source earlier, never physically double-clicked). Seeded a removable custom exercise, dispatched two real pointerdown/mousedown/pointerup/mouseup/click sequences at its x button's exact coordinates: both hit the same pre-render DOM node, and the result was a genuine, confirmed bug -- the exercise WAS removed (gone from the YOURS list) but the screen showed 'Can't remove it -- it already has sets logged', a false and specifically WRONG error for something that had just succeeded. Root cause: onRemove's repo-level guard (deleted=0 check) makes the second call harmless to the DATA, but the UI had no way to tell 'already gone because I just removed it' from 'refused because it has sets', so it displayed the generic failure text for both. Fixed with a useRef<Set<string>> of already-removed ids, checked before onRemove is ever called and populated only on a SUCCESSFUL removal -- a genuinely refused one (real sets logged) stays retryable, only a same-tick duplicate of an already-successful tap is silenced. Verified live: re-ran the identical double-click reproduction post-fix, no false error text appeared. Added test/remove-exercise-guard.test.ts pinning the guard's three lines; reverted the fix and confirmed the test fails with the exact expected assertion message, restored and confirmed 1623/1623 green, tsc clean. Sixth confirmed instance of tonight's one root cause (same-tick double-tap landing on a pre-render DOM node), and the second (after ConfirmSheet's onRemove) where the consequence was a wrong MESSAGE rather than wrong DATA -- worth naming as its own failure mode: the write can be idempotent-safe while the UI's REPORT of what happened is not.
R392 — hunted for other instances of R391's new failure shape (a write succeeds, data is fine, but a same-tick retry reports failure because it can no longer tell 'already done' from 'genuinely refused'). Checked every other boolean/error-returning save function reachable from a Pressable: goals.tsx's createGoal/editGoal (submit, already traced live in R372/R381/R390 -- deterministic upsert, same input always gives the same ok:true both times, no state-dependent flip), measure.tsx's recordMeasurement (creates a new reading keyed on value+timestamp, no 'already recorded' refusal path -- always succeeds if the number is valid, regardless of prior calls) and saveMeasureGoal (create-or-update by kind, same validateMeasureGoal result both times, no first-succeeds-second-fails branch), and clearMeasureGoal (void return, no error message tied to it, so no discrepancy possible even though a second call is a silent no-op). None share removeExercise's specific shape: an explicit refusal branch whose answer depends on state the FIRST call itself just changed. Confirmed real, not manufactured -- removeExercise was the one function in the app with that exact property (its own guard checks 'already deleted', which only exists because deletion is the thing being guarded against). This closes the message-can-lie axis with a genuine negative result rather than forcing a second finding to match the first.

R396 — traced the Goals screen's own UNDO toast (after a single-goal WIPE) live, the last untested primary action reading from React state closure rather than a fresh repo query. R399 — took the peer's time-at-scale suggestion. Measured storage growth directly (not previously measured -- prior perf tests only checked state()'s speed at 6000 sets/5 years, never the actual localStorage footprint): a realistic 3x/week, 5-set-average user hits 78 sessions/390 sets in 6 months (140KB sqlite / 187KB base64, 3.6% of a 5MB quota) and 780 sessions/3900 sets over 5 years (668KB sqlite / 891KB base64, 17.4% of quota) -- growing roughly linearly at ~178KB/year of base64. Extrapolating, a genuinely multi-decade user (25-30+ years of consistent training) would be the first to realistically approach a conservative 5MB localStorage quota. Checked whether that failure mode is handled: yes, already -- src/data/web-db.ts:93-103 wraps the debounced localStorage.setItem in try/catch with the exact scenario named in its own comment ('Over quota, most likely. Losing the dev snapshot is acceptable; taking down the screen mid-workout is not.') and openWebDb's initial read (line 79-84) has the matching try/catch for a corrupt/oversized entry on load. This axis produced a real, useful measurement (nobody had sized the actual storage footprint before) and confirmed the one failure mode it points at is already gracefully handled rather than an unhandled crash -- a genuine positive result, not manufactured. Native builds use a real file-based SQLite (see repo.ts's dual web/native Db split), so this quota ceiling is web-preview/PWA-specific and does not apply to a native install at all.
R400 — measured the Progress screen's own render-path functions at genuine long-term scale (10 years, 3x/week, 1560 sessions / 7800 sets -- beyond the 5-year/700-session scale the existing NowScreen guard test uses). Real numbers, 20-call averages: progressRows 3.96ms, recentSessions 0.60ms (confirms the prior session's own fix -- picking which sessions survive before building summaries -- still holds at double its original test scale), hiddenRowCount 0.23ms, weeklyLine 1.80ms. Combined, well under 7ms for everything Progress computes on one render, comfortably inside a 16ms frame budget with room to spare. No perf cliff found across the whole Progress screen at 10-year scale, not just the one function (state()) already guarded by an existing test.
R401 — checked whether achieved goals (uncapped, never prompted for cleanup since only ACTIVE goals count toward MAX_GOALS) become a real problem over years. First attempt used a flawed fixture -- seeded 260 goals with no sets logged against any of them, so every single one legitimately read as unachieved and correctly hit the real 100-active-goal cap on the 101st save. Caught this as a fixture bug before reporting it as a repo bug: re-read repo.ts's actual check (saveGoal:556-563, activeGoals(...).length >= MAX_GOALS) and confirmed the cap logic itself was correct all along -- my test just never gave any goal a real reason to count as achieved. Rebuilt the fixture to genuinely achieve each of 260 goals (a real matching set logged at/above target, immediately after creation) across a simulated 10 years, none ever deleted. Real numbers: listGoals stayed at 0.55ms average over 20 calls with all 260 correctly read back as achieved, and saving goal #261 on top of the 260 succeeded without error, confirming 'achieved goals do not occupy a slot' holds at real accumulated scale, not just in the unit tests that assert it in isolation. Clean result, self-corrected fixture flaw caught before it became a false bug report.
R402 — checked a different access pattern from the whole-database scans already measured: a SINGLE lift's full history at scale (squat trained 3x/week for 10 years, 7800 sets all on one exerciseId -- the worst case for any per-exercise scan, since Progress/PR logic elsewhere gets to split load across a dozen lifts). findPRs averaged 0.34ms and bestWeightAtReps 0.14ms over 20 calls each -- both trivially fast, no scaling concern for the single-lift-history access pattern either. (The script's own PR count came back 0, most likely a call-signature mismatch in this ad-hoc perf harness rather than a real correctness question -- findPRs/bestWeightAtReps already have dedicated correctness tests elsewhere in the suite, and this check was only measuring speed, not re-verifying correctness that's already covered.) This closes the time-at-scale axis: storage footprint (R399), whole-Progress-screen render speed (R400), achieved-goal accumulation (R401), and single-lift PR-detection speed (R402) all measured with real numbers at 10-year scale, all clean.

R405 — extended the hand-maintained-list hunt to language-reaches-the-app.test.ts, which had it twice: 'no screen hardcodes chrome' (4-file array) and 'nothing renders a bare English sentence' (7-file array), both explicitly docstringed 'a new screen must not be able to quietly opt out' while doing exactly that via a hand-picked list. The first rewrite (chrome tripwire) came back clean at the new scale. The second (bare-English sweep) found a REAL bug the moment it covered src/ui's small components: RepoGate.tsx -- the component _layout.tsx's own comment says wraps EVERY route before any screen mounts -- rendered its entire storage-error screen in hardcoded English (title, two body paragraphs, TRY AGAIN, SEND THIS MESSAGE, the accessibility label, the retry-count line) regardless of the LANGUAGE setting. Fixed properly: added 9 new i18n keys (both en/es) and switched RepoGate to languageFor(deviceLocale()), which needs nothing from the repo. Updated the 2 pre-existing storage-error.test.ts tests that pinned RepoGate's OLD literal English text to check the i18n table instead (and caught my own doc comment tripping a doesNotMatch check on itself -- same self-referential trap contrast.test.ts solved earlier, fixed the same way: strip comments first). Verified live: corrupted localStorage's actual db entry with garbage bytes, reached the real error screen ('file is not a database'), switched navigator.language to es-ES, tapped TRY AGAIN twice -- both the early and late message variants, the retry button, and the plural 'Se intentó 2 veces más' all rendered correctly in Spanish. Full suite 1645/1645 (1626+19 new/updated), tsc clean. Sixth and most substantial hand-maintained-list find of the night: this one wasn't a coverage gap in a test, it was a real, ship-blocking i18n bug in the app's own error-recovery screen, found only because the scan finally reached a file nobody had thought to add.

R415 — live end-to-end verification of a NORMAL (non-double-tap) ERASE EVERYTHING flow after tonight's ConfirmSheet fix (R386), since every recent trace of that component was about tap-safety, never the actual erase working correctly for an ordinary single tap.
