R488 -- §11's promise had a hole: data the app was holding that the user had no way to erase. `eraseAll` deletes sets, sessions, goals, custom exercises, measurements, measurement targets and every `pref.%` row — its own comment says of the last of those "their chosen jump amounts are theirs too" — and the control that invokes it was gated on `counts.sets > 0`. So somebody who set their units, recorded a bodyweight on YOU and invented a movement before ever logging a set had all three sitting in the database with **no control anywhere to remove them**, reachable only by logging a set first. §11 makes the export file the only backup and treats every one of those as the user's own; being able to destroy it is the other half of that promise. Gated on `erasureCounts` now — already the single place that decides what counts as erasable, and already what the confirmation sentence is built from, so the button and the sentence answer to one list and cannot disagree about whether there is anything there. Verified live in BOTH directions on the running app: loaded a database with 0 sets, 1 measurement, 1 preference and 1 custom exercise and the ERASE EVERYTHING control appeared, its dialog reading **"1 measurement, 1 custom exercise and 1 setting will be deleted from this device"** — correct categories, correct singulars, which is R480/R481 paying off; then cleared to a virgin install and confirmed the control is absent, because the first thing a new user sees on this screen must not be an offer to destroy nothing. **A second finding fell out of the first**: the same memo computed `sets`, `sessions` and `goals` on every render and, once the gate stopped reading `sets`, nothing read any of the three. Removed. New `test/erase-reachable.test.ts` covers a measurement-only, a preference-only and a custom-exercise-only install, keeps the untouched-install case as the guard, and pins the screen's gate at the source level. Proving it fails is worth reading carefully: reverting the gate fails only the two SOURCE tests while the three model tests stay green — because `erasureCounts` was always right and it was the gate that was wrong, so the model tests document the premise and the source tests are the ones that catch the regression. Suite 1810 green (6 new). | next: Measure's target sheet dates a 30-day "month", so "3 MO" can name a date two months out — the last of the R478 sweep's findings. After that the sweep is exhausted and the loop needs a fresh source of defects; the two owner-decidable items from R483 are still open (delete `lastSetOf` plus its unused `idx_sets_exercise_at`, and whether `db.ts` should adopt an async `openOnce` instead of keeping two copies of that rule).
R489 -- the last finding from the R478 sweep, and reading the code rather than accepting the report changed what the defect actually was. Measure's target sheet offers three chips — 3 MO, 6 MO, 12 MO — computed the date as `now + months * 30 * DAY`, and rendered it as a bare month NAME. Measured across a year of start dates: 3 MO names the wrong month on 20 of 365, 6 MO on 37, and **12 MO on 60** — a one-year bodyweight target set on 1 January displayed "Dec 2026", a month inside the year the lifter was still in. `targetDate` is SAVED, so that was the real deadline and the pace it drives, not merely a label. **The reframing matters**: the same nominal 30-day month lives in `goals-model.ts`'s `DAYS_PER`, with a comment explaining it is deliberate — and Goals is NOT broken, because it renders "90 days — 2 Dec 2026", so the nominal rule is disclosed and checkable (§16, which the comment there cites). The difference is disclosure, not arithmetic: Measure showed a chip that says MONTHS beside a month name with no day, so the two contradicted each other and nothing on the row could reconcile them. So the fix is scoped to Measure and states its boundary rather than drifting into it — new `monthsFrom` in measure-model.ts does real calendar months, clamped with `setDate(0)` so 31 January plus a month lands on 28/29 February instead of JavaScript's roll into March (that overflow is exactly why the nominal version was chosen originally, and the clamp is its answer), and the sheet now shows the DAY as well, the way the Goals sheet already does. New `test/measure-horizon.test.ts` sweeps all three chips across all 365 start dates in a year (1,095 cases, with `checked` asserted so it cannot pass having run nothing), pins the month-end clamp in both a leap and a non-leap year, checks the time of day survives so a deadline is not quietly moved, and — the important one — asserts **`DAYS_PER.months` is still 30**, so anybody "fixing" Goals to match would fail here and be made to read why, rather than silently changing the deadline on every goal already saved. Proved by reverting to the 30-day arithmetic: three of five fail, and the Goals guard keeps passing. Verified live on the running app with today at Thu Sep 3 2026: **12 MO now reads "Sep 3, 2027"**, and the old arithmetic computed in the same call for contrast reads **"Aug 2027"** — the wrong month, with no day to catch it. Suite 1815 green (5 new). | Two harness mistakes of my own, both the same shape — selecting by the wrong predicate. I picked the bodyweight input with `find(i => i.placeholder)` and got the NOTE field, which is the one that HAS a placeholder; the reading silently did not save and the screen still read "Not recorded yet". Targeted by `aria-label` instead. | next: **the R478 sweep is now exhausted** — every finding that survived checking has been fixed across R478-R489. The loop needs a fresh source of defects. The two owner-decidable items from R483 are still open (delete `lastSetOf` plus its unused `idx_sets_exercise_at`; whether `db.ts` should adopt an async `openOnce` rather than keep two copies of that rule), and HANDOFF's "Still open, needing a device or people" list is unchanged — the first EAS build, the Live Activity, §13's kill test, and the clip itself, which is the biggest remaining gap between spec and build.
R490 -- the R478 sweep is exhausted, so this round went looking for a fresh source and mostly found that the app is in good shape, which is worth writing down as plainly as a defect. Two things were tried. **First, a sweep for the shape that produced five of the last twelve defects**: prose asserting a fact that was true when written and quietly stopped being true (R220's "recap.js never reads heaviest", `lastSetOf`'s "the single hottest read in the app", `onChanged`'s doc comment, Spark's "pulled out once Measure needed it", R221's coverage claim). Grepped `src/` and `app/` for absolute claims in comments — "the only", "only place", "only caller", "no other", "nothing else" — and got 45 hits, most of them rationale rather than mechanically checkable. Verified the checkable ones by hand. `progress-model.ts`'s "`lastAt` is the only field the ORDER depends on" holds; `now-model.ts`'s "the only one that is LIVE" holds. **One was half false**: `locale.ts` says it is "the only file that touches a native module to obtain [a locale]" — still true, nothing else imports `expo-localization` — and then "Used solely to choose lb vs kg for a first-ever session (§8)", which is not: `RepoGate.tsx` reads it to pick the LANGUAGE of the database-error screen, deliberately, because that screen renders exactly when the stored preferences may be unreadable and its own comment says so. Corrected in place rather than deleted, naming both callers. A stale clause, not a defect — no user-visible consequence, and the honest yield of the sweep is one comment. **Second, walked journey E end to end on a genuinely cold install**, which is the loop's own designated unit of work and something this whole session had not done: cleared the database, chose PUSH/PULL/LEGS, chose PUSH, logged 135x8, 155x8 and 175x5, finished, read the recap, tapped SHARE. Everything correct. The running total read "3 sets 3,195 lb" and 135x8 + 155x8 + 175x5 is 3,195. The recap claimed SESSION ONE rather than a personal record, which is right — §8 forbids a PR in an exercise's first three sessions — and drew no streak cell, which is `streakWorthShowing` refusing a 1. SHARE failed soft with "Share is not supported in this browser" rather than throwing, which is the documented catch around `Share.share` for platforms with no sheet. **Rendered the recap and measured it**, since screenshots do not work here and I had not looked at a screen picture all session. The composition has a 186px void between the claim slab and the single lift row — on the first recap a user ever sees (§6's hook), where a first session has exactly one lift, so it is the common case rather than an edge one. Checked whether that is a regression before saying anything about it: it is not. `slackTop` is `flexGrow: 0.5` and `slack` is `flexGrow: 1`, so free space splits 1:2, and the measured 108px above / 186px between matches that. The comment records why — a SINGLE spacer put 380px in one gap and "reads as a broken card rather than a short workout" — and `test/recap-layout.test.ts` already pins the split, including the subtle trap that two ADJACENT spacers distribute nothing because real content has to sit between them. So the void is a considered trade with a measured rationale and a test, and changing it would be overruling a design decision on taste, which this project treats as the owner's call. Recorded for them with the numbers rather than acted on. Suite 1815 green, no code changed beyond the comment. | next: the loop has now fixed everything it can find without a fresh signal. Three sources remain, in order of likely yield: another defect sweep across dimensions the R478 one did NOT cover (it skipped performance, the goals screen, the rest timer, session lifecycle and the predictor entirely); the two owner-decidable items from R483 (delete `lastSetOf` plus its unused `idx_sets_exercise_at`; whether `db.ts` should adopt an async `openOnce` instead of two copies of that rule); and HANDOFF's device-or-people list, where the first EAS build is the real gate and the clip — §5's primary shareable, still unbuilt — is the biggest gap between spec and build.
R491 -- swept a dimension the R478 sweep never touched (the rest timer) and found the same fact R485 turned up about Progress, wearing different clothes. `NowScreen`'s rest clock is a `setInterval` whose effect depends on `[lastAt]` alone — and `lastAt` does not change when the workout ENDS, nor when another screen opens over this one, and NowScreen stays mounted through both. So the clock went on re-rendering the whole Now tree once a second behind the recap, which is the screen a lifter sits on longest after a workout, and behind Progress or Goals if they check either mid-session. **Measured rather than reasoned**: instrumented `setInterval`/`clearInterval` in the running app and counted live 1000ms timers through the real flow — log a set, one exists; tap FINISH, **still one**, with the recap on top. Worth recording how nearly I mismeasured this: I also counted TICKS either side, got 2 in 3.2s before and 0 in 4s after, and that comparison is worthless, because a hidden Browser pane throttles background timers (HANDOFF's own note: `setTimeout(240)` measured at 992ms). The registration count is a structural fact and survives the throttle; the tick rate does not. Nothing was ever WRONG on screen, which is why this survived: `restSince` is computed from the last set's timestamp and `Date.now()`, so it is correct whenever it renders. This is pure waste — but it is exactly the waste the effect's own comment was written to avoid ("doing it once a second would get slower the longer someone has used the app"), just aimed at the wrong half of the problem. Gated on focus with the codebase's own `useFocusEffect` idiom, one hook. **The existing tests caught the change and were right to** — three of them pinned the old shape exactly, including `}, [lastAt]);`. Updated rather than loosened, keeping each original reason: the "keyed on anything broader restarts the clock constantly" rule still holds, and `focused` satisfies it because it only moves when the screen is actually covered or uncovered, which is precisely when the interval should stop and start. Added a test for the new behaviour, including that the focus flag is both SET and RELEASED — a flag that is only ever set would make the gate permanently true and the whole thing vacuous. Verified live through the full cycle: set logged 1 interval, navigate to Progress 0, back to Now 1 with RESTING still on screen, FINISH 0. Suite 1816 green (1 new). | next: two more R478-uncovered dimensions are untouched — session lifecycle (`autoEnd`/`isStale`, the 90-minute idle rule, which has real edge cases around a phone left on a bench overnight) and the predictor (`rankExercises`/`recommendNext`). Performance is a third: this codebase has form there (48ms `rankGoals`, 45.6ms `allSets`) and nothing has re-measured since the goal cap went to 100. The two owner-decidable items from R483 also remain open.

R493 — the predictor had never been measured, only reasoned about, so I built the instrument before touching it: fourteen weeks of simulated routine (PPL / upper-lower / full-body × Mon-Wed-Fri, four-day and six-day schedules, with and without a 30% chance of a dropped or swapped accessory), walk-forward, predicting each of the last eight sessions from prior history only. Two results. First, `WEEKDAY_BOOST` is VALIDATED and load-bearing: with it, an aligned split predicts 100% of the day's lifts and 100% of its openers; with it off, the same histories score 0%. Where the split length does not divide the week it is neutral, not harmful. Second, and the defect: next-lift accuracy was **0%** on the very rows where the set prediction was flawless. `nextCandidates` widened the pool to `predictSession(..., 12)`, which on a three-day split spans the whole routine, and `predictSession` sorts its pool by `typicalPosition` — a WITHIN-session number. Compared across days it puts every day's OPENER at the front, so on push day, after Bench Press, the swipe target was SQUAT. Score already had it right: all five push lifts outscored every leg lift, and the widening discarded exactly that ordering. Fixed by keeping the predicted session at its natural size in position order, then appending everything else in SCORE order as overflow — the only ranking that means anything between days. Re-measured: 0% to 100% on aligned rows, 0% to 90-92% under jitter, 0% to 63% on full-body (which is its set-overlap ceiling, so it is now as good as the selection allows). Four new tests, three of which fail against the pre-fix function; one existing harness bug found and fixed in the writing of them — my Mon/Wed/Fri builder was actually laying sessions on Wed/Fri/Sun, which made even the control assertion fail. Suite 1824 green (4 new), tsc clean, driven live to confirm the rail still populates and the console is clean. | next: performance is the last unmeasured dimension named in R478 — 48ms `rankGoals` and 45.6ms `allSets` are the standing figures and nothing has re-measured since the goal cap went to 100. Also worth noting what this round did NOT change: `typicalPosition` averages over ALL history with no decay while the selection score decays on a 28-day half-life, so a lifter who moves a lift earlier in their session is ordered by where it used to sit. That asymmetry is real, measurable with the same instrument, and untested. The two owner-decidable items from R483 remain open.

R494 — performance, the last dimension R478 named, and the standing figures were stale in a way that mattered. Benchmarked the model layer against the database `tools/stress-web.ts` builds (14,000 sets, 700 sessions, 100 goals) rather than trusting the numbers in the comments. `listGoals` — the call carrying the bucketing optimisation and the 48ms comment — came in at 1.76ms. Its neighbours did not: `canAddGoal` 14.57ms and `goalLifts` 15.97ms, for what is nominally a cap check and a picker list. Both are almost entirely `activeGoals`, which asks `isAchieved` once per goal and handed each one the WHOLE history — the exact O(goals x sets) shape `rankGoals` was fixed for, in a function on far more paths: `canAddGoal`, `goalLifts`, `validateNewGoal` (twice per call) and `Repo.saveGoal`. The optimisation had been applied to the call that had the comment, not to the call that was slow. Fixed by bucketing the history by exercise once, identically to `rankGoals`, with the single-goal case left on the direct path so the common shape pays nothing for the index. Re-measured: `canAddGoal` 14.57 to 1.09ms, `goalLifts` 15.97 to 2.49ms. Four tests: equivalence in both directions, the cross-lift leak guard, a millisecond budget in house style, and — the real gate — a COUNTED one, because a timing budget proves a regression is absent on fast hardware whether or not the fix is there. It hands `activeGoals` a history whose iterator reports every element yielded and asserts the whole list is walked at most twice regardless of goal count; the quadratic version reads 100x higher. Both gates fail against the pre-fix function. Two of my own mistakes caught in the writing: the fixture had every goal on the same side of achieved, so the equivalence test would have proven nothing — caught only because I had asserted the fixture was mixed — and tsc rejected the counting iterator's type after `node --test` was already green, which is the R484 lesson landing again. Verified live: stress database loaded into the running app, Goals renders 89 open / 11 done at the cap with a clean console — and those counts ARE `activeGoals`' output, so the bucketed function is answering correctly on the real screen at full size. Suite 1828 green (4 new), tsc clean. | next: all three dimensions R478 named are now swept. Standing leads: the `typicalPosition` decay asymmetry flagged in R493 (ordering averages over all history while selection decays on a 28-day half-life — measurable with the walk-forward instrument, currently untested); `model.state()` at 8.36ms and `progressRows()` at 6.66ms are now the slowest things measured, both inside a frame but both worth a look before anything else is added to them; and the two owner-decidable items from R483.

R495 — `state()` was the slowest thing R494 left standing, and it is the one function on the logging path: it runs on every tap. Profiled it at 14,000 sets rather than guessing, and had to fix the instrument before believing it — the first version timed `repo.setsInSession(model.state().sessionId)`, which put a whole `state()` call inside the thing it was measuring and reported 5.78ms for a memoised read that actually costs 0.01ms. That is trap 10, self-inflicted. Corrected, the profile read: `state()` 5.93ms, `nextCandidates` 1.51ms, `weekStreak` 1.48ms, `pickerFor` 0.88ms. Then counted PASSES rather than milliseconds, with an iterator probe: one `state()` walks the entire history FOUR times — twice inside `nextCandidates`, once in `pickerFor`, once in `weekStreak` — and three of those four collapse the identical sets into the identical per-exercise occurrences, because every one of them reads the same memoised array. Fixed by caching that collapse on the array's identity, one entry, no clock in the key. The soundness argument is a property `Repo.allSets` already guarantees for its own unrelated reason: the array it returns is FROZEN and every write drops the memo, so identity changes exactly when the contents could have — the cache cannot go stale without the caller holding a different object. Re-measured: `state()` 5.93 to 3.98ms, `rankExercises` 0.64 to 0.05ms, four walks down to one. Six tests, five of them about invalidation rather than speed — a longer history, an array appended to in place, two histories interleaved through a one-entry cache, the clock still decaying scores (the collapse is cached, the SCORE must never be), and a caller mutating what it was handed. The sixth is the gate, and the only one that fails without the fix: it counts what the collapse reads and asserts five reads of one history walk it once. Verified live on the stress database — three sets logged into a 14,000-set history, the running total and the rail both updating correctly to PULL DAY with Lat Pulldown next, which is the invalidation working on the real screen. Suite 1834 green (6 new), tsc clean. | next: `weekStreak` at 1.48ms is now the largest single cost in `state()` and is a fifth full walk that could ride the same collapse, though its buckets are weeks not exercises so it needs its own. `progressRows()` is 6.66ms but off the logging path. Also found while reading: `now-model.ts` around line 1098 carries a long comment describing the very defect R493 fixed at the source — every day's opener has position 0 — and the `onThisDay` workaround built on top of it. The workaround is still doing separate work and should stay, but the prose now describes the world before last round, which is exactly the pattern this log keeps catching. The R493 `typicalPosition` decay asymmetry and the two R483 owner-decidable items remain open.

R496 — followed R495's parting note about stale prose in `now-model.ts` and found a live defect underneath it, not a comment problem. `onThisDay` filters the UP NEXT candidates with `dayOf(id) === day`, where `day` is a push/pull/legs `SplitDay`. That is exactly right for a PPL lifter and a category error for UPPER/LOWER — a split the app offers in its own picker — because `DAY_OF` files bench under push and row under pull, which are the SAME day on that plan. Measured on fourteen weeks of an upper/lower routine: the lifter benches, `nextCandidates` returns ROW first off their own history, and UP NEXT showed OHP, because the filter walked past row looking for something filed as push. The app knew what they do and recommended something else. Two wrong turns before the right fix, both caught by the existing suite rather than by me: I first tried trusting the predicted session outright, which broke three §7 tests because a lifter is free to depart from the weekday prediction and then the "next lift of your routine" is the next lift of a routine they are not having; then I tried requiring an overlap between the predicted session and what they had trained, which still failed because with a small library the top-5 by score spans two days and bench and squat both sit in it. The actual fix was already in the codebase: `planDay` is computed three lines above, `inPlanDay` exists for precisely this comparison, and `sessionPlanDay` carries the same written argument about why the push/pull/legs level is the wrong one to count at for a lifter whose day spans two of them. This was the one place still asking the narrower question. For PPL the plan day IS the split day, so nothing about that case moves — which is why the §7 suite passes unchanged, and is stated as its own test. Three new tests; the first fails against the pre-fix line. Verified live: seeded a fourteen-week upper/lower history into the running app, chose UPPER, logged a bench set, and the rail reads NEXT ON UPPER DAY / Barbell Row. Suite 1837 green (3 new), tsc clean. Tidied up after the last two rounds: removed the ad-hoc seed I generated and added `public/stress.b64` to .gitignore, since a committed tool generates it and it is a 3 MB binary. | next: `weekStreak` at 1.48ms is the largest remaining cost in `state()` and the one full history walk the R495 cache does not cover — its buckets are weeks, not exercises, so it needs its own. `progressRows()` at 6.66ms is larger but off the logging path. The R493 `typicalPosition` decay asymmetry is still untested, and the two R483 owner-decidable items are still open. Worth noting the shape of this round for the next one: R493 fixed a defect in the domain, and the UI still carried a workaround for it written in the pre-R493 world. That workaround turned out to be independently wrong. It is worth asking, whenever a domain fix lands, what the screens were already doing to compensate.

R497 — took R496's closing lesson as an instruction and swept for the same question asked at the wrong level, rather than waiting to trip over it again. Grepped every `dayOf(` outside `split.ts`: four callers, and the answer was informative in both directions. `now-model.ts:1496` — the day RAIL — already used `inPlanDay` and was already right, which means before R496 the Now screen was internally contradictory: the rail said NEXT ON UPPER DAY and listed Barbell Row while UP NEXT, six lines away, pointed at Overhead Press. The fourth caller was a second live defect. `goal-filters.ts` hardcoded `GOAL_FILTERS = ['open', 'push', 'pull', 'legs', 'done']` for every lifter: an UPPER/LOWER lifter got chips for days they do not have, and a FULL BODY lifter got three chips that all mean the same thing to them. Worse than cosmetic, because the counts come from the same filter — a chip could read PULL 9 to somebody whose every session is an upper day, and the chips for the days they DO have did not exist. Fixed by deriving the chips from `PLAN_DAYS[plan]` and filtering with `inPlanDay`, so chips and counts are one decision; `filterCounts` now takes the plan for the same reason. `FILTER_KEY` gained the three plan-day words, reusing exactly the keys `DAY_KEY` already uses so a chip and the Now rail cannot name one day two ways. Six tests, five of which fail against the pre-fix constant, and the sixth pins that PPL — the plan this always worked for — is unchanged. Verified live: fourteen weeks of upper/lower plus six goals seeded into the running app, Goals reads OPEN 6 / UPPER 4 / LOWER 2 / DONE 0, and tapping UPPER lists the bench, the row and the pulldown together, which is the whole argument in one screenshot. Suite 1843 green (6 new), tsc clean; scratch seed removed. | next: `weekStreak` at 1.48ms is still the one full history walk the R495 cache does not cover. The R493 `typicalPosition` decay asymmetry is still untested. And the sweep above is worth repeating for the OTHER thing R496 taught: `sessionDay` (the SplitDay-level function) still has callers alongside `sessionPlanDay`, and it is worth checking which of those genuinely want the narrow question. The two R483 owner-decidable items remain open.

R498 — followed R497's own next-line and swept `sessionDay` against `sessionPlanDay`. One caller left, and it was wrong in the way the codebase had already written down. `now-model` computed the day it SHOWS the lifter as `planDayFor(sessionDay(trained, ...), plan)` — tally in push/pull/legs, then translate — while `sessionTitle`, on the recap, has always called `sessionPlanDay` and tallies in the lifter's own vocabulary. Those are not the same function of the same input, and `sessionPlanDay`'s own comment says exactly why: an upper/lower lifter's upper day is push AND pull, so bench + row + squat splits two upper votes across two buckets, reads as a 1-1-1 tie, and the tie-break then sends the answer to whichever lift they happen to be standing on. Counted where the lifter actually lives it is 2 upper against 1 lower and not a tie at all. Enumerated the disagreement rather than reasoning about it: five session shapes across two plans, one differed — bench + row + squat, standing on the squat. Fixed by calling `sessionPlanDay` directly; `day` stays a `SplitDay` because `groupBySplit` and `companionFor` still want the narrow question, and only the day shown to the lifter moves. `planDayFor` left the file entirely, orphan-scan clean. Four tests: the two surfaces agree, the majority answer is the one given, a day the user CHOSE still wins over inference (§4 unchanged), and PPL is unaffected — two fail against the pre-fix line. Verified live on the real screen, both directions: seeded a live upper/lower session already holding bench, row and squat with the lifter standing on Squat, and the rail heading reads NEXT ON UPPER DAY; reverted the one line in place and the same screen reads NEXT ON LOWER DAY. Suite 1847 green (4 new), tsc clean, scratch seed removed. | next: three rounds of the same defect class are now closed (UP NEXT R496, the Goals chips R497, the day heading R498) and the sweep that found them is exhausted — every `dayOf`/`sessionDay` caller outside `split.ts` has been checked. Remaining leads unchanged: `weekStreak` at 1.48ms is the one full history walk R495's cache does not cover, the R493 `typicalPosition` decay asymmetry is untested, and the two R483 owner-decidable items are open. Worth recording the pattern that produced three rounds: the codebase had ALREADY written the correct argument down, in `sessionPlanDay`'s docstring, and three call sites had not been migrated to it. A written-down rule with unmigrated callers is a reliable place to find live defects.

R499 — took the R493 lead that had been sitting in the next-line for six rounds: `typicalPosition` had no decay while the score it sits beside had a 28-day half-life. Measured rather than argued, with a fixture that holds the LIFTS fixed and reverses only their order, so selection cannot mask or explain the answer: the predictor never adapted. Fifty-three days after a lifter reordered their session it still opened on the lift they had moved to last. Then measured the recovery time, which is the part that makes it a defect and not a preference — four weeks of the old order took 35 days to displace, ten weeks took 77, twenty weeks took 147. The lag is proportional to how long the person has used the app, which is precisely the failure `predict.ts`'s own opening docstring says the decay exists to prevent: "a predictor that merely counted would get worse the longer someone used the app, which is the failure mode that matters most because it only hits the users who stayed." That argument was written down, applied to which lifts get picked, and never applied to the order they are offered in — a plain unweighted count-mean left in the middle of the loop that computes the decay one line above it. Fixed by weighting the position sum with the decay already in hand. Deliberately WITHOUT `WEEKDAY_BOOST`: the boost answers "is this lift part of today", a selection question, and where a lift sits inside a session is not something a Wednesday knows better than a Friday. The same three cases now take 21, 28 and 35 days — bounded, and no longer a function of history size. Five tests: the month-old reorder is adopted, the wait does not grow with history (the defect in one assertion, 4/10/20 weeks all adapted by eight), one odd session does NOT rewrite ten weeks of routine (adaptive is not credulous), a steady lifter sees no change at all, and the weekday boost stays out of the position weights. Two fail against the pre-fix line; the other three are guards that must stay green in both worlds, and do. Verified live as an A/B on the real screen with one database: a seeded lifter who reordered their leg day four weeks ago opens on CALF RAISE with the fix and on SQUAT with the line reverted in place. Suite 1852 green (5 new), tsc clean, orphan-scan unchanged, scratch seed removed. Two things worth recording honestly rather than tidying away. First, a cost: on the jittered synthetic histories the next-lift figure moved 92% to 91% in one cell of thirty-six, and that is the expected price — the jitter is NOISE, so a predictor that tracks recent sessions more closely also tracks recent noise more closely. Every unjittered cell is byte-identical, which is the right shape for this change. Second, my own gate was worthless on the first attempt and I nearly shipped on it: the revert script matched a CRLF string against an LF file, silently changed nothing, and reported the tests "passing without the fix" — which I read as the fix being unnecessary rather than as the instrument being broken. It was broken because an earlier edit in this same round had inserted a CRLF comment block into an LF file. Trap 10 arriving through trap 7. | next: `weekStreak` at 1.48ms is still the one full history walk the R495 cache does not cover, and is now the oldest untouched lead. One full-suite run in this round reported a single failure I could not identify before it went green, and four consecutive clean runs since have not reproduced it — worth catching the name next time it appears rather than re-running until it passes. The two R483 owner-decidable items are still open.

R500 — first round under AGENT_LOOP.md (ideate → build → review → ship). IDEATE shortlist, written before building: (a) `weekStreak` at 1.48ms, rejected as an instance fix nobody can perceive; (b) re-open R499's unidentified one-off suite failure, kept as a live lead but not reproducible on demand; (c) the ship gate's test glob; (d) exported-but-uncalled helpers, already covered by orphan-scan. Picked (c). It began as a wrong idea and survived being checked, which is the only reason it is worth the entry: I suspected `npm test` (`test/*.test.ts`) was already skipping files that my own `test/**/*.test.ts` runs were catching, which would have invalidated seven rounds of evidence. It was not — both globs find the same 123 files, no subdirectory tests exist, and I retract that. What is real is the SHAPE: the pattern is hand-maintained and stops at one level, so the hole opens the first time anybody groups files into `test/ui/`. Demonstrated rather than argued, per the doc's preference for a defect you can drive: planted `test/sub/canary.test.ts` containing `assert.equal(1, 2)` and ran the real ship command — 1852 passed, 0 failed, EXIT CODE 0. A deliberately failing test could not fail the build. This is the worst class of defect this repo can hold because it is not wrong about the product, it is wrong about the EVIDENCE, and every round's "suite green" is an inference from that one command. BUILD: pattern widened to `test/**/*.test.ts`, plus a new gate that derives its population from the DISK — walks the tree and requires every `.test.ts` found to be somewhere the configured glob reaches — rather than asserting the script equals an expected string, which would pass happily while the hole reopened underneath it (HANDOFF #13's rule: derive it from source, never hand-maintain the list). Three tests, one of them a guard on the instrument itself, since an empty walk or an unreadable script line would make the other two vacuous. REVIEW: planted the original narrow glob back with the canary in place and both real tests failed BY NAME, on different grounds — the pattern check catches the latent hole, the disk check catches an actually-missed file — then restored and re-ran clean. Two self-inflicted errors on the way, both caught: I first wrote raw double quotes into package.json and broke it as JSON (npm error EJSONPARSE), then repaired it with `json.dumps` and silently escaped every em-dash in the file to `—`; re-read the file rather than trusting the edit, and rewrote with ensure_ascii=False. Worth naming because fitness-app is UNTRACKED inside the home repo — there is no git history to recover from, so an unnoticed reformat is permanent. SHIP: `npm test` → 1855 pass / 0 fail, exit 0; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current". `node link/build.cjs` NOT run and not required — nothing under link/ or the share path changed this round; saying so rather than skipping it silently. The shipped-build check for this round is the exit code itself, driven in both directions, because the change lives in the gate and not in the product: no app source was touched and the product is byte-for-byte unaffected. | next: the R499 phantom failure is now the strongest open lead, and this round is a direct argument for taking it seriously rather than re-running until green. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms and the two R483 owner-decidable items remain.

R501 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) hunt clock-dependent tests, (b) `weekStreak` perf, (c) audit check-deps.cjs's allowlist since each exemption is an unverified claim, (d) sweep "fixed X" comments. Picked (a) to chase R500's own next-line — R499's single unreproducible suite failure — because the loop doc rates a re-opened "known flake" verdict as wrong about half the time. (a) died honestly: four tests mention `Date.now()`, three of them only in prose or in a source assertion, and the fourth (`cry-wolf.test.ts`) anchors a fixture to the wall clock but feeds it to `findPRs`, which never reads an absolute time — `at` only orders sets. Retracted. The next hypothesis was the productive one: `npm test` runs the suite as ~120 SEPARATE PROCESSES, so shared filesystem state is the obvious candidate, and `bundle-parity.test.ts` rewrites `dist/proof-domain.js` — the real shipped artifact — twice, while `card-sheet-is-hard.test.ts` `require`s that exact file at load time from another process. `writeFileSync` truncates before it writes. Measured rather than argued: hammering 400 rewrites while a second process read the path, 39 of 50 reads saw ZERO bytes instead of 160,188. The window is not narrow, it is most of the write, and a require landing in it loads a module with no exports. That is a sufficient mechanism for the phantom, found two rounds after I logged it as unexplained and one round after I said re-running until green was the wrong response. BUILD: `build-domain.cjs` now writes to a pid-named temp file and renames, and `bundle-parity`'s two writes do the same through a local `swap()`. REVIEW is where this round earned its keep, three times. First, the review caught a defect in MY OWN FIX: on Windows `renameSync` onto a path another process currently holds open fails with EPERM — and a concurrent reader is precisely the case the rename exists to protect, so the two collide by construction. Unretried, the fix would have traded a rare torn read for an outright build crash. Both sites now retry on EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY with a short delay; the first retry loop had no delay and still threw, because 200 instant attempts all land inside one open handle. Second, the review caught a worse design error: the first version of the new test raced the REAL dist/proof-domain.js, including a control that wrote it non-atomically on purpose — which would have caused the exact failure it exists to explain, in every other test process, on every run. It now races a copy in a temp dir; the claim is about the technique, so the technique is what gets raced, and a separate source-level check pins that the build actually uses it. Third, the instrument guards fired twice and stopped two vacuous passes: a `SIGTERM` handler that never runs on Windows (child died with empty stdout), and a wall-clock read budget that expired after exactly one batch because the writer starves the reader. Both are recorded in the file next to the code that works around them. Tests: three, with the positive control as a permanent proof that the probe can still SEE tearing — if it ever stops finding short reads, the real assertion beneath it is passing for free. Planting the pre-fix direct write back fails the build check by name; the two race tests stay green, which is the intended split. Tuned down from 22s to ~4s because it runs on every commit. SHIP: `npm test` → 1858 pass / 0 fail, exit 0 (suite 7.6s → 11.5s, the cost of the race); `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `node link/build.cjs` not required, nothing under link/ or the share path changed. | next: R499's phantom now has a mechanism but NOT a confirmed identity — I never saw which test failed, and `card-sheet-is-hard` is only the most likely candidate, so this is "sufficient cause found", not "closed". If a one-off ever appears again, capture the name. Two general leads this round argues for: the suite mutates real artifacts in at least one other place (`screen-render.test.ts` also writes files) and that deserves the same look, and shared mutable state across ~120 concurrent processes is a class nobody has swept. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms and the two R483 owner-decidable items remain.

R502 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) a NUL byte in R500's own new test file, (b) sweep the other tests that mutate real artifacts (`screen-render.test.ts`), the class R501 opened, (c) `weekStreak` perf, (d) audit check-deps.cjs's allowlist. Picked (a): a demonstrable defect sitting in the working tree, and mine. Found by accident and worth recording how, because the finder was not a test: a routine `grep -rln` for leftover canary strings answered "Binary file test/every-test-file-runs.test.ts matches". That file is TypeScript. R500's glob-to-regexp parks `**/` under a placeholder while the lone `*` is expanded, so the second replace cannot chew through the first one's output, and the placeholder had been written as a raw control character — two 0x00 bytes at offsets 3257 and 3308. It WORKED, which is the problem: NUL is a legal string character and no path contains one, so every test passed and will keep passing, while the file is binary to grep, to diff, and to every review tool a person or a hook would use on it. An invisible byte is not something a reader can check. Replaced with a named `__GLOBSTAR__` token, equally safe and readable, and while writing the comment for it I caught a second latent bug in the same three lines: `.replace(token, ...)` with a STRING argument replaces only the first occurrence, so a pattern containing two `**/` would have left a live token in the compiled regexp. Now `.replaceAll`. Nothing in the current pattern has two, so no test would ever have caught that — it is the kind of thing only re-reading the edit finds, which is the review step the loop doc asks for by name. REVIEW: control-byte count 0; planted the pre-R500 narrow glob back with a canary in a subdirectory and both gate tests failed BY NAME alongside the planted test (1856 pass / 3 fail); restored and confirmed package.json byte-identical to the R500 restore by sha (8a0b3fabc3125925), canary directory gone. SHIP: `npm test` → 1858 pass / 0 fail, exit 0; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `node link/build.cjs` not required, nothing under link/ or the share path changed. Product check, stated honestly rather than dressed up: R500 through R502 touch gates only and the app is byte-for-byte unaffected, so there is no product change to see. What was verified in the running app instead is that it still starts clean — loaded localhost:8099, correct §6 cold start (empty database after R499's seed was removed), BENCH PRESS / "First time" / the split picker, and ZERO console errors. R499 remains the last round with a product-visible change, and it was A/B'd live at the time. | next: (b) from this round's shortlist is now the strongest lead and inherits R501's argument — `screen-render.test.ts` also writes files, and shared mutable state across ~120 concurrent test processes is a class nobody has swept. Two smaller ones fall out of THIS round: the same placeholder trick may exist elsewhere (worth a control-byte scan across the whole repo, since a scan is cheap and the failure is invisible), and `.replace` with a string argument where `.replaceAll` was meant is a one-line grep. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms and the two R483 owner-decidable items remain.

R503 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) a repo-wide control-byte scan, since R502's defect is invisible by construction and a scan is cheap, (b) `.replace` where `.replaceAll` was meant, (c) `screen-render.test.ts`'s real-artifact writes, (d) `weekStreak`. Took (a) as the sweep, and it found something considerably worse than what R502 fixed. One file in the whole repo carries control bytes: `test/recap-layout.test.ts`, two 0x08s. The assertion reads `doesNotMatch(block, /PERSONAL RECORD|\bPR\b/)` — a first-session recap must never say either — and the `\b` had collapsed into a literal BACKSPACE, so the second alternative was `<BS>PR<BS>`, a pattern matching a control character that occurs in no rendered text and no source file. Half of that assertion had never been evaluated, in any run, ever. Proven in BOTH directions rather than asserted: planting `// PR planted` into recap.tsx's first-session block, the backspace version passes 32 of 32 and the `\b` version fails by name on the right test. The product itself is clean — with the boundary restored and nothing planted, the suite is green — so what was broken was never the app, it was the check, which is the failure mode that leaves no trace anywhere else. BUILD: restored the escape, then wrote the class gate rather than stopping at the instance. It walks app/ from disk (skipping node_modules, dist, build output) and rejects any control character outside tab, newline and carriage return, on the reasoning that every one of them can be written as an escape and a byte a reviewer cannot see is a byte nobody is reviewing. Derived, not a list of known offenders — R500's NUL and this 0x08 were found by two different accidents, and the third instance will not announce itself either. Guarded on its own instrument: an empty walk would pass for free, so the file count is asserted first. REVIEW: planted a 0x08 into `src/domain/predict.ts` and the gate failed by name; restored, sha c6b82d6ef4028ff3; `recap.tsx` restored to b82adcec8f6756cc after the two plant-and-check cycles. SHIP: `npm test` → 1860 pass / 0 fail, exit 0; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `node link/build.cjs` not required, nothing under link/ or the share path changed. No product change this round either — the app is untouched; this fixes what the suite can SEE, which is the same category as R500 and R502. | next: worth naming that three consecutive rounds have all found defects in the EVIDENCE rather than in the product (R500 a gate that could not see a failing test, R502 an invisible byte, R503 an assertion that had never run), which suggests the instruments deserve at least as much suspicion as the code for a while longer. Immediate leads: (b) from this shortlist is still untouched and is a one-line grep; (c) `screen-render.test.ts` writes real files and inherits R501's argument about ~120 concurrent processes; and the same collapse hazard applies to any regexp built from a heredoc, so a scan for suspicious single-letter escapes (`\s`, `\d`, `\w`, `\b`) that survived as literals is the natural follow-on to this gate. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms and the two R483 owner-decidable items remain.

R504 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) `.replace` with a string argument where `.replaceAll` was meant, the second bug R502 found in its own three lines and never swept; (b) `screen-render.test.ts`'s real-artifact writes; (c) `weekStreak` at 1.48ms; (d) the two R483 items, which are owner-only and get filed rather than decided. Picked (a). Four call sites in the whole repo, and the honest answer for three of them is that they are safe by construction — a URL protocol has one colon, a URL has one fragment. The fourth is on the SHIP path: `link/build.cjs` rewrites `../spike/recap.js` to `./recap.js` as the landing page is copied into a self-contained dist/, and it did that with a string `replace`, which rewrites the first occurrence and no others. What made this look safe is a guard that is genuinely there and genuinely insufficient: the build already refuses a rewrite that matched NOTHING. It cannot see the other failure. Add a second `<script src="../spike/recap.js">` and the build reports success while deploying a page whose script path does not exist inside dist/ — a 404 on the one page the product exists to share, with a green build. There is exactly one occurrence today, which is the reason nobody would catch the day there are two. BUILD: `replaceAll`, plus a check that does not depend on counting anything — dist/ is self-contained, therefore no `src`/`href` in it may point outside itself, which is wider than the single path this build knows how to rewrite and will stop a NEW asset added with a parent-relative href rather than deploying a broken link. REVIEW: three tests driving the real build script, because the claim is about what deploys. Planting the string `replace` back fails the two-reference test by name. Two corrections along the way, both mine: my first count assertion expected two occurrences of `./recap.js` in the built page and got three, because the page names `./recap.js` in a COMMENT explaining this very rewrite — the assertion failed on the fix rather than on the bug, and now counts `src="./recap.js"` specifically. Then I restored `link/build.cjs` from a backup taken BEFORE the round's own edit, silently reverting the fix while the tests still sat there passing from the previous run; caught it by checking the invariant string was present rather than trusting the copy, and re-applied. That is the second time in three rounds that verifying a restore, instead of assuming it, was what saved the round. SHIP: `npm test` → 1863 pass / 0 fail, exit 0; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `node link/build.cjs` → "dist/ ready", REQUIRED this round because link/ changed. Confirmed in the built product rather than the source: every `src="./…"` in link/dist/index.html resolves to a file that exists in dist/ (recap.js, share-url.js, copy.js all present), and the deployed page contains zero parent-relative paths. | next: (b) `screen-render.test.ts` writes real files and still inherits R501's argument about ~120 concurrent processes — it is now the oldest untouched lead from that class. The wider version of THIS round is also open: `link/build.cjs` is one of several build scripts, and none of the others has been checked for a transform whose guard only catches the zero case. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms remains, and the two R483 owner-decidable items are filed and still owner-only.

R505 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) `screen-render.test.ts`'s real-artifact writes, R501's oldest open lead; (b) the wider version of R504 — other build scripts with a transform whose guard only catches the zero case; (c) `weekStreak`; (d) R483's owner-only items, filed not decided. Took (a) first and RETRACTED it: the inputs go to `mkdtempSync`, the outputs land in `app/out/` under names that do not collide with `card-sheet.test.ts`'s, and `out/` is gitignored so nothing leaks into what ships. A real answer, just not a defect. Moved to (b), which paid. `build-domain.cjs` collects each module's exports with a regexp that understands exactly ONE shape, `export const|let|function|class NAME`, and takes one name from it. That is every export in the eight bundled modules today, so the bundler is correct today; what makes it worth a gate is how it fails when that stops being true. `export const A = 1, B = 2;` strips to a valid `const A = 1, B = 2`, the bundle builds, runs, and PASSES ITS OWN "do the exports load" check — because that check only verifies the exports it managed to collect. B is never published, and the harness gets `undefined` for it somewhere far from the cause. `export async function`, `export default` and `export *` fail the same way from other directions. The existing guard cannot see any of it: it only asks whether the rewrite matched nothing, which is R504's finding in a second build script. BUILD: the bundler now asks the opposite question — is there an export here I did not account for — and refuses to build, naming the file and the line. Plus `topLevelComma`, depth-aware because a comma inside `= { a, b }` is not a second declarator. One false positive on the way, and the fix for it is the interesting part: the scan ran on the TypeScript source and tripped on `export const MIN_INCREMENT: Record<Unit, number>`, whose comma sits inside a generic my bracket-counter does not track. Rather than teach it TypeScript, the scan moved to run on the type-STRIPPED output, where annotations are already gone and `export type`/`export interface` have already been erased — narrower code and a stronger check. `SRC` and `OUT` are now overridable by env var, purely so the gate can be exercised against a temp copy of the module tree instead of editing real sources while ~120 test processes read them, which is the defect R501 spent a round removing. REVIEW: six tests, including a control that an untouched copy still builds (without it, every other assertion could be passing because the override is broken) and a test that a type-only export is still allowed through (the half a careless gate gets wrong, rejecting every module in the tree). Two bad plants before a good one, both caught: a stray `open('/dev/null')` crashed the plant script BEFORE it wrote, so the suite ran green against the FIXED build and proved nothing; then cutting the gate out by line range also removed the export-stripping replaces that sit between it and `const prologue`, breaking the build entirely — the control test caught that, which is exactly what it is for. The good plant disables only the gate's two branches, and then precisely the three gate tests fail by name while the control, the type-only test and the real-bundle check stay green. SHIP: `npm test` → 1869 pass / 0 fail, exit 0; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `node link/build.cjs` not required, link/ unchanged. Confirmed in the built artifact by loading it: 91 names published, R499's decay-weighted position present in the shipped bytes. One correction to my own check while doing that — I first reported "1 export" and that was my harness being wrong, not the bundle: it publishes a single `Domain` namespace, and 91 names sit inside it. | next: loading the shipped bundle turned up a LIVE defect that is not this round's and gets its own — `Domain.sessionTitle` throws `TypeError: sessionPlanDay is not a function`, because `split.ts` is not in MODULES while `session.ts` imports from it. This round's gate guards the EXPORT side; nothing checks that every imported name resolves. Taking it next. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms remains, and the two R483 items stay owner-only.

R506 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) the live crash R505 found while loading the shipped bundle; (b) the class behind it, that nothing checks whether an imported name resolves; (c) `weekStreak`; (d) R483, owner-only. Took (a) AND (b) together, because fixing the instance alone leaves the next missing module exactly as silent. The defect: `session.ts` imports `sessionPlanDay` from `split.ts`, and `split.ts` was not in the bundler's MODULES list at all. Each module's imports are destructured out of the shared registry when its IIFE runs, so the name came out `undefined` and `Domain.sessionTitle` threw `sessionPlanDay is not a function` for anyone who called it. Sized honestly before fixing: exactly one unresolved name in the whole bundle, and nothing in spike/, harness/ or link/ calls `sessionTitle` today — so this was a shipped function that throws when called, not a crash anybody had hit. Latent, but on the artifact the harness runs. Why nothing caught it is the part worth keeping: the build DOES verify itself, loading the bundle in a bare scope and confirming every export is present — but it walks a HAND-WRITTEN list of 28 names and it asks only about exports. An import resolving to nothing is invisible to that question: the module loads, the export publishes, and the hole appears only on the call. The suite was green throughout too, because `session.ts` is tested directly, where the real import resolves normally. Only the bundle was broken, and only by loading the built file and CALLING things in it does that show. BUILD: `split.ts` added to MODULES before `session.ts` (order matters, and now says so in a comment), plus a derived gate — every name a module imports must already be published by a module EARLIER in the list, checked from the sources on both sides so adding or reordering a module needs no edit here. REVIEW: proved the gate catches both failure shapes, naming file and symbol — split.ts absent, and split.ts present but listed after session.ts. Four tests, run against the BUILT artifact rather than src, which is the whole point; rebuilding a deliberately broken bundle fails three of them by name while the instrument guard stays green. One correction to myself mid-round: I first reported `sessionTitle` still throwing after the fix, and that was my own call signature — it takes (sets, lang, plan) and I had passed the plan as the second argument; `upper-lower`, not `ul`, is also the real plan key. SHIP: `npm test` → 1873 pass / 0 fail, exit 0; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `node link/build.cjs` → "dist/ ready". Confirmed in the built product by loading it and calling through it: 108 names published (up from 91, since split.ts now contributes), `sessionTitle(bench+row, en, upper-lower)` returns UPPER DAY, and zero unresolved imports. | next: the `EXPORTS` list in build-domain.cjs is still hand-maintained — 28 names checked out of 108 published, and the doc's own rule says derive it rather than keep it. That is the direct follow-on and it is now the oldest instance of that rule being broken in this file. Worth noting three rounds running that the SHIP step, not the suite, is what found the defect: R504 and R506 were both invisible to 1800-plus green tests because the tests exercise src/ and the product is the bundle. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms remains; the two R483 items stay owner-only and are filed, not decided.

R507 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) the hand-maintained `EXPORTS` list in build-domain.cjs, R506's direct follow-on; (b) other consumers of the bundle that call names no test exercises; (c) `weekStreak`; (d) R483, owner-only. Picked (a), and measuring it first changed what the round was about. The list is not merely stale, it is wrong in BOTH directions at once: the bundle publishes 108 names so it verified a quarter of them, and the harness — the only consumer of this artifact that exists — calls exactly TWO, so it was not a contract either. A list that is neither complete nor accurate still reports success, which is exactly how R506's broken bundle passed this very step while `Domain.sessionTitle` threw on the first call. BUILD: both questions now asked of the sources instead of a memory. COMPLETENESS — every name the bundler collected while parsing the modules must survive into the registry, which is the thing the string surgery can actually get wrong, now covering all 108. CONTRACT — what the harness needs is read out of the harness, so adding a `Domain.foo` call there makes the next build check for it with nothing here to update. The old list was deleted rather than lengthened; a longer list is the same defect with a later expiry date. Backup at ~/bd507.keep per the standing rule. REVIEW is where most of this round went, and three of the four problems were mine. First, my "a collected export that fails to publish stops the build" test PASSED for the wrong reason: it planted `export const` inside an `if` block, which is a SyntaxError, so the build died in the type stripper before the completeness check ever ran — a non-zero exit proving nothing about the thing under test. Replaced with `export let X;`, which is genuinely collected and genuinely lands as undefined, and the assertion now matches the check's OWN message rather than the exit code. Second, an existing test (`harness-loads`) broke, and correctly: it grepped build-domain.cjs for each harness-called name inside the array I had just deleted. The guarantee did not disappear, it got stronger, so that test now asks the ARTIFACT whether it publishes those names instead of grepping a source file for a quoted string. While fixing it I found my own build change was NARROWER than what it replaced — that test scanned harness/clip.js and encode.js as well as index.html, and I had read only the page. Widened to every harness file the repo owns, excluding the vendored muxer. Narrowing a check silently while calling it a refactor is the failure this round exists to stop, and I nearly committed it inside the fix for it. Third, my own new test ran the REAL `node build-domain.cjs` with no overrides, rewriting the shipped bundle while ~120 test processes read and mutate it: it passed alone and failed in the full suite, which is R501's defect reintroduced by me. A test for a build must not BE a build of the product; it now builds in a temp sandbox like the others. Planting the hand-written list back fails all four tests by name. SHIP: `npm test` → 1877 pass / 0 fail, exit 0, and three consecutive clean runs because two of this round's failures were order-dependent; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `node link/build.cjs` → "dist/ ready". Confirmed in the built artifact: 108 names published, both harness-called names present as functions, zero unresolved imports. | next: the build now reports "verified all 108 collected exports load... and the 2 the harness calls", which makes a real question visible that the old list was hiding — 106 of the 108 published names have NO consumer outside the app's own src/, where they are imported directly rather than through the bundle. That is either dead weight in a 168 kB artifact the harness downloads, or a contract nobody has written down; worth measuring before assuming either. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms remains, and the two R483 items stay owner-only, filed not decided.

R508 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) the 106 published-but-unconsumed bundle names R507's new output exposed; (b) `weekStreak`; (c) whether the harness's entry points are exercised through the bundle at all; (d) R483, owner-only. Started on (a) and it split cleanly into an owner decision and a defect, which is the useful outcome. MEASURED, then FILED, not decided: the harness's transitive closure is six modules — types, i18n, measure, pr, split, session — so `predict.ts`, `goals.ts` and `coldstart.ts` are bundled and unreachable from any consumer. Building without them still verifies and still meets the harness contract, at 125,452 bytes against 173,412: about 48 kB, 28% off an artifact the harness downloads. Whether this bundle is harness-only or a general domain artifact for spike/ and link/ is a scope decision about the product, so it is filed here with the number attached and NOT acted on. Then (c), which I expected to be the gap and was not: `bundle-parity.test.ts` already calls `D.buildRecap` and `D.findPRs` through the bundle and compares byte for byte against source. Good to have checked rather than built a duplicate. What that reading DID turn up is the round's actual defect, and it is the third hand-written list in three rounds: parity's first test is titled "the bundle exposes everything the harness needs" and checks seven names — the harness needs two of them, the bundle publishes 108, and `sessionTitle` is not among the seven. That is precisely why this test sat green through R506 while `Domain.sessionTitle` threw `sessionPlanDay is not a function` in the shipped bundle. A title that overclaims is worse than no test, because it answers the question somebody would otherwise ask. BUILD: derived on both sides — namespace-import every bundled module, and require that every value it exports reaches the bundle with the same typeof and the same arity. Adding an export to a module extends the check by itself. The two the harness actually calls keep their own named test, because those are a contract and not merely presence. REVIEW: measured before asserting (all 108 match on type and arity today), then planted three mutations into the built bundle. A deleted export: caught. A function replaced by a number: caught. An arity change: MISSED, and the miss is the part worth keeping — `Function.length` counts only parameters before the first default, so `sessionTitle(sets, lang = 'en', plan = 'ppl')` has length 1 whatever you do to its tail. Re-planted against `findPRs`, which has no defaults, and that was caught. The comment now states that limit instead of the claim I first wrote. Two of my three plants also silently failed to apply on the first attempt and I read "0 failures" as "not caught" — the run was meaningless either way, so the planting helper now asserts the file actually changed before the test is trusted. Same trap as R507's, one round later. Also hit the heredoc backslash collapse again: `problems.join('\n')` reached the file as a literal newline inside a string literal, which the type stripper reported as "Expected ',', got 'string literal'". SHIP: `npm test` → 1878 pass / 0 fail, exit 0; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → "dist/proof-domain.js is current"; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `node link/build.cjs` → "dist/ ready". Confirmed in the built artifact: 108 names, 168.6 kB, and `findPRs` called through the bundle returns a real answer. | FILED FOR THE OWNER: drop predict.ts, goals.ts and coldstart.ts from the bundle to save ~48 kB (28%), or state that the bundle is deliberately the whole domain — one line either way, and the build will tell the truth afterwards either way. | next: three rounds have now each removed a hand-maintained list that was silently wrong, and the remaining one worth checking is `MODULES` itself in build-domain.cjs — it is hand-written, and R506 showed the cost when it is incomplete; deriving it from the import graph is the same move again. `weekStreak` at 1.48ms remains, and the two R483 items stay owner-only.

R509 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) derive `MODULES` from the import graph, R506's root cause; (b) `weekStreak` at 1.48ms; (c) the product itself, untouched since R499; (d) R483, owner-only. Retracted (a) after checking rather than building: R506's gate already enforces the invariant that made it a defect — a module importing an unlisted one, or listed after its consumer, fails the build by name. What remains in MODULES is SCOPE, which is the owner decision already filed in R508. Then spent real time on (c) and found nothing, which is worth recording as an answer rather than a gap: seeded fourteen weeks into the running app and read Progress and Goals on real data. `20 TO 225` on the Squat row looked wrong and is not — gap 20, target 225, documented in `goalTag` and consistent with the 205 shown beside it. Goals reads "20 lb from a 225 squat / 60 days left · on pace". Also checked whether any domain module lacks tests: all fourteen have them. Three candidates retracted honestly, which left the one item with a MEASURED basis, open since R495. Re-measured rather than trusting the ten-round-old number, and it was worse than recorded: at 14,000 sets `weekStreak` costs 3.84 ms, not 1.48, and `longestStreakBefore` another 2.70 — and they each walk the entire history to build the SAME set of week indices. That is the one full walk R495's collapse cache never covered, because its buckets are exercises and these are weeks. BUILD: one identity-keyed cache shared by both, mirroring R495's pattern and sound for exactly the same reason — `Repo.allSets` hands out a frozen array and drops the memo on every write, so identity changes exactly when contents could have. 3.84 ms to 0.002 and 2.70 to 0.008. `now` is deliberately NOT in the key: what is cached is which weeks were trained, a property of the sets alone, so a cached entry cannot freeze a streak as the weeks roll over. REVIEW: a cache is only worth having if it cannot be wrong, so five of the six tests are about staleness rather than speed — alternating histories, two histories of the SAME LENGTH (the case a length check alone misses), an array appended to in place, and the clock one, which pins that three weeks of nothing reports 0 rather than a streak the lifter can disprove. Planted two realistic cache bugs and each was caught by exactly the test written for it: dropping identity fails "two histories of the same length are not confused", dropping the length check fails "an array edited in place". Verified in the PRODUCT, not just the model: reloaded the running app on the seeded history and the Now header still reads 14 WK, the same number it showed before the cache existed. SHIP: `npm test` → 1884 pass / 0 fail; `node build-domain.cjs --check` → current; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `node link/build.cjs` → "dist/ ready". Confirmed in the built artifact by calling through it: `trainedWeeks` is present in the bundle, `weekStreak` returns 5 and 2 for a five-week and two-week run, and 0 for a run three weeks lapsed. | next: a SECOND unidentified one-off suite failure happened this round — one run reported 1883/1 and I could not name it, because the command that produced it filtered the output down to the counts. Five subsequent runs including a deliberate replay of the same command sequence are clean. R501 found a real mechanism behind the first one; this is now twice, so the actionable item is not "investigate the flake" but "stop discarding the evidence": any command that runs the suite should capture full output to a file rather than pipe it through grep. That is the next round. `weekStreak` is now closed; the R508 bundle-scope decision and the two R483 items remain owner-only and filed.

R510 — IDEATE shortlist: (a) stop discarding the evidence when the suite fails; (b) hunt the flake by repeated runs; (c) more product exploration; (d) owner-only items. Picked (a) and explicitly rejected (b), which was the tempting one: two full-suite runs (R499, R509) have reported a failure that was never identified, and both times the cause was not the flake being elusive but the command that ran the suite piping stdout through grep for the counts. Twice the answer was on screen and thrown away. "Capture the output next time" is not a fix, it is the instruction already being ignored, so the RUNNER now keeps the evidence rather than the discipline of whoever invoked it. BUILD: `tools/failure-log.mjs`, a `node --test` reporter that writes each failure — name, file, line, assertion message, stack — to `test-failures.log`, and yields nothing so the spec reporter still owns the console. A file survives any pipe, filter or truncation applied downstream. Rewritten per run rather than appended, because a stale entry read as a live failure is worse than no log at all, and because a log that grows forever gets ignored. Wired into `npm test` alongside the spec reporter; gitignored. REVIEW: four tests, all against a THROWAWAY suite in a temp directory rather than the real one (the mistake R507 made). Four of my own errors on the way, and the last two are the interesting ones. `const log = fs.readFileSync(log)` shadowed its own parameter. An absolute glob is not expanded by the runner, so the first version ran ZERO tests — caught only because the test asserts the planted failure actually failed the run. `stdio: 'ignore'` closes the reporter's own destination, so the run then failed for that reason instead of the planted one; piping stdout and discarding it is what `| grep` really does, and that is what the test now does. And the one that took longest: `NODE_TEST_CONTEXT` is set by the runner and INHERITED by a spawned child, which makes node treat that child as part of the parent test protocol — reporters do not run and the exit code stops meaning what it means. The identical spawn worked perfectly from a plain script, which is exactly why it was hard to see. Planted three reporter defects; counting suite-level failures and appending instead of rewriting were each caught by the test written for them. The third — dropping the assertion message — was NOT caught, because the stack repeats the message and my match was too loose; tightened to require the `error:` line itself, then re-planted and caught. That is the second round running where a test of mine passed for a reason other than the one it claimed. SHIP: `npm test` → 1888 pass / 0 fail, exit 0 (two type errors found and fixed on the way, both in the new test's env handling — the tsc step in the ship gate is what caught them); `node build-domain.cjs --check` → current; `node link/build.cjs` → "dist/ ready". Verified end to end in the exact shape that lost the evidence twice: planted a failing test, ran `npm test | grep` for the counts only, and the name, file, line and assertion were all sitting in test-failures.log afterwards. | next: THE REPORTER FOUND A REAL FLAKE ON ITS FIRST RUN. That end-to-end check reported 2 failures, not 1 — alongside my canary, `a plain in-place write IS observable as a torn file` failed with "only 100 reads — the probe measured nothing". That is my own R501 probe: its instrument guard requires the reader child to complete 200 reads, and under the extra load of one more concurrent test file it managed 100. So the guard is not wrong, the threshold is — it fires as a false failure exactly when the machine is busy, which is the condition a full suite creates. This is almost certainly the R509 one-off, and it is a flake I introduced. Fixing it is the next round, and it is now a named, reproducible-under-load defect rather than a phantom. R499's remains unexplained and predates R501. The R508 bundle-scope decision and the two R483 items stay owner-only and filed.

R511 — Stage 0 first, and it changed the round. OWNER.md exists now and its "## Next" outranks my shortlist, so the flake fix I had queued from R510 became a prerequisite rather than the subject. Two corrections to my own earlier reading before anything else: fitness-app IS its own git repo (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel` returns it), so committing here is not the home repo — my R500 note to the contrary was wrong, and wrong because that `git status` ran after cwd had drifted to C:\Users\srobs. And the repo carries a baseline commit from today containing R500-R510, so the only uncommitted work was this round's. PREREQUISITE (one line, gate hygiene, because REVIEW cannot report a real suite count from a gate that invents failures): R501's tear-probe asserted the reader child completed 200 reads, and R510's failure log caught it managing 100 under full-suite load — the guard is right to exist, its number described an idle machine, and the condition it must survive is a busy one. Floor is 50 now; tearing shows up within tens of reads when it is there at all. That is the R509 phantom, named. PICK: OWNER.md #1, the main screen redesign. Judged the real screen against the owner's words — "too together", "sloppy and AI-generated" — and the specific finding was hierarchy, not decoration: the exercise name was 22px at letterSpacing 2, which is the treatment `topLink` and `railLabel` and every other CHROME label on the screen use, only bigger. Wide tracking on a short all-caps string reads as a category heading, so the one thing the screen is ABOUT was dressed as furniture and nothing claimed the top of the hierarchy. Tracked at 0.6 now; the labels keep their wide tracking, so "this is the thing" and "this is a label" are told apart by the type rather than by size. Plus room to breathe at the top (paddingTop 8 to 16, nav links 11/1.6 to 12/1.2). The size was ALSO raised to 26 and that was a real regression, caught by the suite: `layoutFor` floors `hero` at 24, so a 26px name outgrows the weight itself on the smallest viewport. I had been about to dismiss the test that caught it as another hand-pinned constant of the kind R507 and R508 removed — it pinned the literal 22 and said nothing about why — and it was RIGHT and I was wrong. Kept 22; the polish came from the tracking, not the size. Then improved the guard rather than the value: it now reads `hero: Math.max(24, ...)` out of now-model.ts and requires the name to be under that floor, so it states the reason and would stop the same restyle again. Proven to reject 26 AND the exact boundary 24. REVIEW: 1888 pass / 0 fail; verified in the running app on seeded history, the title now reads as a name and the top has air. Hit the heredoc backslash collapse a third time, and this time it produced a literal BACKSPACE in my edit script's regex — the exact defect R503 found in the repo, now in my own tooling. R512 — Stage 0: OWNER.md unchanged, #1 still top and still open. IDEATE within it: (a) the logging area has no surface while the app's own card vocabulary already exists on the plan chooser; (b) the rail cuts a chip mid-word with nothing saying it scrolls; (c) THIS WORKOUT reads as a debug grid. Picked (a) — and did not build it, because reading the fit math first turned up something that had to come first. `fixedHeight` decides whether the Now screen fits, from constants hand-copied out of NowScreen's stylesheet, and its own comment admits the price: "every constant here is duplicated from the stylesheet... a periodic job, not a one-off". The file records two times that copy went stale, STEP_HINT 12 against a real 40 and HEADER_TEXT 58 against a real 79, both silent, both making the screen promise a fit it did not deliver. It had just happened a THIRD time, by my hand, one round earlier: R511 raised `root.paddingTop` from 8 to 16 for the breathing room OWNER.md asks for and left ROOT_PAD at 8. Every fit test still passed, because they check that arithmetic against itself — the exact sentence already written in the file, and I still did it. Correcting ROOT_PAD to 16 is what made the round: four tests failed immediately, and one of them said 624px against a 568px screen. The drift had been HIDING a real regression. The shortest shipping phone has no 8px to give and LOG SET goes below the fold, so R511's padding change is reverted outright — air at the top has to come from `layoutFor`'s scaled gaps, which shrink on a short screen, not from a fixed padding that does not. R511's letterSpacing win is untouched and verified still live at 22px / 0.6px on the running app. The deliverable is the guard, not the constant: `fixed-height-no-drift.test.ts` reads `root.paddingTop` out of the stylesheet and requires ROOT_PAD to equal it, with a guard on its own regexes so a rename cannot make it pass vacuously, and a second check that it is reading paddingTop rather than paddingHorizontal — two unrelated numbers that would otherwise have compared by luck. Proven from BOTH directions: moving the constant fails it, and moving the stylesheet fails it. The composite constants (HEADER_TEXT is three lines plus gaps) cannot be derived from a single declaration and are named in the test as still hand-measured, so the file states what it does not cover. REVIEW: 1892 pass / 0 fail.
