R513 — Stage 0: OWNER.md unchanged, #1 still top. IDEATE within it, using R512's constraint that any chrome added to the fixed column costs height a 568px phone does not have: (a) the THIS WORKOUT block, which sits inside the SCROLLER and so costs the fixed column nothing; (b) the rail's mid-word cut, which needs a gradient and therefore a dependency §12 forbids; (c) the logging-area surface, now known to need budgeting in `fixedHeight`. Picked (a). The finding was an inverted hierarchy rather than anything decorative: each lift's set chips are 15px at #E8EAED and the lift NAME that groups them was 12px at #9AA5AF — the label was quieter than its own contents, so nothing anchored a group and three exercises read as one undifferentiated field of small numbers. That is what makes a list look like a debug view instead of a workout, and it is the concrete thing behind the owner's "sloppy". BUILD: the name is the anchor now — 14px, #C7CED6, tracked IN rather than out because it is a name and not a category — and the blocks get room (paddingVertical 9 to 12). It deliberately stays below `chipText`, so the numbers a lifter actually reads are still the loudest thing in the row, and `liftNameCurrent` keeps its brighter tone so the lift you are on is still marked. Verified on the running app: the three exercise names now read as group headings and the list scans as three groups. REVIEW is where this round earned its entry. I wrote four tests, planted three regressions, and the FIRST plant — restoring the exact pre-R513 values — produced no failure at all. The assertion was "the lift name is larger than the chrome label", and 12px was already larger than the 10px label, so it passed against the precise state it had been written to rule out. It was decoration, and only planting the old values exposed it; the suite would have carried it forever. Rewritten to ask which TIER the name is nearer, which is the only form of the question that discriminates: before, 12px sits 2 above the chrome label and 3 below the set chips, so it is nearer the chrome and read that way; after, 14px sits 4 above and 1 below. Now the pre-R513 values fail by name, an 18px over-correction fails the opposite guard, and 9px padding fails the spacing one. That is the third time in recent rounds a test of mine passed for a reason other than the one it claimed (R508's arity, R510's assertion message, this) — the pattern is that a test written from the FIX rather than from the DEFECT tends to assert something the defect already satisfied. Planting the original state, not merely a mutation, is what catches it. R514 — Stage 0: OWNER.md unchanged, #1 still top. IDEATE: (a) the rail's mid-word cut, (b) the logging-area surface. Picked (a) because of the constraint R512 bought — an absolutely positioned overlay costs ZERO layout height, and the logging-area surface does not, on a column the 568px phone already overflows. The defect: the chip row scrolls and nothing said so, so it stopped mid-word at the screen edge ("DB Shoul"), which reads as breakage rather than as more-to-come. BUILD: a gradient is the standard answer and is a dependency §12 forbids, so this is a ramp of five solid BACKGROUND slices at rising opacity, absolutely positioned, pointerEvents none. Two properties worth recording because they are why this works rather than merely renders. It needs no is-it-overflowing check: the slices are the same colour as the background, so when the chips do not reach the edge the fade is background drawn over background and cannot be seen — self-hiding by construction rather than by a measurement that could be wrong. And the wrapper introduced to give the overlay a positioning context deliberately sets no size, because `railBand`'s own comment records being pinned to a model number twice and being wrong both times. REVIEW: verified in the running app by MEASURING the rendered result rather than looking at it — five slices, ascending 0.12 to 1 across a 32px overlay, pointerEvents none, spanning the 52px rail row — which is stronger than a screenshot and was necessary here, since the Browser pane does not support region zoom and the fade is subtle at full-page scale. Five tests, one per way this could be built wrong, and all five plants caught by name: in the layout flow rather than absolute (the R512 constraint, now a test rather than a memory), an overlay that eats taps on the very chip a user is reaching for, a grey bar instead of a fade, a ramp that never reaches opaque so text bleeds through, and a ramp that descends. That is the next thing to try. After it, #1 is worth re-judging as a whole against a real fitness app's home screen rather than continuing to pick at parts. R515 — Stage 0: OWNER.md unchanged, #1 still top. Took the last increment I had identified on it, the one blocked by height: the logging controls had no surface, so the screen was a flat field with everything floating on it and nothing grouping the three rows that are in fact ONE control. That is most of what "too together" and "not app-appropriate" point at, and the app already owned the vocabulary for it — #111417 on #2A323A at radius 12-14, on the plan chooser — and had never applied it to the control the screen exists for. The whole difficulty was that a card pads its contents and this column has none to give: R512 measured the 568px phone at 624px of unshrinkable content, and eight pixels of padding was enough to put LOG SET below the fold, which is precisely how R511 broke it. BUILD: the panel is an ABSOLUTE child with negative insets, reaching out past the rows to look like padding while contributing no height — the same trick as R514's rail fade, pointed the other way. REVIEW: the load-bearing claim here is "costs nothing", and that is not something to argue, so I A/B'd it in the running app: reverted the file, reloaded, measured, restored, measured again. LOG SET at y475 and the document 1175px tall, with the surface and without it, identical to the pixel. Four tests, and the reason they exist is worth stating: this property is INVISIBLE on a big screen. The panel would look perfectly correct while quietly costing 24px, and the phone it breaks is the one nobody develops on. So the tests pin absolute-with-negative-insets, a container that adds nothing of its own (a wrapper is the easy place to reintroduce exactly the cost this design avoids), pointerEvents none (it covers the entire control — without it, a 294px button that does nothing sits over every stepper), and `columnHeight` at 320x568 rather than at a comfortable size. All three plants caught by name: a real card, a padding wrapper, and a tap-eating surface. R516 — Stage 0: OWNER.md unchanged, #1 still top. This round did what the item itself asks and I had not yet done — judge the screen AS A WHOLE against a well-known fitness app's home screen — and it ships a decision rather than code, because the judgement found nothing left to fix. The single most useful thing in it: I judged at real phone size (375x812) for the first time. R511 through R515 had all been looking at an 800px-wide browser pane, where the app is a narrow column floating in a wide dark field, and that is not the product. At phone size it holds up — the R515 panel groups the control, LOG SET is unmistakable, the hierarchy reads top to bottom. THREE suspected defects, all retracted after measuring rather than after arguing. (1) The nav links measure 36px against a 44px standard — and already carry `hitSlop={14}`, so the real target is about 64px. The codebase had solved it the exact way I was about to propose, and only checking first stopped me rebuilding it. (2) "LB" looks orphaned beside a 112px hero; measured, `baselineDrop` is 0 and the gap is 6px, so it is aligned precisely as its comment intends — the 149px line box on a 112px font is what makes it LOOK low. Taste, not defect. (3) The first-run split sheet appeared to render transparent with the Now screen showing through and text overlapping text — genuinely alarming on the first screen a new user sees, and it is a mid-animation frame. It settles correctly four seconds later. Worth recording that my check for it was itself worthless: I asserted the page text contained both "LOG SET" and "HOW DO YOU SPLIT", which is true whether or not anything overlaps, because the Now screen sits BEHIND the sheet in the DOM. A text-presence test cannot see occlusion. That is the fourth instrument this session that measured nothing, and the pattern is the same each time — I asked a question the defect and the healthy state both answer the same way. DELIVERABLE: #1 moved to OWNER.md's ## Done with the round numbers and what each one changed, plus TWO things deliberately not done and filed as owner decisions rather than made — a bottom tab bar is what every well-known fitness app uses and this app structurally cannot have one (it costs about 50px and R512 measured the 568px phone at 624px of unshrinkable content already, so it means dropping something else off the screen), and the centred layout is taste rather than defect and touches every row. It is the largest item in the file, the owner asked for it twice (in Vision and in Next), and it is completely untouched. R517 — Stage 0: OWNER.md #1 is in ## Done, so #2 is now top: the AI coach. Took the domain half only, because that is what the architecture asks for and because the two halves fail differently — the engine can be proven right against fixtures and against real data, and the screen half is a layout problem the engine should not be waiting on. BUILD: `src/domain/coach.ts`, a local rule engine over the last two weeks of a lift's top sets — progressive overload, plateau, deload, tuned to strength/size/consistency. No network, no key, no new dependency, exactly as OWNER.md asks, and the seam for a model call is documented and unused because the same line says not to add it unasked. Two design rules carried the design. It returns null readily, which is §8's never-cry-wolf applied to advice: a coach that speaks when it does not know teaches you to ignore the times it does. And it returns an i18n KEY plus values rather than a sentence — a string built in the domain would be English on a Spanish phone and no test would catch it, which is the whole reason §16 exists. THE ROUND'S REAL FINDING came from running the engine over the app's OWN SEEDED HISTORY rather than only over fixtures. Every fixture I wrote holds the weight constant across sessions, so `atSameWeight` was always >= 2 and one case never arose in any test — and on real data it is the COMMON case, because a lifter on linear progression moves up every single session. The engine told them "235 last 1 — stay here and add a rep": a count of one rendered as a streak, and hold advice given to somebody who had added weight every session for three months. Both halves wrong, and invisible to twenty passing tests. It now has its own case with its own reason — first time at this weight, repeat it before adding — which is the same ACTION as hold for a completely different reason, and the reason is the half the owner actually asked for. REVIEW: 20 tests grouped by how a coach can be bad rather than by function (it can talk when it does not know, push a tired lifter, only ever say "go up", be right in English and wrong in Spanish). Six plants, all caught by the test written for them, including the one that matters most — moving the deload check after the progress check, so a lifter grinding out a bad week gets told to add weight. Restored from a backup taken BEFORE the round's own fix once again and caught it by checking rather than assuming, the same slip as R504. SHIP: `npm test` exit 0, 1925 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; committed as 1b2d7ee. Two of my own gates caught my own work in this round, which is the first time that has happened in the same round: `no-control-bytes` found a `\b` that had collapsed into a literal backspace inside the new test (the R503 defect, third occurrence, now caught automatically instead of by accident), and `orphan-scan` refused to let an unwired export sit quietly and demanded a decision. | next: the screen half of #2 — one line on the Now screen, for the exercise in front of you. The hard part is not the rendering, it is that the Now column has no vertical room: R512 measured the 568px phone at 624px of unshrinkable content, and R511 put LOG SET below the fold by adding eight pixels. So the line has to either replace something already there (the "Just did 75 x 12" line is the obvious candidate — it is the same slot, saying less) or be budgeted properly in `fixedHeight` and accepted as a trade. That is the decision the next round has to make and it may be an owner call. `coachSuggestion` is registered in orphan-scan with exactly that as its removal condition: if it is still listed several rounds from now, the engine is speculative code and should be deleted rather than kept. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R518 — Stage 0: OWNER.md #2 still top. Took the screen half, and the layout problem I flagged last round turned out to have a clean answer rather than a trade: the suggestion TAKES OVER the header slot instead of getting a row of its own. That is the right place and not a compromise — the slot said "Last time 185 x 5" for any lift with history, and the coach line is that same fact plus what to do about it, in the position a lifter already looks, directly under the exercise name. It is also the only place it could go: R512 measured the 568px phone at 624px of unshrinkable content and R511 put LOG SET below the fold with eight pixels, so a new row (about twenty) was never available while reusing a budgeted one costs nothing. Two details that are load-bearing: the coach outranks "Last time" and never "Just did", because that line confirms the set you just logged and swapping advice onto it answers a question nobody is asking mid-set; and history is read through `historyInSessionUnit` because a LoggedSet carries no unit (HANDOFF trap 9), so raw history would compare kilos with pounds and suggest a jump in the wrong currency. THE ROUND'S FINDING, and it is R517's finding arriving from the opposite side: wiring the engine to a real screen made an EXISTING fixture fail, and the fixture was right. `trained()` in now-model.test.ts is four weekly squats at 200, 205, 210, 215 — a lifter adding five pounds a week and making every one — and the engine said "first time at 215, repeat it before adding". R517 had added that case to stop it saying "last 1", and the conservative answer is just as wrong when the lifter's plan is working. Climbing and settling are indistinguishable from `atSameWeight` alone (both are one session at this weight) and the correct advice is opposite, so they are now told apart by whether the weight rose across the window. The climb suggests THEIR step — 5 for the squat, 2.5 for the row, taken from their own last increment rather than from the goal table — which is the personalisation OWNER.md asks for, arrived at because a test insisted. R520 — Stage 0: OWNER.md #3 top, "Personalization: goals, units, split, jump amounts and history should visibly shape what the app shows, not just what it stores". First, the derived scan found a preference my hand-written audit had missed entirely — `pref.language`, which is the one with the strongest claim to be in the file. Enumerating by hand covered six and missed the seventh; deriving the list found it in one line. Second, and more useful: the audit was WRONG FOUR TIMES before it was right, and every wrong answer looked exactly like "the app is broken". A fixture where the coach happened to be silent, so flipping the goal changed nothing. A fixture with no machine, so the machine preference had nothing to act on. A live session whose unit a display preference cannot change, which is documented correct behaviour and not a defect. And a `machine` field silently dropped on insert because `equipment` was not set to 'machine'. Four false alarms in one sitting, on ground where a real defect would look identical — so every case in the gate now carries a PRECONDITION that proves the path it feeds is live before the comparison is allowed to conclude anything, and the precondition failing is itself a test failure with its own message. That is the same lesson as R516's occlusion check and R513's decorative assertion, arrived at from a third direction: an instrument that cannot distinguish "no defect" from "not exercised" is not measuring the thing it names. R524 — Stage 0: the only OWNER.md item is the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner, and nothing should be built on top of an unmade decision, so this round took the oldest defect I had filed and not fixed — and it was one I shipped. R518's climbing rule takes the lifter's own increment, which is right, and trusted it with no bound, which is not: two sessions at 185 then 320 produced "320 and climbing, 2 sessions — try 455", and even +45 produced "try 275". FIRST, REPRODUCED IT PROPERLY, and the first attempt did not: a three-session fixture with a 135 lb jump came out as "repeat it before adding", because `rising` requires EVERY consecutive pair to ascend and my fixture had a flat pair. The live bug needs exactly two sessions in the window. Worth recording because a reproduction that fails to reproduce looks identical to a bug that is already fixed, and I would have closed it. THE FIX IS NOT A CAP ON THE NUMBER, which was my first instinct. A 73% jump in one session is not evidence of a repeatable increment, so "keep climbing" is the wrong KIND of advice rather than merely the wrong size — and the engine already has the honest thing to say about a weight hit once, which is to repeat it before adding. So a step past `MAX_CLIMB_FRACTION` stops the run being a climb at all and falls through to settle, which is a sentence that was already there and already right. A FRACTION rather than a number of pounds, because 5 lb is ordinary on a 185 bench and enormous on a 45 lb one, so any fixed cap has to be wrong for one of them; a test plants the fixed-pounds version specifically and catches it. Measured every case before and after rather than reasoning about the boundary: 185 to 320 and 185 to 230 now settle; 185 to 190, 185 to 195, 100 to 102.5, 45 to 47.5, 400 to 410, and steady 5s across three sessions all still climb. Four tests, three plants, each caught by the test written for it, and the boundary test derives its numbers from the exported constant so moving the constant moves the test rather than leaving a number here that quietly disagrees. Verified in the running app: the same 320 lb jump that produced "try 455" last round now reads "First time at 320×5 — repeat it before adding". R525 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner, so this round took the strongest unfollowed lead: `state()` runs on every tap and sat at 5.7ms against the 3.98ms R495 achieved, and R522 had ruled out the coach and PR marking without isolating what HAD grown. That function touches `history` three times and filters by `goal.exerciseId` every one of them, twice through `bestAt` and once for `trainedSince`, so it walked 14,000 rows to look at a few dozen. Fixed with a by-exercise index cached on `allSets()`'s identity — the same pattern as R495, R509 and R522, and the same insight R494 had about `activeGoals`, which was a function scoped to one exercise being handed the whole log. A/B'd in identical scripts, three passes each: 5.7ms to 4.4ms, a 23% cut on the logging path. Behaviour-identical rather than an approximation, and the tests prove it rather than assert it — the same goal scored both ways must agree exactly, and a 500 lb squat must not move a bench goal by a pound. A FALSE ALARM WORTH RECORDING: `goalProgress` across the stress database's 100 goals measures 140ms, which looks like a serious defect on the Goals screen. It is not a real path — only `now-model` calls that function, once, for the lift in front of you, and the Goals screen goes through R494's already-bucketed route. Checking who actually calls it is what stopped me optimising something nobody has, and that check cost one grep. THE INSTRUMENT LESSON THIS ROUND, and it is the sharpest yet: THREE successive versions of my empty-bucket test could not fail, each for a different reason, and only planting the bug exposed it. First I used `squat`, which has sets in the fixture, so the lookup never missed. Then I removed the goal, and `goalHint` returns before the lookup happens at all, so the path was still never reached. It needs a goal ON an untrained lift — which is also the case a new user is in for every lift but one. Two of the three plants I ran were not caught, and the second miss was informative in the other direction: flattening every bucket into one array does not fail anything, because passing the whole log gives the same answer, which is precisely the correctness property the round is built on. A plant that cannot fail is sometimes the proof rather than the problem. R526 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Picked from AGENT_LOOP's own yield-ordered list, the one entry I had never swept: "exemption / allowlist entries — each reason is an unverified claim". Enumerated every exemption in the suite and checked each stated reason against the current source, which is a cheap grep per claim. Four held. One was FALSE, and it was hiding exactly what the suite it lives in exists to catch: `recap-fields-reach-consumers.ts` exempted `lang` from the recap.tsx check on the written grounds that "the live screen already knows its own language — `lang` and `kind` exist specifically for the OTHER renderers", and `recap.tsx:155` reads `payload.lang` to format the volume, because a thousands separator is a locale decision (11,130 against 11.130). So a field the live screen genuinely depends on was being skipped by the test whose whole job is to notice a payload field no consumer reads. The same field is exempt from the shareText check and THAT one is correct — `shareText` takes `lang` as its own parameter and never touches `payload.lang`, which the comment there had already anticipated in a sentence that reads like pedantry until you check it. Two exemptions on one field, one true and one false, separable only by reading the code: which is the argument against a reason written as prose above a bare Set, and exactly the correction R464 made in `accent.test.ts` and nobody swept anywhere else. BUILD: exemptions prove themselves now. Each asserts the consumer does NOT read `payload.<field>`, so an exemption that goes stale fails the build rather than quietly widening. THE ROUND'S OWN INSTRUMENT FAILED THE SAME WAY, and it is the sharpest instance of this all session: my new guard shipped blind for about ten minutes because inside a TEMPLATE LITERAL `payload\.${field}\b` loses its backslashes — the compiled pattern was `payload.kind` followed by a literal BACKSPACE, which matches nothing. It passed while being incapable of failing, in the code written to catch precisely that. Caught only by planting the defect and noticing the plant did not fire, then reading the emitted regexp rather than the source I thought I had written. That is the backslash-collapse trap R503 first found, arriving for the fourth time and through a new door — this time not the Bash heredoc but JavaScript's own template literals. R527 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Finished the sweep R526 started, across the two allow-lists it named. `language-reaches-the-app.ts` allows ten bare strings past the "nothing renders untranslated English" check. Nine are real; `←` exempted NOTHING. The arrow lives inside the TRANSLATED string `editWorkout` — '← EDIT THIS WORKOUT' and '← EDITAR ESTE ENTRENO' — so it was never a bare glyph needing permission, and both languages already control it. An allow-list entry for something that does not exist is a claim about the code that has quietly stopped being true, which is the same shape as R526's false `lang` exemption one screen over. The gate is the deliverable rather than the deletion: an entry appearing in no screen now fails the build, so the list can only shrink by being wrong. Both plants caught, including re-adding the exact arrow I had just removed. The other half of the sweep came back empty and that is worth recording as an answer rather than a gap — `check-deps.cjs` carries no exemptions at all, which I established by reading it rather than by assuming, because "probably fine" is how the first two survived. WORTH NOTING WHAT THE MEASUREMENT ACTUALLY SHOWED, since it was more nuanced than the fix: of the ten entries, only six are currently rendered as a bare `<Text>` — PROOF, ▴ and · appear in the screens but inside larger expressions. I did NOT remove those. An entry that is present but not currently bare is permission that may be needed the moment a screen changes shape; an entry that appears nowhere at all is dead by any reading. The gate draws the line at the second, which is the only one that cannot be argued with, and being able to say precisely why the line is there is the difference between a rule and a preference. The probe hit the backslash-collapse trap a FIFTH time — the Bash heredoc this round rather than R526's template literal — and the answer was to stop fighting the quoting and write a plain .mjs file with no regex escaping in it at all. That is now the third distinct mechanism for the same defect (heredoc, template literal, and R503's original), and the only reliable defence has been to remove the escaping rather than to get it right. R528 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Took AGENT_LOOP's next untried source, "comments that say fixed X / same bug as Y — each is a class where only one instance was swept", which is how R526 and R527 both started. Three leads, and TWO CAME BACK CLEAN — which is worth recording as an answer rather than skipping to the one that paid. First, the benchmark class: `recap-layout.test.ts` records an instrument that timed `render()` and `encodeSync('png')` in one region and printed the sum as "avg / frame", so 0.54ms of drawing read as 68ms and the headline was seventeen times over a budget the thing being measured was comfortably inside. That is the same mistake I made in R495. It is fixed, gated by two tests, and `spike/render-frames.cjs` turns out to be the only timed region in the repo outside throwaway probes — so the class is swept. Second, the drifting-copy class: `spark-is-shared.test.ts` names three siblings, and all three are accounted for — the sparkline by its own gate, `SettingsSheet.tsx` by having been deleted, and the Swift port by `swift-parity.test.ts`'s acknowledged list. Followed up rather than trusted, because a comment naming three siblings is worth exactly as much as whether anybody checked them. THE THIRD LEAD PAID, and it was inside the comment doing the naming. It cites the Swift port as "four changes behind `recap.js`"; HANDOFF.md says FIVE, and `KNOWN_DRIFT` has five entries. FOUR THINGS I SUSPECTED AND RETRACTED, each after measuring rather than reasoning. And I hypothesised that the other screens lacked the narrow-width gates the Now column has, which is false: `goal-card-name-room` and `progress-row-fits` both assert at 320pt, and the recap's action row is guarded STRUCTURALLY — no third child in the row that shares SHARE's width — which is stronger than a width number and exists because that exact failure happened. Worth recording as a result: after nine rounds of finding real defects by sweeping claims, a round that sweeps and finds nothing is evidence about the codebase rather than a wasted round — and the temptation at that point is to lower the bar for what counts as a defect, which is how "every sparkline looks the same" nearly became a bug report. R531 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY BEFORE REWRITING rather than from memory, which mattered: the call timed out once and then succeeded on immediate retry, which is exactly what the tool's own error message instructs. So the true statement is narrower and still worth having — a hidden or minimised pane can stop the page drawing and the call times out after five seconds, and calling it again works. `screen-render.cjs` now survives on its real merit instead of a false monopoly: a photo cannot tell you an element is 3px wide or 8px past the fold, and the layout defects this session turned on exactly that kind of number. R533 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Third round of the trap audit, taking 10 and 12 — the two with the most direct evidence from this session. TRAP 12 IS TRUE and re-measured precisely: dispatching `click` on LOG SET and reading `document.body.innerText` in the SAME execution reports 0 sets, and reading after a delay reports 1. The press landed both times; only the read was early, which is exactly what the trap says and exactly the mistake that produced three false "this control does not respond" conclusions before R277. TRAP 10 WAS THE FIND, and it is the same class R529 found in HANDOFF's suite count: a number that has quietly stopped being true. It said an instrument here "has silently measured nothing THREE times", and eleven further rounds have hit it since — R500, R501, R510, R512, R513, R516, R520, R525, R526, R529, R532 — each by a genuinely different mechanism, which is what makes the tally worth keeping rather than rounding off: a gate whose glob could not see a planted failing test, a reporter that passed while incapable of failing, an assertion that passed against the exact state it was written to rule out, a text-presence check that cannot see occlusion, four fixtures in one sitting that never exercised the path they judged, three successive tests that could not fail, a regexp whose backslashes had collapsed so it matched nothing, and plants that silently did not apply and were read as "not caught". The count IS the entry's argument, so being three times out of date made the most common failure in this repo read as a curiosity rather than as the thing to expect. Corrected to fourteen with the rounds named, so the next session can check any of them. MORE USEFUL THAN THE NUMBER, the trap now carries the defence that emerged across those eleven: plant the defect, then check the plant ACTUALLY FIRED AND ACTUALLY APPLIED — because no failure from a plant means either the instrument is blind or the edit never landed, and both are findings rather than a pass. That rule is the single highest-yield thing this session has produced, it was learned the same way eleven times, and until now it lived only in scattered LOOP_LOG entries nobody would read in order. This round's own three plants were run under it and all three were caught. An anchored insert into a document is exactly as capable of landing in the wrong place as one into code, and nothing said so: the suite was green, the claim was true, the sentence was broken, and every check I had built pointed at whether the CONTENT was accurate rather than whether it had landed where I put it. R535 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Audited trap 13, hand-maintained lists drift. It already prescribes the right fix — derive the population from source, exempt explicitly with a stated reason, prove the gate can fail — so the count was the expected find: it said "Twice" and six more have happened since (R507's 28-name EXPORTS list against a bundle publishing 108, R508's seven-name parity check under the title "everything the harness needs" when the harness needs two, R520's preferences, R526 and R527's two allow-lists, R529's test count in that same file). Corrected to eight with each named. THE REAL FIND WAS ITS EXEMPLAR. Trap 13 cites `lang`/`kind`/`watermark` as its model of "exempt explicitly, with a stated reason" — and R526 found the `lang` exemption FALSE: `recap.tsx` reads `payload.lang` to format the volume, because a thousands separator is a locale decision. So the field was being skipped by the very test written to catch an unread field, for the stated reason that it did not need checking. An out-of-date count misleads about FREQUENCY; a wrong exemplar misleads about METHOD, and that is worse, because anyone following the entry would have copied the pattern it was demonstrating — a reason written in prose above a bare Set — which is exactly what this session proved insufficient twice. The entry now carries what R526 established: a stated reason is necessary and not sufficient, because prose does not fail, so each exemption must assert that the consumer genuinely does not read the field. Worth noting the shape: trap 13 was RIGHT about everything it prescribed and wrong about the case it prescribed it from, which is a failure mode I had not seen before — the advice survived while the evidence for it rotted. REVIEW: both lessons and both counts gated; four plants, all caught by name. One inconsistency I found while planting and fixed rather than argued for: trap 13's count was ungated while trap 10's was gated, and both are frequency claims whose entire force is the number. R536 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Audited trap 7, the backslash collapse, on the reasoning that six hits by three mechanisms almost certainly meant another undercount. It was worse than undercounted, it was MIS-SCOPED: the entry is titled and framed around the Bash heredoc, and two of the six hits came through doors it never mentions, so a session reading it feels safe the moment it switches to python or writes the regex in JavaScript. Measured the second door properly rather than describing it — a template literal holding a single-backslash dot and word-boundary compiles to a pattern whose final character is codepoint 8, a real BACKSPACE, matching nothing, while the doubled forms give the intended 92 46 ... 92 98. That is precisely what made R526's guard pass while structurally incapable of failing. The third door is a doubled carriage-return escape arriving as a real CR inside a regex literal, which at least fails loudly. The entry now carries the defence that has worked every single time: do not escape more carefully, REMOVE A LAYER — build with `chr(92)`, or Write the file, or Edit the one line. THE TRAP DEMONSTRATED ITSELF THREE TIMES INSIDE THE ROUND THAT FIXED IT, which is the entry earning its place. The `node -e` proof was mangled by Bash before it could prove anything. The correction, written through a heredoc, had every example in it eaten — the word-boundary vanished entirely, the doubled forms collapsed to single ones, the carriage-return escape became nothing — leaving an entry about backslashes being eaten visibly contradicting itself on disk. Then the Edit tool could not match the damaged text at all, because the file now contained literal control bytes where the escapes had been. Fixed by replacing the block BY LINE INDEX, which needs no pattern matching, and the entry is now deliberately written with no literal escapes in it, because an entry about this cannot survive being written through the thing it warns about. SECOND FINDING, stumbled on while reading past the first: HANDOFF states the goals cap TWICE — 100 at line 309, 12 at line 596, 287 lines apart, with the code at 100. R529's gate passed it, because `.exec` returns the first match and the first one happened to be right. A document can contradict itself and still satisfy a check that stops reading at the first agreement, which is a new shape of blind instrument and belongs with trap 10's list. The gate now checks EVERY mention; planting the contradiction back fails it by name. R537 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Six documentation-audit rounds in a row had each found something real, but the marginal value was dropping and AGENT_LOOP prefers a defect you can demonstrate in the product, so this round took the one trap that is actually ABOUT the product: trap 9, "a cross-unit weight bug does not look like a bug". A LoggedSet carries no unit — the SESSION does — so anything comparing weights across sessions has to convert first, and the coach I built in R517 compares across sessions by construction: it reads two weeks of top sets and decides whether they are climbing. It turns out to be protected, because R518 wired it through `historyInSessionUnit()`, and NOTHING TESTED THAT. Measured the unprotected path rather than describing the risk, which is what made it concrete: three pound sessions plus one 86 kg session, and the app says "189.5 and climbing, 4 sessions — try 194" — correct, because 86 kg IS 189.5 lb and 4.5 is the lifter's own step — while the identical call on raw `allSets()` reports `recentWeight = 86` and advises settling there. No error, no crash, a plausible sentence about a weight nobody lifted, which is precisely the invisibility trap 9 is warning about. THE SUBTLER HALF IS WORSE THAN THE NUMBER: unconverted, 185 to 86 reads as a 54% DROP, so under R524's bound the run stops being a climb entirely and a lifter on working linear progression is told to settle. The advice is wrong in KIND, not merely in magnitude — the same failure shape R518 and R524 each fixed once, arriving this time through a unit conversion rather than through a rule. Four tests, and the plant is the one-word change somebody would actually make in good faith: `allSets()` in place of `historyInSessionUnit()`, which is faster, is what every other call site uses, and looks equivalent. Three of the four fail on it, including the two behavioural ones rather than only the source check. Verified live on a purpose-built mixed-unit seed: the screen reads 189.5 and the hero reads 189.5 LB, with no 86 anywhere on it. R538 — Stage 0: still only the tab-bar decision waiting on the owner. Took R537's own closing lesson as the instruction and pointed the audit at more code I wrote this session: R525's by-exercise index, which buckets `allSets()` UNCONVERTED and which R537's finding made worth re-examining. IT IS CORRECT. Whole history and bucketed agree exactly under mixed units, `current` is 189.5 from an 86 kg session, `remaining` 35.5, and the screen reads "36 to 225 × 5". `goalProgress` takes `sessionUnits` and converts per set internally, so raw history is precisely what it wants. No defect, and that is the second "probably fine" this session that turned out to be actually fine — worth saying, because the value of asking does not depend on the answer being bad. WHAT IT EXPOSED IS THE SEAM UNDERNEATH, and that is the round. `now-model` feeds two consumers from the same history and they want it in OPPOSITE forms: the coach needs it ALREADY CONVERTED because it takes a unit and converts nothing itself, while `goalProgress` needs it RAW because it converts per set against each set's own session unit. So `historyInSessionUnit()` for one and `setsFor()` for the other, eight lines apart in the same method, reading exactly like an inconsistency somebody ought to clean up. CLEANING IT UP IS NOT A ROUNDING ERROR. Measured rather than imagined: hand `goalProgress` a pre-converted history and it converts a second time — `current` becomes 418 instead of 189.5 and `remaining` becomes 0, so a lifter benching 189.5 is told they have HIT a 225 lb goal. Nothing throws, nothing looks wrong, and the failure is in the direction that feels like success. That is trap 9's "does not look like a bug" at its most convincing, produced by a change made in good faith for the sake of tidiness. Four tests; both directions of the tidy-up planted and caught, and the `goalProgress` one fails BEHAVIOURALLY rather than only on the source check, which is the difference between a rule and a gate. Verified live on a purpose-built mixed-unit seed with a goal on it: the header reads "189.5 and climbing, 4 sessions — try 194 · 36 to 225 × 5" — both consumers correct, from one history, in one line. R539 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Took the last unaudited piece of this session's code, R522's PR marking, and found the defect R538 went looking for and did not find. IT IS NOT A UNIT BUG. `findPRs` takes `sessionUnits` and converts internally, and `now-model` hands it raw history, which is exactly right — same shape as R538's `goalProgress`. THE BUG IS IN THE CACHE AROUND IT. R522 keyed the memo on `allSets()` array identity and its own comment ended "nothing else can" invalidate it. `findPRs` is also handed `measurements()`, because the four bodyweight-carrying lifts are judged on real load — belt weight plus what the lifter weighed that day — so the scale can change what a pull-up weighed without a single set being written, and the key never moves. A confident sentence in a comment turned out to be the thing that was wrong, which is the same failure as R531's screenshot trap in a different file. Fix: key on both, using the identity trick the repo already relies on twice, because `measurements()` is a frozen memo dropped on every write on exactly the same terms as `allSets()`. THE PRODUCT PATH IS NARROWER THAN THE BUG, and finding that out was the real work of the round. My first demonstration — log the set, then weigh yourself — showed nothing, and I nearly filed it as "the fix did not take". `readingAt` looks BACKWARD only, so a reading recorded after a set never changes that set, and the app was right both times. The reachable case is DELETING a reading: that changes what OLDER sets weighed with no set written. Verified end to end on a seed built for it, driving the real UI: Now open showing no star, push to Progress -> YOU -> remove the 300 lb reading -> back, and the star appears on the still-mounted screen. Then planted the one-line revert, let Metro reload, and walked the identical path: star stays false. before=false after=true with the fix, before=false after=false without it, on the same six clicks. Also repaired R522's own source-shape test, which read the literal `this.repo.measurements()` in the call and failed on the change that strengthened what it protects — it now checks the argument and, separately, that the local is bound to the repo. R540 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. IDEATE came straight out of R539's lesson, sharpened: the thing that hid R539's defect was a COMMENT MAKING AN ABSOLUTE CLAIM about what cannot happen ("nothing else can" invalidate the cache). Grepped for the pattern and found two more, both of the same family — `session.ts` and `weekly.ts` each claim they make "the same comparison `findPRs` makes, so the two can never disagree". `weekly.ts` is honest: it calls `bestWeightAtReps` with measurements, unit and sessionUnits, so it really is the same rule. `session.ts` IS NOT, and the disagreement is the worst kind the app can have. `findPRs` holds a bodyweight movement to TWO scales — more total load AND more added weight than ever — because on a pull-up the one way real load can rise with no training is the lifter getting heavier, which `pr.ts` calls "the purest cry-wolf in the app: a badge for eating". `bestYet` compared load alone. Measured: 25 x 5 pull-ups three times at 180 lb bodyweight, then the identical 25 x 5 at 192. `findPRs` correctly awards nothing — and BECAUSE there is no record, the `headline` suppression that would normally hide `bestYet` cannot fire. The recap card said BEST YET, UP FROM 205, for a set the lifter had already done three times, on the surface people SHARE. The comment was not describing the code; it was standing in for a test, and it survived every round that touched the file. Fix is four lines, `findPRs`' own rule and its reason. VERIFYING IN THE PRODUCT COST MORE THAN THE FIX and taught two things worth keeping. First attempt showed no difference with the defect PLANTED, which I nearly filed as "not reachable from the UI": a single-set session is `thin` and the screen holds its message back. Second attempt still showed nothing, and this time I checked the actual bundle rather than trusting the screen — the plant WAS live, so the fault was mine: the seed logged sets at now-120s while `startSession` stamps startedAt at now, so today's own sets satisfied `x.at < session.startedAt` and became their own prior best. A seed can be wrong in a way that looks exactly like a fix working. With the timestamps right: planted build shows BEST YET / PULL-UP / UP FROM 205, fixed build shows nothing, same six clicks, and the bundle grepped for the guard both times so neither reading was on trust. SHIP: `npm test` 1997 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; app reseeded. | next: `weekly.ts` carries the same sentence and IS correct, which is worth a test of its own — the claim is only safe while `bestWeightAtReps` keeps being handed all three of measurements, unit and sessionUnits, and nothing enforces that. More broadly the grep from this round has more in it: `types.ts` "that never changes", `session.ts` "touches the row and nothing else", `coldstart.ts` "can never go below". Each is a claim a reader trusts instead of checking. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R541 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Third round on the same seam and it is still producing, so I kept pulling: comments that make an ABSOLUTE CLAIM about what cannot happen. `coldstart.ts` states a floor — "the empty version of each thing: a bar with no plates, the lightest dumbbell, the first pin on a stack. The floor a suggestion can never go below" — and the coach engine, which I wrote in R517, had never heard of it. Measured: three bench sessions at 45 lb with reps falling and the app says "45 is grinding — back off to 41". THE BAR ALONE IS 45. §16 asks that every number be checkable against a rack and this one cannot exist, and it is aimed at the exact person least able to spot it — a beginner, at the empty bar, having a bad week. Same shape as R539 and R540: the claim was true of the file it sat in and false of the app, because a module written later never read it. THE OBVIOUS FIX IS A SECOND BUG. Flooring `back` and letting the branch decline hands the question to PLATEAU, which fires on the identical condition (three sessions, one weight, reps not improving) and says "try 46" — telling somebody grinding out a bad week to add load, which is precisely what the deload branch exists to prevent. So the protection stays and only the ACTION changes: hold at the floor, with a new key saying why, en and es both, because a domain key with no Spanish is a blank line no other test would notice. `base` is optional and defaults to 0, so every existing caller keeps the old arithmetic rather than inheriting a wrong floor — and one test pins that, because a silent default is how a fix becomes the next round's defect. The floor is the EQUIPMENT'S: a dumbbell bottoms out at 5 and a pull-up at 0, and flooring everything at 45 would be a different bug wearing the same fix. Six tests, and both halves planted separately — remove the floor, two fail; remove the wiring in now-model, one fails — because a fix in two files can be half-live and look whole. Verified in the running app with the bundle grepped both ways: planted reads "back off to 41", fixed reads "45 is grinding — hold here, 3 sessions in". Also worth one test: `weekly.ts` makes R540's claim and IS correct, but only while `bestWeightAtReps` keeps being handed measurements, unit and sessionUnits. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R542 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. FOUR ROUNDS HAD LANDED ON THE SAME SEAM from four different sides — R537 the coach reading kilos as pounds, R538 converting twice and reporting a goal met, R539 the PR cache, and R525's index before them — and every one was a single line in `now-model` judged by a rule that existed only in my head. So this round wrote the rule down somewhere a test can read it, which is worth more than the fifth instance would have been. THE RULE IS DERIVABLE, not a list (HANDOFF #13): a function handed raw history must either never read a weight, or take `sessionUnits` and convert them itself. The population comes from the source — every raw-history expression in now-model, walked back to its enclosing call, resolved to its defining module through the import statements, and checked against that FUNCTION'S body rather than its module's. Per-function matters and is not pedantry: `session.ts` reads `.weight` ten times and `weekStreak` reads none, so a module-level check fails a correct function and teaches the next reader to distrust the gate. Its value is that a consumer added tomorrow is covered by nobody remembering anything, which is precisely what failed four times. MY OWN SCAN WAS BLIND TWICE, and both are the round's real content. First it matched `f(rawHistory` by regex and missed `findPRs` — the most important consumer in the file — because raw history reaches it as the SECOND argument; a gate silently covering less than it claims is the exact failure the gate is about. Then the fix for that, walking back over balanced parens, ran clean out of the statement and reported `sessionStats` for five bare assignments like `const all = this.repo.allSets();`. I INVESTIGATED A CONSUMER THE SCAN HAD INVENTED before catching it, and I nearly shipped the comment crediting the discovery to the gate. Stopping the walk at `;` `{` `}` fixes it, and the false finding was still worth something: `sessionStats` genuinely does read weights out of raw sets and is genuinely correct, because it is fed ONE session's and takes that session. That is the rule sharpened — the hazard was never "raw", it is comparing across SESSIONS, since the session owns the unit — and it is pinned by its own test so the exemption cannot outlive its reason. Proved the gate bites by planting the two cases it exists for: restore R537's original defect and it names `coachSuggestion`; add a brand-new unregistered consumer and it names `topSetPerExercise`. SHIP: `npm test` 2007 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; app healthy on the seeded history. | next: the gate covers `now-model` only, and `recap-model` and `progress-model` consume history the same way — extending it is mechanical now that the walker and `fnSource` exist. The other claim from R541's list is still open: `types.ts` "every set is stored in the unit it was logged in and that never changes" — I checked `src/data` and `portable.ts` by hand this round and it holds, but nothing enforces it, and it is the assumption all five of these rounds rest on. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R543 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Extended R542's unit gate to `recap-model` and `progress-model`, which consume history exactly the same way and were unwatched — a gate covering only the file where the defect already happened is a gate against the past. First pass over the new files produced THREE FLAGS AND ALL THREE WERE FALSE, which is the round's actual work, because a gate that cries wolf gets switched off — §8's rule, applied to tests. Two causes, both real limits rather than bad luck. The scan matched locals by NAME across a whole file, and `now-model` has two methods each opening `const all = ...`, one raw and one converted, so `prefillFor` — which is handed the converted form — was reported as a raw consumer. Scoping each binding to its own method body fixes it. Then the body finder walked straight PAST every annotated function, because `function progressRows(...): ProgressRow[] {` has a head ending in `]` rather than `)`, so it handed back the whole module as the scope: the same "covers less than it claims" failure the gate exists to catch, this time in the gate. Both false alarms were worth having, because they sharpened the rule — the hazard was never "raw", it is comparing across SESSIONS, since the session owns the unit, and `sessionStats` reads weights out of raw sets and is correct for exactly that reason. AND THEN THE GATE SILENTLY SCANNED NOTHING. Composing the patterns through a rewrite turned the word-boundary escape into a real BACKSPACE byte, so `RAW[0]` read as a control character followed by `repo\.allSets\(\)` and could never match — trap 7's third mechanism, hit in the file that carries the warning about it, and the second time in this round I built a blind instrument. Everything the scan reported after that came from one surviving code path. What caught it was R542's own "the scan finds the call sites it is supposed to" test, which asserts the scan sees `findPRs`, `weekStreak` and `pickerFor` by name — written precisely because a silent gate passes forever, and the only reason this was a detour instead of a shipped no-op. Fixed by removing a layer: the patterns are now built with String.raw and `new RegExp`, and the block was written by line index rather than by anchored replace. Re-proved it bites in the NEWLY covered file, not just the old one: an unsafe consumer planted in `progress-model` is named. SHIP: `npm test` 2007 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; Progress screen healthy on the seeded history. | next: `types.ts` "every set is stored in the unit it was logged in and that never changes" is still the open claim and still unenforced — I have now hand-checked it twice, which is exactly the pattern that precedes finding it false. The suite also has a `no-control-bytes` gate that did not catch today's backspace, and finding out why is worth a round: either it does not cover `test/`, or it looks for the wrong thing, and both are the same class of defect as everything R539 onward has been about. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R544 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Started with R543's own lead — the suite has a `no-control-bytes` gate and it did not catch yesterday's backspace — and the answer is that THE GATE IS FINE AND I WAS THE GAP. Planted a backspace in a source file and it names the file and the byte, first try. It never fired in R543 because I iterate on one test file and only run the full suite at SHIP, so the byte existed for exactly the window nothing was watching. Worth writing down plainly rather than turning into a code change: the fix is running the suite before believing a green single file, not another gate. So the round went to the item that was actually open. `types.ts` states the invariant EVERYTHING from R537 to R543 rests on — "every set is stored in the unit it was logged in and that never changes; a 225 lb bench stays 225 lb in the database for ever" — and nothing enforced it. I had hand-checked it twice across those rounds, which is the exact pattern that precedes finding a claim false, and it is also the wrong instrument: the way this breaks is a FUTURE write path, and no amount of reading today's code tests that. Four tests, in two directions, because either alone is easy to satisfy wrongly. Behavioural: switching the display unit to kg through the real path (`setPref` then `adoptChosenUnit`) leaves every stored weight byte-identical, and an export taken on a pound device and restored onto a kilo one comes back with the same numbers AND the same per-session units. Structural: nothing under `src/data` calls `convertWeight` at all, comments stripped first so quoting the rule is still allowed — that is the half that catches the next write path rather than the current ones, because the moment storage converts, the number in the table stops being the fact. PROVED EACH ONE FAILS ON THE WAY IT WOULD REALLY BREAK. A `logSet` that normalises kg to lb on write fails three of the four, including the structural one, which is what a plausible "let's just store everything in pounds" refactor looks like. A `restore` that drops the session's unit and calls everything lb fails only the round-trip test — confirming that test is load-bearing on its own rather than passing on the first one's coat-tails. SHIP: `npm test` 2011 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; app healthy. | next: the unit seam is now closed on both sides — the storage invariant beneath it (R544) and the consumer rule above it (R542, R543) — after five rounds of finding one instance at a time. Worth stopping to say the pattern that produced all of them: a comment asserting what CANNOT happen, checked against the app rather than against its own file. The remaining unaudited HANDOFF traps are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 14 and 15, and that same question is the one to ask of each. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. R545 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Took the question that produced R539 through R544 — does this claim hold against the APP, not just against its own file — and pointed it at an unaudited HANDOFF trap instead of at code. Trap 14 says a `<Text>` child gives a control no accessible name. IT IS TRUE, and re-measuring it turned up a detail the entry did not have. Planted four probes into the running app: `<button>PLAINTEXT</button>` came back `button "PLAINTEXT"`, while a real `<button>` wrapping its text in a `<div>`, the same with a `<span>`, and a `<div role="button">` all came back with the button ANONYMOUS and only the inner node named. So the effect is not react-native-web's and not specific to a div-role-button, which is how the entry reads: any real `<button>` loses name-from-content the moment its text sits inside a child element. That distinction matters because the current wording invites the next reader to conclude their case is different. CHECKED THE OTHER DIRECTION, which is the half that proves the app is not accidentally fine: every named control on the Now screen — LOG SET, PUSH, PULL, LEGS — has an explicit `aria-label` AND a `DIV` child, so each would be silent to VoiceOver without the label, and removing one fails `accessibility.test.ts` by name. The trap is real, and a gate is the only reason it is invisible. THEN R534's GATE CAUGHT MY OWN EDIT, which is the round's second half. It requires a measurement note to follow a finished sentence, and I put a blank line before mine — a paragraph break, which finishes nothing. That is the gate being slightly wrong rather than the edit being wrong, and relaxing a gate to let your own change through is exactly the move to distrust, so the fix had to preserve every failure it could previously catch: skip blank lines and test the last NON-BLANK one, which is still the text the note lands after. Re-proved it by planting R533's original shape — a note inserted mid-clause after "react-native-web renders" — and it fails by name with the sentence quoted. SHIP: `npm test` 2011 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; probe removed from the running app and the screen verified clean. | next: traps 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 15 remain unaudited. 15 is the one worth doing next and the most likely to have rotted, because it is a claim about a DEPENDENCY VERSION — "react-native-web 0.21 dropped `accessibilityState` from its forwarded props" — and the probe for it is the same shape as today's: plant a control with the prop and read what reaches the DOM. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R546 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Trap 15, picked because it is the one kind of claim that rots with nobody touching the repo: a statement about a DEPENDENCY VERSION. BOTH HALVES HOLD. react-native-web is still 0.21.0, and a probe putting `accessibilityState={{ selected: true, disabled: false, busy: true }}` on LOG SET rendered a node carrying `aria-label`, `role`, `tabindex`, `type`, `class`, `style` — and not one of `aria-selected`, `aria-disabled`, `aria-busy`. The prop is dropped whole. Learned something on the way that cost me a probe: `data-*` attributes are dropped the same way, so my first attempt tagged the control with `data-probe546` and found nothing, which reads exactly like "the prop was dropped" and is actually "every unknown prop is dropped" — a probe that cannot distinguish its two outcomes measures neither. The second half reproduced MORE strongly than written: selecting a rail lift left `className` carrying the new background class within 1ms while `getComputedStyle` still read the old `rgb(16, 19, 22)` at 1, 30, 80, 150 and 300ms, long past the 90ms transition. AND I STOPPED SHORT OF THE EXPLANATION, deliberately. Every reading was taken with `document.visibilityState === "hidden"` — it stayed hidden even after fronting the tab — and a hidden page defers style recalculation, which is the same condition that stops `rAF` firing and killed two of my measurement scripts by timeout this round. That is a plausible mechanism and it is NOT established, so the entry records the advice as verified and the mechanism as untested, with a line saying not to repeat it as though it were. Recording a good guess in the voice of a measurement is how trap 11 became false. Pinned both: the evidence strings, the caveat sentence, and a check that the react-native-web version HANDOFF names is the version installed — planted 0.19 against the real 0.21.0 and it fails telling the next session to re-probe rather than inherit. SHIP: `npm test` 2012 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; both source probes reverted and the running app confirmed clean (`aria-busy=null`). | next: traps 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 remain, and they are a different species — all five are about npm and the toolchain rather than about the product, so probing them means touching dependency state, which is the one thing worth being careful with while the app is running. Reading them for internal consistency first is the cheap half. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R547 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Cleared the last five unaudited traps, and one of them is FALSE. Traps 1, 2, 3 and 6 check cheaply and all hold: `C:\Users\srobs` really does carry a rival `package.json`, an `app.json` with Expo plugins and a 400-package `node_modules` at DIFFERENT versions (expo-router 6.0.23 against the app's 6.0.24), which is exactly Expo-shaped enough to fool a drifted command; the `bundledNativeModules` lookup trap 2 prescribes returns `~16.0.10` for expo-sqlite; `npm run check-deps` exists and reports 20 Expo-managed packages matching SDK ~54. TRAP 5 DOES NOT REPRODUCE. It says a transparent `Modal` on react-native-web stays on screen when you toggle `visible`, and on 0.21.0 it does not: forcing `visible={false}` onto the `<Modal>` inside `ScreenModal` and driving the CLEAR confirm sheet produced nothing — no sheet, no CANCEL — and the same clicks after reverting the one-line probe produced "Clear this workout? ... CANCEL / CLEAR". Ran it in both directions on purpose, because "no sheet appeared" is worth nothing until the same steps are shown to produce one; a probe that fails to open the sheet at all looks identical to a modal that hides correctly. That is the second trap found false after trap 11's screenshots, and both were believed for the same reason — nobody re-ran them because they read like settled facts. THE ADVICE STILL STANDS, for a better reason than the one it gave: `ScreenModal` returns null when unfocused, and that conditional render is what makes the exit animation possible at all, since a modal held mounted behind `visible` has no unmount to animate out of. The entry now carries the measurement, the correction and the real reason, and both halves are pinned separately — planted against each and each fails alone, because losing the first restores a false claim and losing the second invites somebody to delete a conditional render the animation depends on. The document is no longer the weakest thing in the repo, which means the next round should go back to the product. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. R548 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Back to the product, following R541's thread past the branch it fixed. That round stopped a DELOAD suggesting a weight below the empty bar; every other branch was still free to name a weight nobody can load. Measured across both units and all three goals: a lifter plateaued at 60 kg on the size goal was told "Stuck at 60 for 3 — TRY 61.25". A 1.25 kg total increase is 0.625 kg a side and no such plate exists in any gym. In pounds it said 137.5, which is off the app's OWN 5 lb stepper — the lifter cannot even dial the advice in without typing it. Cause: the engine rounded to `MIN_INCREMENT`, which is the resolution of the DATA (1 lb, 0.5 kg), not of a barbell. Fix is `WEIGHT_STEP`, passed in the way R541 passed the floor, and it is the right grid for a reason worth writing down: it is simultaneously what the +/- buttons move by and the smallest standard plate pair (2x2.5 lb, 2x1.25 kg), so a suggestion on it is both reachable in the app and loadable on the bar. MY FIRST VERSION BROKE ITS OWN CONTRACT and a test I had just written caught it. I defaulted `grid` to `MIN_INCREMENT`, which reads like "unchanged" and is not — the plateau branch never rounded at all, so a caller passing nothing went from 61.25 to 61.5. Defaulting to zero, meaning no snapping, is the actual no-op. That is the second round running where the test pinning a default earned its place. THEN THE FIX HAD A CONSEQUENCE I HAD TO FOLLOW THROUGH rather than leave. The goals differed by 2.5 lb of step, and a 2.5 lb difference cannot survive rounding to 5 — so Settings' "strength adds weight in bigger steps, size in smaller ones" became false in both units the app ships. Rewrote it, en and es, to describe the difference that is real and survives any grid: strength releases the weight at 5 reps, size waits for 8. R519's test asserted the old difference and failed; the easy move was to weaken it, and instead it now asserts EQUALITY on a plateau (with the reason) plus a new case at six reps where the goals visibly diverge — strength says "try 210", size says "stay here and add a rep". Whether strength should also climb faster is a training judgement, not a bug fix, so it is filed in OWNER.md as a one-line change I did not make. SHIP: `npm test` 2018 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; verified in the running app on a kg seed with the bundle grepped both ways — planted reads "try 61.25", fixed reads "try 62.5"; reseeded. | next: the coach has had three defects in four rounds (R541 floor, R548 grid, and R537's units before them) and they share a shape — it does arithmetic on weights while knowing nothing about the equipment they sit on. Worth one round asking what else it assumes: the climbing branch reads the lifter's OWN increment, which is the one place that is self-correcting, but `MAX_CLIMB_FRACTION` and the 0.9 deload are both bare fractions applied to a number that has to land on plates. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R549 — Stage 0: tab bar still the owner's. Closed the hole R548 left ON PURPOSE, which turned out to be the interesting one. R548 put every suggested weight on the loadable grid and exempted CLIMBING, on R518's rule that a lifter's own working increment outranks the goal table. The rule is right; the exemption was not, because THEIR OWN INCREMENT IS ONLY THEIRS WHEN THEY LOADED IT. With one session logged in kilos, 86 kg reads as 189.5 lb and the step reads as 4.5, so the app said "189.5 and climbing, 4 sessions — TRY 194". Nobody ever put 4.5 lb on a bar; the unit conversion did, and the number came from their history in form only. Snapping the suggestion gives 195. The reported weight stays EXACT at 189.5 — that is what they lifted, and §16 wants it told honestly — so the split is: report the real number, suggest a reachable one. FOUND A SECOND DEFECT WHILE FIXING THE FIRST. `roundTo` goes to the nearest multiple, which can round a suggestion BELOW the weight being climbed from: 191 plus a 1 lb step is 192, and 192 on a 5 lb grid is 190, so the line reads "climbing, try 190" to somebody who just lifted 191 — the advice inverted, not rounded. Reachable exactly when the current weight is off-grid, which a converted history is by construction. Added a `raise` helper so every branch that says "go up" goes through it. AND MY GUARD TEST WAS BLIND. It looped over plateau fixtures and passed against the planted defect, because the size step of 2.5 on a 5 grid is always far enough above to round up — the down-round case never arose, so the test could not reach the thing it was named after. It takes a CLIMBING history with a small own-step to get there. Rewrote it that way and re-planted: now it fails. Both halves planted separately and both bite — remove the snap and the climb test fails, remove the guard and the increase test fails. Verified in the running app with the bundle grepped both ways: planted reads "try 194", fixed reads "try 195", same seed, same screen. SHIP: `npm test` 2021 pass / 0 fail; `--check` current; `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready; reseeded. | next: that is the coach's fourth defect in five rounds and they all had one shape — it does arithmetic on weights while knowing nothing about the equipment underneath. It now takes `base` and `grid` from the caller, which is the right direction, and the remaining bare constant is `MAX_CLIMB_FRACTION`. That one is a TEST rather than a suggestion, so it never has to land on plates — worth stating in the file so the next round does not "fix" it. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's. Filed and still owner-only: the R508 bundle scope (~48 kB), the two R483 items, and R548's strength-vs-size question.

R550 — PICK (logged before building, per AGENT_LOOP): the weight STEPPER after a
unit switch. Shortlist was (a) note in coach.ts that `MAX_CLIMB_FRACTION` is a
test rather than a suggestion so nobody "fixes" it onto the grid, (b) the +/-
stepper, (c) sweep other screens for unloadable numbers. Picked (b): R548 and
R549 put every SUGGESTED weight on plates, and the field the lifter actually
types into was never looked at. R549's own seed shows the problem — the weight
field opens at 189.5 (86 kg converted, honestly reported), and if + adds a flat
5 the lifter walks 194.5, 199.5, 204.5 and can never reach a loadable weight
again without typing one. Contract to check: pressing + or - from an off-grid
weight should land ON the grid, and the app's own suggestion (195) should be
reachable by pressing +.

R550 — BUILD/REVIEW/SHIP on the pick logged above. The hypothesis was WRONG and
measuring it first is what turned the round into a real fix. I expected the
stepper to walk 194.5, 199.5 off-grid forever; it does not — `bumpWeight` has
always snapped to `WEIGHT_STEP`, so from 189.5 the small + lands on 195, which
is exactly the weight the coach suggests. One press, and the lifter is back on
plates. THE DEFECT WAS THE BUTTON NEXT TO IT. `bumpPlate` did not snap, so from
189.5 the big `+45` gave 234.5 and `-45` gave 144.5, and every further press
kept the half — the two controls sit on the same row and disagreed about what a
weight can be, with the large obvious one being the broken half. A lifter who
logged a single session in kilos could never reach a loadable weight through
the plate buttons; their only escape was typing a number, which is §4's "the app
never asks a question it could answer" pointed straight at the thing it just
made unanswerable. Fix routes it through the same rounding, with the grid being
the FINER of the stepper increment and the lifter's own plate jump — a custom
2.5 lb jump means they own micro-plates and are telling the app what they can
load, and snapping that onto the 5 lb default would erase the setting. Their
evidence outranks the default, the same rule R518 and R549 each reached from a
different direction. REVIEW: suite 2027 pass / 0 fail (real count, up 6). Both
halves planted separately and both fail BY NAME — restoring the old `bumpPlate`
fails three tests reporting "+45 from 189.5 gave 234.5" and "-45 ... gave
144.5"; snapping to `WEIGHT_STEP` alone fails "a lifter with micro-plates keeps
them". Verified in the PRODUCT by clicking the real buttons, with the bundle
grepped both ways: planted reads 234.5 and 144.5, fixed reads 235 and 145, and
the ordinary seeded history is untouched (175 +45 -> 220 -> 175). SHIP: `--check`
current, `link/build.cjs` dist/ ready, app reseeded to seed.b64. | next: the
coach and the logging controls now agree that a weight has to exist. The one
place left with a bare fraction is `MAX_CLIMB_FRACTION`, and it is a TEST rather
than a suggestion so it never has to land on plates — worth one line in coach.ts
saying so, because five rounds of grid work is exactly the context in which
somebody "fixes" it. Tab bar remains the top item and the owner's; R548's
strength-vs-size question is filed beside it. Also owner-only: the R508 bundle
scope (~48 kB) and the two R483 items.

R551 — PICK (logged first): finish the grid work by protecting what must NOT be
snapped. Shortlist was (a) the `MAX_CLIMB_FRACTION` note, (b) sweep the OTHER
screens (Progress, Goals, recap) for weights the app invents rather than
reports, (c) the typed-weight path, which is now the only way to reach an
off-grid number. Picked (a)+(b) as one round, because they are the same
question asked twice: after five rounds of "put it on the grid", the live risk
is somebody rounding a weight the lifter actually LIFTED. §16 wants the real
number reported and a reachable one suggested, and nothing states which side of
that line each number is on.

R551 — BUILD/REVIEW/SHIP on the pick logged above, and this round FOUND NOTHING
WRONG, which is the finding. Swept every surface with a converted history: Now
header "189.5 and climbing", the weight field 189.5, Progress `best` 189.5 and
`trend` 14.5, the recap card 86 in kg — the unit it was typed in. All exact, all
correct. What is missing is not a fix, it is the RULE, because five rounds of
putting weights on the grid have made "round it" the obvious move in this repo
and the next person to make it will be right four times and wrong once. §16
draws the line and nothing enforced it: a SUGGESTED weight must exist on a rack
because the lifter is asked to load it, a REPORTED weight must match what
happened because the lifter is asked to recognise it. 86 kg is 189.5 lb, so
"190 and climbing" is a sentence they cannot check against anything they did.
Five tests, one per surface, plus a note on `MAX_CLIMB_FRACTION` — the last bare
fraction in coach.ts and therefore the obvious next target — recording that it
is a TEST rather than a suggestion, applied to weights already lifted, and never
reaches a screen. REVIEW: suite 2032 pass / 0 fail (real count, up 5). Four
plants, each the tidy-up a reasonable person would make, and each fails by its
own name: rounding Progress's `best` fails the Progress test, snapping the
coach's `recentWeight` fails the header test, rounding the prefill fails the
field test, deleting the note fails the note test. Verified in the PRODUCT on
the off-grid seed — Now reads "189.5 and climbing, 4 sessions — try 195" with
the field at 189.5, and Progress reads "189.5 × 5" and "+14.5 lb" — both sides
of the line visible on two screens at once. SHIP: `--check` current,
`link/build.cjs` dist/ ready, plants reverted, app reseeded to seed.b64. | next:
the weight story is now closed end to end — stored exactly (R544), consumed in
the right form (R542/R543), suggested on plates (R548/R549/R550), reported
honestly (R551). Worth moving somewhere else entirely next round rather than
mining the same seam a seventh time; the recap/share surface has had one real

and the owner's; R548's strength-vs-size question is filed beside it. Also
